title: Nepal: Rasuwa Flood Situation Report No. 13 (As of 20 November 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • On 6 November, the National Planning Commission published the preliminary findings of the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA), estimating total damage and losses from the Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi floods at NPR 472.66 billion (USD 3.18 billion) and recovery and reconstruction needs at NPR 706.65 billion (USD 4.76 billion).
  • According to the preliminary PDNA, the disaster resulted in 1,464 deaths, 5,285 people missing, and 13,795 people rescued, underscoring the scale of its human impact across affected districts.
  • CARE Nepal, Plan International, and UN Women released a joint Rapid Gender Analysis (RGA) of the flood response. The assessment found that women, children, persons with disabilities, and other marginalized groups face disproportionate recovery challenges, including livelihood loss, increased care burdens, psychosocial distress, and barriers to accessing services and decision-making, underscoring the need for gender-responsive and inclusive recovery support.

title: Syria: Protection and Reintegration Insights, Voices of returnees and host communities across Syria, July - September 2026
content:
Executive Summary

Syria continues to experience significant population returns, with more than 1.8 million refugees and 2 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) having returned since December 2024. However, the pace of refugee returns has moderated throughout 2026, declining from over 268,000 in Q1 to approximately 131,000 in Q2 and 117,000 in Q3. Findings from the third quarter highlight persistent challenges affecting recovery and sustainable reintegration, particularly economic hardship, inadequate housing, gaps in civil documentation, limited access to essential services and localized protection risks.

This report draws on 9,842 household interviews conducted across all 14 governorates and 187 subdistricts, complemented by community consultations. Respondents comprised refugee returnees (45%), IDP returnees (29%) and host community members (26%). Building on three rounds of monitoring in 2026, the report identifies both improvements in selected indicators and persistent vulnerabilities, with variations across population groups and geographical areas.

Most surveyed returnees intend to remain in their current locations, although conditions for sustainable reintegration remain fragile. Among surveyed refugee and IDP returnees, 79% and 75%, respectively, reported intending to remain over the following six months. Improved security, family reunification and access to housing, land and property (HLP) were among the main reported factors influencing return decisions. However, damaged housing, limited infrastructure and services, livelihood constraints and security concerns remain important barriers to return. Phased returns, particularly among refugees returning from neighbouring countries, may also be linked to housing and livelihood constraints, although the monitoring does not establish the reasons for these arrangements.

Socioeconomic vulnerability remains a central concern, with important implications for protection and reintegration. Unemployment affected 31% of working-age respondents, rising to 36% among refugee returnees, with pronounced gender disparities. Food and nutrition remained the most frequently reported unmet need across population groups (65–73%), followed by economic opportunities. Financial pressures were also reflected in continued reliance on negative coping mechanisms, including depletion of savings (42%), deprioritization of essential needs (38%) and borrowing (26%). These findings point to persistent household vulnerability and associated protection risks.

Housing insecurity and unresolved HLP issues continue to affect households' living conditions and reintegration prospects. Refugee returnees reported higher unmet shelter needs (49%) than IDP returnees (35%) and host communities (19%). While most respondents expected to remain in their current accommodation, rental insecurity and affordability remained important concerns.

Gaps in civil documentation continue to restrict access to rights and essential services. Although modest improvements were recorded among returnees, 18% of refugee returnee households and 10% of IDP returnee households reported at least one member lacking essential documentation, compared with 6% among host communities. These findings reinforce the importance of accessible legal assistance and strengthened national civil registration systems.

Perceptions of safety and psychosocial well-being show some improvements, although localized protection concerns persist. In Q3, 87% of refugee returnees and 68% of host community respondents reported feeling safe, compared with 83% and 61% in Q2, respectively, while perceptions of safety among IDP returnees declined. Localized insecurity, movement restrictions and explosive ordnance contamination continued to pose protection risks. Reported stress-related symptoms also declined from 47% in Q1 to 38% in Q3, although economic hardship, insecurity and barriers to accessing mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services remained important concerns.

Women and children continue to face distinct protection risks. Community consultations identified concerns related to gender-based violence, harassment, restrictions on women's and girls' freedom of movement and unequal access to resources. Child protection concerns included child labour, child marriage, violence, exploitation and exposure to explosive ordnance. Although reported school non-attendance declined among refugee returnee and host community households, economic pressures, child labour and documentation gaps continued to present barriers to education.

Social cohesion challenges remain localized but require continued attention, particularly in communities experiencing substantial returns and economic pressures. Community consultations identified tensions related to competition over resources, identity-based narratives and perceptions of unequal access to opportunities. Findings also point to the continued use of community-based dispute-resolution mechanisms, highlighting opportunities to strengthen inclusive dialogue and locally appropriate approaches to addressing disputes.

Access to humanitarian assistance has declined despite persistent needs. Only 29% of surveyed households reported receiving assistance in Q3, compared with 33% in Q2 and 45% in Q1. Among households reporting difficulties accessing assistance, service unavailability (64%), limited information (24%) and the absence of service providers (24%) were the most frequently cited barriers. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining assistance responsive to assessed vulnerabilities, particularly in underserved and high-return areas.

Overall, three rounds of protection monitoring in 2026 suggest that improvements in some safety, psychosocial, and education indicators have not yet translated into a corresponding reduction in the structural barriers affecting sustainable reintegration. Economic insecurity, housing and documentation challenges, uneven service availability and localized protection risks remain interconnected, with different implications for refugee returnees, IDP returnees and host communities.

Advancing durable solutions, including sustainable reintegration for those who have voluntarily returned, requires integrated, area-based and protection-sensitive approaches that connect humanitarian assistance with recovery and longer-term development efforts. Priorities include expanding access to livelihoods and essential services, supporting adequate housing and HLP rights, strengthening civil documentation and access to legal assistance, sustaining community-based psychosocial support, mitigating gender-based violence and child protection risks, and reinforcing explosive ordnance risk education and mine action.

Continued support to national and local institutions and coordinated service delivery are essential, with UNHCR contributing through protection monitoring, legal assistance, technical engagement, community consultations and coordination with government counterparts and relevant recovery and development actors. These efforts will be critical to creating the conditions necessary for safe, dignified and sustainable reintegration.

title: WFP Somalia Country Brief, November 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Flood risk remains elevated across Somalia, with further humanitarian impacts expected through year-end. Deyr rainfall triggered flash floods, particularly in Galkacyo, Abudwaq and Baidoa, affecting more than 175,000 people and displacing over 51,000 in October. While Shabelle and Juba River levels have receded, above-average rainfall forecasts and potential El Niño conditions sustain risks through December. An estimated 874,000 people are projected to be displaced between October and December, largely due to flooding.

• In Luuq, some of the 58,500 people displaced by recent conflict are returning following the 29 October peace agreement, however, food insecurity, acute malnutrition and Juba River flood risks persist. Existing WFP programmes continue to be implemented with plans to provide additional cash assistance from December. In Baidoa, renewed violence has affected around 5,600 people amid severe food insecurity and critical acute malnutrition.

• According to WFP’s October market analysis, the cost of living remains high, with the national food and non-food basket reaching USD 210 in October, up 4.2 percent yearon-year. Market pressures persisted in Southwest State due to conflict-related disruptions and reduced Gu crop production, while diesel prices remained 26 percent above October 2025 levels, increasing food, water, transport and humanitarian operating costs.

title: Sudan Conflict and Complex Emergency - Public Health Situation Analysis (PHSA)
content:
Sudan’s war has shattered the country and shows little sign of abating, with the crisis driven by prolonged conflict, widespread displacement, food insecurity, disease outbreaks, and the collapse of essential services. Despite some progress in the first half of the year, including reduced overall displacement and modest gains in food security indicators, Sudan’s humanitarian situation remains extremely severe.

An estimated 19.5 million people, approximately 41% of the population, are currently experiencing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse levels of acute food insecurity. Without immediate action to reverse the current trajectory, the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825 000. Anticipated El Niño-related climate shocks could worsen food insecurity and malnutrition and increase risks of cholera and other waterborne diseases, as well as malaria, Rift Valley fever and yellow fever.

Between 11 January and 15 October 2026, an estimated 119 782 individuals (23 598 households) were displaced from locations across Blue Nile state, placing further strain on health, protection and other essential services. Nearly 12 000 displaced people are sheltering in severely overcrowded schools with limited or no access to sanitation, electricity and other basic services.

The outlook is increasingly alarming as El Niño is driving severe drought conditions across more than half of Sudan, resulting in crop failures, water deficits, reduced agricultural recovery, declining incomes, and rising cereal prices.

Before the current conflict, Sudan had already been grappling with violence and displacement since the onset of the Darfur crisis in 2003. Sudan was home to more than 1 million refugees. Sudan has also been heavily impacted by severe weather events linked to climate change, including floods and droughts. These events have adversely affected hundreds of thousands of individuals throughout the country, leading to crop and livestock destruction and exacerbating food insecurity for families.

title: WFP Mali Country Brief, November 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Mali continues to face food security and nutrition challenges, particularly in the central and northern regions. According to the Food Security Cluster, more than half of the population classified in IPC Phase 3 and above remains unreached. Humanitarian needs persist, driven by conflict, displacement, climate-related shocks and constrained livelihood opportunities affecting vulnerable communities, refugees and internally displaced people (IDPs).

• Climatic conditions continue to influence food security and livelihood outcomes. Irregular rainfall and localized deficits during the 2026 rainy season, partly associated with El Niño conditions, may affect agricultural and pastoral production in some areas of the country. Given the importance of agriculture and livestock to rural livelihoods, reduced production could affect household incomes and food availability, while rising fuel prices continue to put additional pressure on purchasing power.

• Despite recent access gains in some areas, insecurity remains an important factor shaping humanitarian access and response planning.

• Recent improvements in humanitarian access have created opportunities to better understand needs in previously hard-to-reach areas. A multi-sectoral assessment in Diafarabé (Mopti Region) identified food security, nutrition, livelihood and basic service needs.

title: UNHCR: Socio-Economic Update on Refugees in Jordan 2026
content: The Socio-Economic Update on Refugees provides an overview of the socio-economic conditions of refugees in Jordan, with findings intended to inform evidence-based programming, policy development, and assistance planning. The latest data in this report is based on data collected in August 2026. About this Report Starting in 2026, the assessment will transition to an annual reporting frequency and adopt a repeated cross-sectional approach, moving away from the previous panel design in which the same households were followed over time. This change will support regular monitoring of refugees’ socio-economic conditions at the population level, while allowing for more flexible sampling and analysis in each assessment round. To strengthen the comparability of findings over time, data from previous assessment rounds have been re-weighted using the updated weighting approach. This will help produce more consistent estimates and facilitate the comparison of socioeconomic trends across reporting periods. However, re-weighting may result in slight changes to figures previously published. Historical estimates presented in this report should therefore be interpreted in light of these methodological adjustments.

title: Sudan Situation, Refugees and Asylum-seekers Movement and Presence (as of 31 October 2026)
content:
The refugees and asylum-seekers arrival data is based on the joint border monitoring of RRC, UNHCR and IOM collected at official border points. The data does not include refugees/asylum-seekers who crossed through unofficial border points or at night, when the monitors are not present. This data set excludes South Sudanese returnees and third-country nationals.

The refugees and asylum-seekers data is comprised of people officially registered at refugee camps/settlements in UNHCR's proGres database. Data on arrivals at border points and presence in camps/settlements may vary due to people crossing at unofficial border points or finding their own way to these sites for registration.

title: WFP Kenya Country Brief, November 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• October was marked by overlapping humanitarian pressures, with worsening drought conditions in several arid and semi-arid counties, continued concerns over acute malnutrition, and a new influx of people fleeing conflict in Ethiopia into Moyale. While above-average rainfall forecast for the October– December short-rains season offer prospects for improved water availability, pasture and crop production, it also heightens the risk of flooding and landslides, particularly in flood-prone areas of Garissa and Tana River counties, including Dadaab refugee camp. Meanwhile, approximately 30,000 new arrivals from Ethiopia were profiled in Moyale, with urgent needs for food, water, healthcare, shelter and protection. These overlapping pressures underscored the need for simultaneous drought preparedness, anticipatory action against flooding, and emergency assistance for newly displaced populations.

OPERATIONAL UPDATES Refugee assistance

• In September, WFP provided food and cash assistance to 623,000 refugees and asylum seekers in Dadaab, Kakuma and Kalobeyei, covering their September and October entitlements. However, funding shortages have forced WFP to reduce food rations for the most vulnerable households and those with limited capacity to meet basic needs from 80 and 60 percent of the minimum food basket, to 60 and 40 percent, respectively. Rations for partially selfreliant households remain at 20 percent.

title: Yemen Emergency - UNHCR External Update #8 - 23 November 2026
content:
Highlights

▪ Displacement in Yemen continues to rise, with more than 360,000 people newly displaced since 1 August, up from around 321,000 in the previous update. Taiz remains the most affected governorate, accounting for 64% of new displacement.

▪ Cross-border movements continue across the Gulf of Aden, with arrivals reaching 4,9191 individuals, including 4,439 arrivals in Djibouti and 480 arrivals in Somalia. During the reporting period, 115 new arrivals from Yemen were recorded in Somalia.

▪ Insecurity is driving further refugee movements within Yemen, with 4,638 refugees relocating from Kharaz camp to Aden since 7 November. An assisted spontaneous return flight to Somalia for more than 100 refugees has been postponed to 28 December.

title: Occupied Palestinian Territory Emergency Response Activity Update #61, 1 - 31 October 2026 [EN/AR]
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

October marked both one year since the October 2025 ceasefire and three years since the escalation of hostilities. The humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire and extremely fragile, with humanitarian partners warning that funding shortfalls, combined with ongoing Israeli restrictions, have begun to reverse the gains achieved since the ceasefire was announced. One year on, Israeli military operations have continued and approximately 70 per cent of Gaza remains behind the constantly shifting “Yellow Line”. Most of the population remains displaced in worn-out tents, overcrowded sites and severely damaged buildings, with water and sanitation systems devastated. With the rainy season imminent, conditions are likely to worsen.

Needs ahead of winter are acute. The Shelter Cluster estimates that 1.98 million people require shelter and non-food item assistance, yet the supplies available can reach fewer than one in five of those needing shelter for winter. Winter shelter requirements remained severely underfunded, with two-thirds of the USD 283 million required still unmet. Structural safety is a growing concern, with OCHA preliminary estimates – supported by IOMled assessments – indicating that more than 4,000 buildings require full or partial demolition and some 44,000 people living in over 2,300 structurally unsafe buildings.

Briefing the Security Council on 15 October, the UN Acting Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, Ramiz Alakbarov, reported that, for the fourth consecutive winter, Israeli restrictions on the entry of essential equipment, spare parts, engine oil and other supplies continued to impede humanitarian and recovery efforts, and that partners knew what winter preparedness required but lacked the materials to act at the scale required. Without expanded access, the lifting of Israeli restrictions on critical materials, and adequate funding, humanitarian actors will remain unable to move from emergency relief to the recovery that Gaza urgently needs.

title: Yemen — Rapid Displacement Tracking Update (15 – 21 November 2026)
content:
IOM Yemen DTM’s Rapid Displacement Tracking (RDT) tool collects data on estimated numbers of households forced to flee on a daily basis from their locations of origin or displacement, allowing for regular reporting of new displacements in terms of estimated numbers, geography, and needs. It also tracks returnees who returned to their location of origin.

From 1 January to 21 November 2026, IOM Yemen DTM tracked 65,427 households (HH) (392,562 Individuals) who experienced displacement at least once.

Between 15 and 21 November 2026, IOM Yemen DTM tracked 2622 households (15732 individuals) displaced at least once. The majority of people moved into/within the following governorates and districts:

  • Lahj (1589 HHs) – Tuban (1057 HHs), Tur Al Bahah (302 HHs), Al Madaribah Wa Al Aarah (90 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate were internal.
  • Ta’iz (401 HHs) – Sabir Al Mawadim (71 HHs), Jabal Habashi (70 HHs), Ash Shamayatayn (67 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate were internal.
  • Aden (382 HHs) – Al Burayqah (295 HHs), Dar Sad (84 HHs), Kritar - Sirah (3 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate originated from Lahj.

The majority of people moved from the following governorates and districts:

  • Lahj (1732 HHs) – Al Madaribah Wa Al Aarah (1139 HHs), Tur Al Bahah (459 HHs), Al Maqatirah (122 HHs) districts.
  • Ta’iz (750 HHs) – Al Misrakh (130 HHs), Jabal Habashi (122 HHs), Al Makha (93 HHs) districts.
  • Al Hodeidah (81 HHs) – Al Khukhah (45 HHs), Hays (28 HHs), Al Hawak (2 HHs) districts.

IOM identified 442 additional households displaced in the previous reporting period, which covered 08 - 14 November 2026, in the governorates of Aden (178 HHs), Abyan (98 HHs), Ma’rib (76 HHs), Ad Dali (41 HHs), Al Maharah (35 HHs), and Hadramawt (14 HHs). These figures have been added to the cumulative displacement total recorded since the beginning of the year.

title: Europe — Mixed Migration Flows to Europe, Quarterly Overview (July – September 2026)
content:
In late 2015, IOM launched a Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) Flow Monitoring system, aiming to monitor Mixed Migration Flows to Europe by land and sea. Since then, DTM gathers, validates and disseminates information on migrants and refugees entering Europe through four main routes:

  • Eastern Mediterranean route (EMR): arrivals by sea and land to Bulgaria, Cyprus and Greece
  • Central Mediterranean route (CMR): arrivals by sea to Italy and Malta
  • Western Mediterranean route (WMR): arrivals by sea to the Peninsular Coasts of Spain, Balearic Islands, by land to the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla
  • Western African Atlantic route (WAAR): arrivals by sea to the Canary Islands of Spain

DTM also monitors data on migrants in transit through the Western Balkan route (WBR), including data from Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, and Kosovo (UNSCR 1244, 1999). These are considered separately to prevent, to the extent possible, the double counting of the same people, crossing multiple borders. Finally, DTM compiles data on migrants entering Croatia, Romania and Slovenia by land, typically after having crossed the Western Balkans or Bulgaria.

This report presents the latest available data and trends, focusing on the third quarter of 2026 and comparing it with the same period in 2025.

  • In the third quarter of 2026 (Q3 2026), 36,097 migrants arrived in Europe via these four routes. This represents a 42 per cent increase from previous Q2 2026 and a 24 per cent decline compared with Q3 2025. The steepest year-on-year drop was on the CMR (down 59%), followed by the EMR (down 13%). Arrivals were distributed across the CMR to Italy and Malta (24%), the EMR to Greece, Cyprus and Bulgaria (42%), the WMR to Spain (25%), and the WAAR to Spain (9%).
  • According to Eurostat, EU+ countries registered over 99,385 new asylum applications in the third quarter of 2026. Although data on asylum applications remain incomplete at the time of writing, France, Italy and Greece are among the highest ranking countries in the EU27+ in Q3 of 2026. Notably, France registered nearly twice as many first-time asylum applications (27,910) than Italy (15,450) did. Between July and September 2026, the main applicants held nationalities from Afghanistan (10%), Bangladesh (7%) and Sudan (6%), comprising nearly a quarter of all applications registered. These groups are followed by Türkiye, and Pakistan, Ukraine, Syrian Arab Republic and Somalia, averaging at around 4 per cent, respectively.
  • According to IOM’s MMP, 920 migrants died or went missing at sea while trying to reach Europe through the Mediterranean and Western African Atlantic routes in Q3 of 2026. Of these, 141 perished on the Central Mediterranean, and 350 while trying to cross the Atlantic to reach the Canary Islands. This represents a 6 per cent increase compared to Q3 2025 (871).

title: UNICEF Sudan Humanitarian Situation Report No. 47, 1-30 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • In September, over 29,000 people were newly displaced, while more than 8.5 million remain internally displaced, placing immense pressure on basic services and humanitarian assistance.
  • UNICEF enabled 333,500 women and children to access primary healthcare, reached 144,200 people through emergency health services, and supported routine immunization, including 1.2 million children vaccinated with DTP1 and 919,000 with measles vaccine.
  • Nutrition interventions expanded, with 139,000 caregivers receiving IYCF counselling and 41,000 cartons of RUTF dispatched for severe acute malnutrition treatment.
  • UNICEF reached 7.7 million people with safe water services, 1.4 million children with education opportunities, and 184,784 children with psychosocial support.
  • As of 30 September 2026, only 40 per cent (US$382.5 million) of requirements had been secured, leaving a US$580.4 million funding gap, with critical shortfalls persisting in Child Protection, Nutrition, Health and humanitarian supply pipelines.

title: Joint UNICEF-WHO-Ministry of Health Situation Report No. 1 (Syria Polio Outbreak Response), 22 November 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

In October 2026, after receiving initial reports of children with acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) in Deir ez-Zor Governorate, Syria, the Ministry of Health (MoH) mounted a swift response, in coordination with partners.

Conflict, displacement, interrupted immunization and population movement have created immunity gaps. An unrelated variant VDPV1 detection was reported in wastewater in the area in February 2026.

HIGHLIGHTS

The MoH, supported by WHO,UNICEF and partners, is leading the outbreak response, including intensified surveillance and vaccination.

Emergency vaccination activities reached:

  • 34 720 children in October 2026
  • 54 382 in November 2026 (111% of the target of 49 000)

The high coverage can be attributed to population movement. Additional efforts are needed to determine target population in future rounds.

The next campaign is planned for 30 November 2026 in six districts of Deir ez-Zor Governorate, integrating child nutrition assessments, drinking-water chlorine level checks and chlorine distribution.

An expanded scope will follow in December 2026.

The risk of further spread within Syria and to neighbouring countries, including Iraq, remains a concern due to uneven vaccination coverage and immunity gaps, particularly among displaced, mobile and underserved populations.

COORDINATION OF THE RESPONSE

The MoH is coordinating national and subnational actors. WHO and UNICEF are mobilizing regional and global technical expertise, while the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) provides technical and financial support. World Vision and the International Rescue Committee funded the first two vaccination rounds in October and November 2026.

Two coordination meetings involving national, regional and global response teams have reviewed the situation and agreed on priorities. The MoH Incident Management Team meets weekly through its Emergency Operations Centre. The remaining 13 governorates in Syria have been advised to intensify surveillance and preparedness. Cross-border coordination is particularly important for Iraq, given population movements and the history of wild poliovirus transmission across this border in 2013.

title: UNHCR Romania Ukraine Refugee Situation Weekly Update #223 - 23 November 2026
content:
Highlight

In 2026, UNHCR Romania strengthened its commitment to community-based protection and refugee inclusion by partnering with 10 refugee-led organizations (RLOs) and community-based organizations (CBOs) across nine counties. Building on its established collaboration with RLOs and CBOs since 2023, UNHCR recognizes their vital role in ensuring that refugees are not only recipients of support but also active contributors at grass-root level to solutions within their communities. Rooted in the communities they serve, these organizations draw on their experience, knowledge and trusted relationships to respond to local needs, facilitate access to essential services and create opportunities for participation and self-reliance. Their diverse initiatives include psychosocial support and empowerment for women and girls, educational and recreational activities for children and young people, language and employability training, assistance navigating public services, and programmes promoting social cohesion between refugees and host communities. Collectively, their activities directly benefit more than 1,500 refugees, demonstrating the value of locally led responses in strengthening protection, fostering inclusion and building resilient communities. With current funding ending in December 2026, UNHCR is actively seeking resources to sustain these partnerships and enable the organizations to continue their important work in 2027.

title: PAHO Regional Situation Report No.16: Measles in the Region of the Americas (19 November 2026)
content:
Summary of the Situation

Between epidemiological week (EW) 1 and EW 45 of 2026 (which ended on 14 November 2026), the Region of the Americas reported 58,795 confirmed cases of measles in 17 countries and territories, representing a 4.7-fold increase compared with the same period in 2025. Guatemala (34,860), Mexico (14,087), the United States (5,412), Peru (2,985), and Canada (1,128) account for the vast majority (99.5%) of confirmed cases (Map 1). A total of 84 deaths has been reported, including 53 in Guatemala, 23 in Mexico, six in the United States of America, one in Peru and one in Bolivia (1).

During EW 43 and EW 44 of 2026, the Region of the Americas reported 527 new confirmed cases of measles in seven countries and territories (Figure 1). Of the 527 new confirmed cases reported during EW 43–44, the United States accounted for 390, followed by Guatemala 73, Peru with 48, Mexico with nine, Belize with four, Canada with two, and Bolivia with one.

The 10–13 November meeting of the Regional Commission for the Monitoring and Re-Verification of Measles, Rubella, and Congenital Rubella Syndrome Elimination (RVC) reviewed the epidemiological situation of measles across the Region. Based on the Commission’s assessment and recommendations, which were subsequently endorsed by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Director, Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, endemic measles transmission was determined to have been re-established in Bolivia, Mexico, and the United States, resulting in the loss of measles elimination status in all three countries.

title: Humanitarian Feedback Bulletin: Accountability to Affected Populations - Renk, South Sudan I October 2026 Issue #7
content:
The Concern Worldwide Accountability to Affected Populations project, supported by WFP, aims at creating a bottom-up feedback and communication mechanism between responders and people we serve, that is community-based, easily accessible, and built on mutual understanding and genuine information-sharing.

Through local responders and community correspondents, Concern Worldwide, Community Engagement Network (hereafter: CEN), and the Radio Community (hereafter: TRC) work together to set up a complete community feedback mechanism that is accessible to all participants regardless of their literacy levels and access to assets and internet. Drawing on TRC’s and CEN’s extensive experience in radio broadcasting and community engagement, the project ensures a wide outreach beyond people with access to written updates.

Together, and alongside WFP, the project partners respond to information and feedback gaps. This way, and by consolidating and sharing the feedback received, the project increases accountability to affected populations in the targeted areas.

title: Rasuwa Flood Response 2026, Situation Report 16
content:
Situation Update

Following the devastating flash flood, thousands of people remain displaced, and uncertainty remains about the future. The flood response has entered a longer-term relief and early recovery phase, while search and rescue efforts continue in parallel with initiatives to restore access, basic services, and support for displaced and affected families. According to the latest update from the NDRRMA, 1,457 people have lost their lives, 5,285 remain missing, 13,795 have been rescued. To date, authorities have identified and handed over 112 bodies to their families. Currently, 417 people are taking shelter in 11 holding centers across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts, including 229 people in 6 centers in Rasuwa, 67 people in 1 center in Nuwakot, and 121 people in 4 centers in Dhading. Recognizing the need for greater flexibility and dignity among displaced families, the Government of Nepal will provide monthly cash assistance to those who choose not to stay in holding centers. The support will help cover accommodation and livelihood expenses for up to six months, or until alternative housing is arranged. Each family who do not wish to stay in holding centers and until alternative housing arrangement willreceive NPR 15,000 per month for families up to four members, with an additional NPR 2,000 per month for every family member beyond four, enabling families to make decisions that best suit their circumstances during recovery.

title: WFP Kenya External Situation Report on Moyale Emergency Response, 20 November 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Ongoing conflict on the Ethiopian side of Moyale has reportedly displaced approximately 60,000 people into Kenya, with registration continuing as new arrivals are reported. Although a ceasefire has reportedly held since 17 November, the security situation remains fragile, with cross-border humanitarian movements disrupted.

• Displaced populations are sheltering in communal reception centres, including schools, and with host families. Disrupted cross-border trade and livelihoods, coupled with increased pressure on host households' food resources, are heightening food security concerns. Nutrition screening is being prioritized to establish needs among new arrivals and host communities.

• The Government is prioritizing the relocation of displaced populations from school-based reception centres before schools reopen. Qilta is currently the only authorized relocation site, with plot demarcation underway under IOM guidance. Government direction on additional sites is awaited.

title: Doo Tha Htoo District Incident Report: Burma Army air strike killed one villager, injured five others, including two children, and caused destruction to villagers’ houses in Bilin Township (May 2026)
content: This Incident Report describes events occurring in Billin Township, Doo Tha Htoo (Thaton) District, in May 2026. On 12 May 2026, a Burma Army fighter jet dropped two 300-pound bombs onto Zd--- village, Noh Berh Baw village tract. One of the bombs landed in the village, killing one postpartum woman named Naw J--- and injuring five other villagers, including four-year-old Naw R--- and 17-year-old Naw V---. They were all originally from Jv--- village, K’Ter Tee village tract, Dwe Lo Township, Mu Traw (Hpapun) District, and were displaced in Zd--- village. One of the five injured villagers was in critical condition, so he was transported to Vl--- hospital in Thailand, while the others received treatment at Rk--- hospital, located in Rk--- village, Htee Baw Hkee village tract, Bilin Township, Doo Tha Htoo District, administered by the Karen Department of Health and Welfare (KDHW). Additionally, two villagers’ houses were destroyed and four were damaged by the explosion of the air strike. As a consequence, villagers faced livelihood challenges, and some of them displaced to forests in fear of further attack.[1]

title: Mergui-Tavoy District Interview: Fighting, shelling, and air strikes led local villagers to displace resulting in livelihood challenges in T’Naw Th’Ree Township (December 2025)
content: This Interview, conducted in December 2025, describes events occurring in T’Naw Th’Ree (Tanintharyi) Township, Mergui-Tavoy District, including fighting, shelling, and air strikes, which resulted in displacement, travel restrictions, healthcare challenges, difficulties accessing education, and livelihood challenges for local villagers who displaced in Za--- village, Moo K’Hpoh area. In particular, the interviewee, Ma T---, discusses livelihood challenges through the lens of gender and the specific challenges women face in the displacement site. The interview concludes with needs relating to humanitarian support, Ma T---’s hopes for the future, and requests to relevant stakeholders. This interview was conducted as part of a series of interviews examining the experiences in women in displacement in Karen State from January 2024 to December 2025. 1

title: UNHCR Sudan Factsheet, September 2026
content:
The conflict in Sudan has created a complex displacement and protection crisis. Although over 5.2 million people have returned to areas of origin, there are still an estimated 8.6 million people internally displaced.

Over 900,000 refugees and asylum-seekers mainly from South Sudan, Ethiopia and Eritrea reside in Sudan, with few solution options available to them. This multifaceted context is increasing pressure on public service delivery.

UNHCR and partners deliver life-saving assistance and protection through community- based structures and an area-based approach that enables self-reliance.

title: WFP Mauritania Country Brief, November 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Mauritania hosts the largest number of Malian refugees in West Africa; 305,000 refugees and asylum seekers are estimated in the country in which about 178,500 registered refugees reside in Hodh Chargui (HEC). WFP continues to adapt its life-saving food and nutrition assistance for refugees and host communities amid rising needs and reduced resources.

• Mauritania’s import dependence has heightened its exposure to the Middle East and Gulf crisis, contributing to a fourth fuel price hike since March and rising transport and commodity costs, with WFP monitoring impacts on markets, food security and operations.

• WFP completed the third cycle of its lean season response, in the departments of Kankossa and Boumdeid in the region of Assaba, in line with the Government’s National Response Plan (PNR). In addition, in October WFP expanded its coverage to the department of Guerou, in the same region, based on the Cadre Harmonisé classification (IPC Phase 3+) to further complement the PRN.

• The national Food Security Monitoring Survey (FSMS) data collection was carried out in October. Its results will inform the Cadre Harmonisé exercise planned during the first week of November. For the first time, the government funded the whole exercise, including data collection from refugees.

title: Moyale Emergency - Public Health Situation Analysis (PHSA)
content:
Since 18 October 2026, there has been active conflict within the Oromia and Somali regions of Ethiopia.

The conflict on the Ethiopian side of Moyale, has reportedly displaced approximately 60 000 people into Kenya, with registration continuing as new arrivals are reported. Although a ceasefire has reportedly held since 17 November, the security situation remains fragile, with cross-border humanitarian movements disrupted.

A Government led assessment published 3 November 2026 found limited access to health care with 53% of all households (398/755) reporting that they cannot access nearby health centre. Households who reported inaccessible healthcare cited higher costs (49%) and drug stockouts (44%) as the drivers of inaccessibility.

Marsabit is one of Kenya’s 23 Arid and Semi-Arid Lands (ASAL) counties and was already facing food insecurity before the influx, which compounds pressure on local resources. Humanitarian access to some border areas, including Somare, remains constrained.

On 9 November, Kenya’s Prime Cabinet Secretary said Ethiopia had assured Kenya it is working to restore normalcy. Reports indicate that the root cause of clashes between rival forces are long-standing local disputes related to land ownership, governance, ethnic differences and political disagreements. Successful peace talks remain essential for people to return home safely.

The United Nations is appealing for USD 8.9 million to address the most critical lifesaving needs for the next three months.

title: Palestine Logistics Cluster - Concept of Operations (ConOps) November, 2026
content:
Background

For the last 3 years the situation in Gaza has been marked by conflict, mass displacement, widespread infrastructure destruction and the collapse of essential services. The October 2025 ceasefire enabled some operational improvements but has not secured sustained humanitarian access or civilian safety. Continuing conflict, the activities of military and other armed groups, as well as continuing restrictions around demarcation lines threaten civilians, humanitarian personnel and logistics facilities, and impact access to affected communities. Needs remain extensive across food security, shelter, health and WASH sectors. Winter further compounds these needs: an estimated 294,250 families require shelter assistance, while approximately 950,000 displaced people live in sites at medium or high risk of flooding1 . Funding shortfalls are reducing assistance and limiting partners’ ability to replenish supplies, maintain operational capacity and prepare for seasonal emergencies. Humanitarian logistics remain constrained by heavily damaged infrastructure within Gaza, limited operational entry points into the Strip, complex clearance procedures (particularly for items considered “dual-use”), and intensive cargo inspections upstream. Cargo entering through the limited crossing points (at time of drafting only Kerem Shalom/Karem Abu Salem) depends on tightly coordinated movements; additional scanning, detailed inspections, and repeated handling slow down operations and can lead to delays, congestion and higher costs. Inside Gaza, damaged roads and warehouses, restricted routes, and limited access across the military demarcation line all constrain cargo collection, storage and onward distribution. Shortages of fuel, spare parts, lubricants and maintenance equipment undermine vehicle availability, while unreliable electricity and restrictions on equipment further compromise logistics operations. Airstrikes near warehouses, security incidents along key supply routes, and frequent checks and inspections further disrupt operations. Although transport markets in Jordan and Israel remain functional, substantial logistics gaps persist within Gaza. Predictable access, road rehabilitation, secure temporary storage, reliable transport and fuel, and coordinated cargo movements therefore remain essential to sustaining deliveries and reaching populations with lifesaving assistance at the scale required, particularly as winter conditions further impact operations.

title: Concern & partners expand emergency response across Yemen with EU support | Concern Worldwide
content:
Under this new grant, the Irish humanitarian organisation and partners (referred to as the HAYAT* Consortium) aim to reduce morbidity and mortality through lifesaving healthcare and nutrition services to vulnerable people and communities affected by ongoing insecurity, displacement, and worsening economic conditions in Yemen.

The situation in Yemen remains highly volatile, with more than 18 million people facing acute food insecurity. Civilians continue to bear the brunt of the crisis, as persistent security tensions, economic deterioration, and recurring population displacement further exacerbate humanitarian needs across the country.

“By bringing together international and national organisations with complementary experience and capacities, the HAYAT Consortium helps ensure that assistance is informed by local realities, reaches communities most in need, and contributes to strengthening local humanitarian response capacities,” says Victor Moses, Country Director for Concern Worldwide in Yemen.

More than 2.2 million children under the age of five are suffering from acute malnutrition. Health and nutrition services have been among the sectors hardest hit by last year’s funding cuts, leaving millions of people with reduced access to essential care.

Under the HAYAT* Consortium, the organizations will support 64 health facilities and their catchment communities in the governorates of Hajjah, Hodeidah, Raymah, Taiz, Lahj, and Abyan, aiming to reach over 448,000 people. Support will include treatment for malnutrition, healthcare services, safe water and sanitation, and psychosocial support for children and caregivers. The program will also strengthen health facilities and restore water supply systems where necessary.

The regional conflict, and uncertainty regarding commercial shipping in the Red Sea have intensified trade disruptions across the region. The resulting increase in transportation and commodity costs is disproportionately affecting vulnerable households, fishing communities, and coastal populations in Yemen, where 22 million people require humanitarian assistance to survive.

For further information contact Eilis Staunton, Media Relations Officer, Concern Worldwide, at eilis.staunton@concern.net or +353 85 872 0720.

*HAYAT Consortium:

The Health & Nutrition Alliance for Yemen’s Affected Households (HAYAT) consortium brings together Concern Worldwide, Action Against Hunger (ACF), Première Urgence Internationale (PUI), Yemen Family Care Association (YFCA) and Generation Without Qat (GWQ). Funded by the European Union, the HAYAT Consortium delivers integrated health and nutrition services, with mental health and psychological support, and water, sanitation, and hygiene services to the most vulnerable communities.

title: Attacks on Health Care Bi-Monthly News Brief, 01 - 15 November 2026
content:
The Missing Gender Dimension: Sex Is Unknown for Nearly 6 in 10 Health Workers Affected by Violence
Women accounted for 24% and men 76% of health workers affected by violence in cases where sex was reported. But sex was known in only 41% of 15,146 cases recorded by Insecurity Insight (2016-Sept 2026). These figures cannot tell us who faces greater risks. Better sex-disaggregated data is essential to understanding gendered impacts of violence against health workers.

Understanding how armed conflict affects women and men differently requires reliable sex-disaggregated data. Without this information, the gendered impacts of violence against health workers remain largely invisible, limiting our ability to understand who is most affected, assess differences in exposure to violence and develop responses that address people centred needs. The importance of gender-sensitive evidence has long been recognised in the Women, Peace and Security agenda, beginning with UN Security Council Resolution 1325 (2000). Subsequent commitments, including Resolution 1889 (2009) and the Secretary-General’s 2010 report, further emphasised the need for systematic monitoring and the collection of sex- and age-disaggregated data.

Sex is reported for only 41% of health workers affected by violence
Insecurity Insight's monitoring shows that of the 15,146 health workers recorded killed, injured, kidnapped and arrested between January 2016 and September 2026, sex was reported for 6,167 (41%). Reporting rates of sex also varied by incident type, reaching 61% for health workers who were killed, compared with 25% for those who were injured. One reason for these reporting gaps is that many organisations omit sex to protect the privacy and confidentiality of affected health workers and reduce the risk of their identification. While this is an important ethical and protection measure, it limits the availability of sex-disaggregated data and, consequently, the ability to understand gendered patterns of violence against health workers. This presents a challenge for efforts to improve monitoring while ensuring that the safety and privacy of affected individuals remain paramount.

Available data cannot establish whether women and men experience violence differently
Among the 6,167 health workers whose sex was reported, 1,410 (24%) were women and 4,419 (76%) were men. However, these figures should be interpreted with caution. As sex was reported for only 41% of recorded cases where health workers were killed, injured, kidnapped and arrested, the available data cannot establish whether this distribution reflects the actual gender composition of affected health workers or differences in reporting. Drawing conclusions about the relative exposure of women and men to violence based on these figures alone risks producing a misleading picture. It is also important to consider how many women and men work in healthcare overall. Without knowing the gender composition of the health workforce, it is impossible to determine whether women or men face a greater risk of violence. These findings highlight the need for more systematic and ethically responsible approaches to collecting sex-disaggregated data, so policymakers can better understand the gendered impacts of violence against health workers and develop evidence-based responses.

title: Syrian Arab Republic: Humanitarian Update No. 8 | September - October 2026 [EN/AR]
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Israeli military activity intensified across southern Syria, with around 280 armed incursions recorded in September alone, increasing protection concerns and affecting civilian movement, agricultural livelihoods and access to services in border communities.
  • Agricultural recovery remains at risk despite improved 2026 harvest conditions,with underfunding contributing to emergency agriculture assistance reaching only 12 per cent of its annual target by end-September, even as the 2026–2027 planting season was already underway.
  • Food affordability remains a major concern across Syria, with monitored food prices in September 25 per cent higher than a year earlier, while gaps in regular food assistance persisted across some of the country’s highest-severity areas.
  • Humanitarian partners reached an average of 2.48 million people per month with humanitarian assistance between January and September 2026, with 325 organizations operating across 5,097 communities.
  • The Syria Humanitarian Fund allocated US$5 million to address growing needs in south-west Syria, targeting more than 100,000 people across prioritized areas of Quneitra, Dar’a and Rural Damascus through integrated humanitarian assistance.

title: Rwanda Population Movement 2025 - DREF Final Report MDRRW024
content:
What happened, where and when?

On 7 December 2025, renewed fighting in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, particularly in South Kivu Province, triggered a significant movement of people towards Rwanda. The initial influx was concentrated in Rusizi District, with asylum seekers arriving through border entry points and being received at the Nyarushishi Transit Centre and surrounding reception sites. The sudden increase in arrivals placed additional pressure on existing shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene, health, protection and basic assistance capacities

The IFRC-DREF operation was launched on 16 December 2025 to support the Rwanda Red Cross Society in addressing the immediate humanitarian needs of people arriving from eastern DRC. While the initial operation was designed around an estimated 2,000 people, implementation took place in a context of continued population movement and evolving needs. During the four-month implementation period, the Rwanda Red Cross Society provided assistance through shelter and non-food items, health and first aid, WASH, Protection,
Gender and Inclusion (PGI), and Community Engagement and Accountability (CEA) activities. The response also focused on strengthening the capacity of volunteers to provide timely assistance and referrals at reception and transit locations.

By the end of the operation on 30 April 2026, the Rwanda Red Cross Society had assisted 3,100 people . Assistance included 400 households receiving shelter and essential household items, health and first-aid support, WASH assistance, protection and child-focused services, as well as community engagement and feedback activities.
The response therefore evolved from an initial emergency response to a broader effort to address the needs of both newly arriving asylum seekers and people already accommodated in or around the reception areas. The operation also strengthened the preparedness and response capacity of Rwanda Red Cross volunteers through training in first aid, epidemic control, psychosocial support, WASH, shelter, PGI and CEA.

title: Colombia: Informe de Tendencias e Impacto Humanitario en 2026 | Datos acumulados entre enero - agosto de 2026 | Fecha de publicación: 23 de noviembre de 2026
content:
MENSAJES CLAVE

  • Entre enero y agosto de 2026, Colombia continuó enfrentando una crisis humanitaria marcada por la acumulación de impactos del conflicto armado y de eventos de origen natural recurrentes. La situación se agravó tras el terremoto de agosto, que incrementó las necesidades humanitarias en territorios que ya enfrentaban los efectos de la violencia, la pobreza y una limitada presencia institucional. Esta combinación de emergencias puso aún más presión sobre las capacidades de respuesta de las autoridades locales y nacionales.
  • La intensificación de las hostilidades y el control territorial de grupos armados siguen deteriorando las condiciones de vida de comunidades rurales y étnicas.
  • Los confinamientos, restricciones a la movilidad y limitaciones de acceso a bienes esenciales persisten como una de las afectaciones más críticas, incrementando riesgos de protección, inseguridad alimentaria y vulneración de derechos.
  • El terremoto de magnitud 7,4 ocurrido en agosto evidenció la fragilidad de territorios ya vulnerables y donde las capacidades de respuesta locales ya enfrentaban desafíos y limitaciones. Más allá de la emergencia inmediata, el sismo incrementó las necesidades, mientras confirmó la urgencia de fortalecer la preparación, resiliencia comunitaria y capacidad de respuesta frente a crisis complejas y concurrentes.
  • Los ataques indiscriminados con drones cargados con explosivos siguen en aumento ocasionando daños a la infraestructura civil y aumentando los riesgos a los que se exponen los civiles.

title: Zimbabwe - Drought Anticipatory Action | DREF Operation (MDRZW031)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

11-09-2026

What happened, where and when?

Existing vulnerability and drought risk

Zimbabwe remains highly vulnerable to recurrent droughts driven by climate variability, El Niño events and the growing effects of climate change. Repeated drought episodes have increasingly affected agricultural production, food security, water availability, livestock health and household livelihoods, particularly in rural areas that depend heavily on rain-fed agriculture and natural resource-based livelihoods. Communities in drought-prone areas continue to face constrained coping capacities due to successive climate shocks, limited livelihood diversification and persistent economic challenges.

The impacts of the 2023/2024 El Niño-induced drought demonstrated the magnitude of these vulnerabilities. Reduced agricultural production, depletion of household food stocks, deterioration of water sources and declining livelihood opportunities contributed to widespread humanitarian needs across the country. The 2024 Zimbabwe Livelihoods Assessment Committee (ZimLAC) assessment estimated that approximately 5.9 million people were food insecure in rural areas, while access to basic water services declined significantly. Although these figures relate to the previous drought season, they highlight the scale of humanitarian impacts that can result from severe rainfall deficits and underscore the vulnerability of communities entering another potentially poor season.

Current food security and livelihood conditions indicate that many households have not fully recovered from previous shocks. According to the FEWS NET Food Security Outlook Update (August 2026-January 2027), poorer households in districts such as Chivi and Buhera had already exhausted own-produced food stocks earlier than normal and were increasingly dependent on market purchases. The April 2026 Second Round Crop, Livestock and Fisheries Assessment (CLAFA 2) similarly reported below-average agricultural production in several drought-prone districts. At the same time, elevated staple food prices, declining water availability, deteriorating pasture conditions and reduced livelihood opportunities continue to increase household vulnerability.

These underlying vulnerabilities are particularly pronounced in Chivi, Buhera, Mudzi, Mbire and Kariba districts, where many households are entering the 2026/27 agricultural season with limited food reserves, fragile livelihoods and reduced capacity to absorb further climate-related shocks.

Forecast evidence and anticipated drought risk

The operation is triggered by credible seasonal forecast information indicating an elevated likelihood of drought conditions during the 2026/27 rainfall season. The Meteorological Services Department (MSD), through the National Climate Outlook Forum (NACOF) held on 11 September 2026, forecast a high probability of below-normal rainfall across much of Zimbabwe between October 2026 and March 2027, associated with the development of a strong El Niño event and the potential influence of a positive Indian Ocean Dipole. These conditions are expected to increase the likelihood of delayed rainfall onset, prolonged dry spells, above-average temperatures and reduced soil moisture availability during critical stages of crop production.

This outlook is consistent with forecasts issued by the Thirty-Third Southern Africa Regional Climate Outlook Forum (SARCOF-33), which highlighted an elevated probability of below-normal rainfall and above-average temperatures across much of Southern Africa, including Zimbabwe. The convergence of national and regional forecasts indicates an increased risk of drought-related impacts on rain-fed agriculture, water resources, livestock production and rural livelihoods during the 2026/27 season.

Forecasts indicate that rainfall deficits during the October-December planting period could negatively affect planting decisions, crop establishment and germination, while continued moisture deficits during January-March could increase crop stress, reduce yields and worsen existing livelihood vulnerabilities. These projected conditions present a clear opportunity for anticipatory action before impacts materialize fully.

Anticipated humanitarian impacts

If forecast conditions materialize, vulnerable households are expected to experience further deterioration in food security, agricultural production and livelihood outcomes. Delayed rainfall, prolonged dry spells and above-normal temperatures may result in poor germination, reduced crop establishment, lower agricultural productivity and declining seasonal labour opportunities. Consequently, households may become increasingly dependent on markets at a time when purchasing power remains constrained.

Reduced rainfall and elevated temperatures are also likely to place additional pressure on water resources for domestic use, livestock and agricultural activities. Declining pasture availability, reduced livestock productivity and increased competition for limited water resources may further undermine household resilience and increase vulnerability among farming and agro-pastoral communities.

Without early intervention, affected households may increasingly resort to negative coping strategies such as reducing food consumption, selling productive assets, withdrawing children from school, distress livestock sales or accumulating unsustainable debt. These impacts are expected to be most severe among already vulnerable populations, including women-headed households, childheaded households, older persons, persons with disabilities, chronically ill individuals and extremely poor farming households.

Rationale for anticipatory action

The convergence of forecasted rainfall deficits, increasing climatic risk and pre-existing food security and livelihood vulnerabilities provides sufficient evidence to justify immediate anticipatory action. The forecast window provides a limited but critical opportunity to protect livelihoods before the most severe impacts of drought materialize. Delaying intervention until the effects of drought are fully observed would significantly reduce the effectiveness of agricultural support measures and increase the likelihood of humanitarian deterioration.

Through this DREF operation, the Zimbabwe Red Cross Society (ZRCS) will implement forecast-based anticipatory actions aimed at reducing the projected impacts of drought on vulnerable households. The operation will prioritize the timely distribution of droughttolerant and short-season crop varieties to 1,800 vulnerable farming households in Chivi, Buhera and Mudzi districts, combined with the dissemination of localized drought early warning information, climate adaptation messaging, water conservation measures and livestock protection advisories across Chivi, Buhera, Mudzi, Mbire and Kariba districts. These interventions are intended to support informed decision-making, protect agricultural production and strengthen household resilience before drought conditions worsen.

To complement implementation, ZRCS will concurrently conduct operational monitoring and assessment activities across the five targeted districts. These activities will support the monitoring of drought progression, identify emerging vulnerabilities, assess the effectiveness of anticipatory actions and strengthen evidence-based decision-making should conditions deteriorate beyond the forecast scenario. The assessments are therefore a supporting component of the operation and do not determine whether anticipatory actions are undertaken.

Implementation of planned early actions, particularly seed distribution within the critical planting window, will proceed independently of assessment activities.

The operation is therefore designed to act on available forecast information and existing vulnerability evidence now, while using concurrent monitoring and assessment to refine operational understanding, support accountability and inform any future preparedness or humanitarian response decisions that may become necessary should drought conditions worsen beyond anticipated levels.

title: BRA: Drought - 11-2026 - BRA: Drought and Forest Fire (2026-11-20)
content:
Sources for data marked as Other

The information was collected directly from the Brazilian Government’s Integrated Disaster Information System

Description

The state of Para is facing an environmental and humanitarian emergency streaming from a combination of prolonged drought. reduced water availability and the spread of forest fires.

This situation has impacted native vegetation, conservation areas, indigenous territories and traditional communities, while also compromising economic activities and the basic living conditions of rural and riverin populations.

The severity of the scenario extends well beyond the areas directly consumed by the flames. The drought increases community vulnerability by limiting access to water for consumption, hygiene, livestock and agricultural production.

Simultaneously, smoke from the fires can exacerbate respiratory issues. hinder de movement of people and disrupt local services. In November 11th by the Decree 5767 the Federal Government declared a state of emergency in 61 municipalities across Para affected by forest fires. This declaration allows the municipal governments to request for federal support for emergency response and humanitarian assistance. In the Marajo region. the municipalities of Cachoeira do Arari and Soure require particular attention regarding the protection of rural areas and the stenghtening of local reponse capacities.

In Santarem the situation is particularly complex: the drought is compromising water supplies and river transport and livelihoods while fires are degradating air quality and threatening conservation areas creating a situation that must be addressed as environmental, public health and humanitarian crisis.

In Alter Do Chao, the gravity of the situation stems not only from fires within the APA but also within the Borari territory home the indigenous borari community (12000 people) that is organised in local brigades essential for a response that respect social, cultural and traditions.

From a humanitarian perspective, immediate priorities must include ensuring access to potable water and food security, providing healthcare, protecting traditional communities, and offering logistical support to response teams.

At the same time, it is necessary to strengthen prevention, oversight, and environmental restoration efforts to reduce the risk of future fires and prevent the emergency from persisting even after the flames have been brought under control.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: -

NS Requests International Assistance: Yes

Information Bulletin Published

Requested

Actions taken by National Society

General

  • Other

ICMBio – Combating fires in federal conservation units, mobilizing firefighting crews, aircraft, and vehicles, protecting traditional communities, and distributing water and supplies to affected families. Ministry of the Environment and Climate Change (MMA) – Coordination and alignment of environmental initiatives between federal and state governments, monitoring of risks, and integration of the institutions involved. Ministry of Integration and Regional Development (MIDR) / National Civil Defense – Recognition of emergency situations, analysis of work plans, and release of funds for humanitarian assistance and disaster response. National Public Security Force: Operational support for environmental teams and reinforcement of firefighting efforts in priority municipalities. Ministry of Justice and Public Security: Support for the mobilization of the National Public Security Force, and the provision of operational and aerial resources to the most affected regions. Ministry of Defense / Armed Forces: Institutional and logistical support for federal firefighting operations. Ministry of Agrarian Development and Family Farming (MDA): Support for vulnerable rural populations, including preventive food security measures and the early distribution of basic food baskets. Chief of Staff of the Presidency of the Republic: Interministerial coordination via the Situation Room for Forest Fire Control. Pará Military Fire Brigade (CBMPA): Direct firefighting, mobilization of specialized teams, coordination of operations, and protection of threatened communities. State Civil Defense Coordination (CEDEC-PA): Monitoring of climate-related risks, issuance of alerts, coordination of the state-level response, and liaison with municipal and federal civil defense agencies. State Secretariat for Environment, Climate, and Sustainability (Semas): Environmental monitoring, provision of equipment, and support for the organization of firefighting and prevention operations. Public Security Air Group (Graesp): Provision of helicopters for the transport of personnel, reconnaissance, and support for aerial operations. Pará Military Police (PMPA): Reinforcement of security and support for integrated firefighting operations. Civil Police / Specialized Environmental Agencies: Support for the investigation of arson and the identification of those responsible for illegal burning.

title: PER: Earthquake - 11-2026 - 6.7 Earthquake Junin (2026-11-21)
content:
Sources for data marked as Other

(1) COEN-INDECI, REPORTE-COMPLEMENTARIO N.° 16238 - Sismo de Magnitud 6.7 con Epicentro en Junín, 21 November 2026 (official situation report). (2) RPP Noticias. “Fuerte sismo en Junín: Indeci reporta ocho heridos y más de 120 viviendas afectadas en su más reciente balance” (21 November 2026): https://rpp.pe/peru/junin/fuerte-sismo-en-junin-indeci-reporta-ocho-heridos-y-mas-de-120-viviendas-afectadas-en-su-mas-reciente-balance-noticia-1718981 (3) Infobae Perú. “Sismo de 6.7 en Junín dejó 128 viviendas afectadas, 4 destruidas, 8 heridos y una universidad comprometida” (21 November 2026): https://www.infobae.com/peru/2026/11/21/sismo-de-67-en-junin-dejo-128-viviendas-afectadas-4-destruidas-8-heridos-y-una-universidad-comprometida/ Note. Estimated affected population (450 people) calculated from 128 affected households reported by INDECI using an average household size of 3.5 persons per household.

Description

On 20 November 2026 at 19:10 hrs local time, a magnitude 6.7 earthquake struck the Junín region of Peru, with impacts reported across Junín, Pasco and neighboring areas. According to the latest official COEN-INDECI report, issued on 21 November 2026 at 01:40 hrs, six people were reported injured, while no deaths or missing persons had been officially recorded at the time of publication. Initial assessments identified damage to housing, public infrastructure and basic services, including temporary power outages and road access restrictions caused by landslides and rockfalls. REPORTE COMPLEMENTARIO N.º 16249 - 21/11/2026 / COEN - INDECI / 08:20 HORAS (Reporte N.° 3) SISMO DE MAGNITUD 6.7 CON EPICENTRO EN EL DISTRITO DE JUNÍN - JUNÍN - INDECI Tarea de Todos

Subsequent updates communicated by INDECI and reported by national media indicate that the number of injured people increased to eight, with 128 houses affected and four houses destroyed. Damage was also reported to two churches, one hospital, one health centre and facilities of the Universidad Peruana Los Andes in Chanchamayo. Based on the reported number of affected households and applying an average household size of 3.5 persons, an estimated 450 people may have been affected by the earthquake. Damage and needs assessments remain ongoing, and figures may be revised as additional information becomes available.

At the time of reporting, all IFRC personnel present in the country have reported being safe, with no injuries or operational impacts affecting personnel confirmed.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: No

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by others

Following the earthquake, the National Emergency Operations Center (COEN) and INDECI activated monitoring and coordination mechanisms to assess damages and support response actions in the affected areas. Local and regional authorities, together with sectoral institutions, continue conducting damage and needs assessments, while emergency response teams have been deployed to verify impacts on housing, health facilities, public infrastructure and road access. Authorities also reported ongoing efforts to restore access in areas affected by landslides and rockfalls and to coordinate assistance for affected households. According to statements by Luis Vásquez, Head of INDECI, emergency authorities continue to update impact figures and coordinate humanitarian assistance for affected families, including support for households whose homes were damaged or destroyed.

title: Afghanistan: Monthly Market Report Issue 77: October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

Markets remain functional, but persistent trade disruptions, elevated commodity prices, rising transportation costs and limited employment opportunities continue to constrain household purchasing power.

MACROECONOMIC AND TRADE DEVELOPMENTS

Economic Growth and Household Welfare

Afghanistan's economy continues to recover, with real GDP projected to grow by 3.0% in 2026. However, rapid population growth, partly driven by returning Afghans, continues to outpace economic gains, limiting improvements in per-capita income which is projected to contract by 3.3 percent in 2026. Weak investment, limited job creation and restrictions on women's economic participation continue to constrain household incomes and economic opportunities.

Trade Routes and Supply Network

One year after the Pakistan border closure, Afghanistan's import networks remain increasingly reliant on alternative routes through Iran and Central Asia. Iranian direct trade and transit routes accounted for 56.6 percent of trade flows, while Central Asian corridors contributed 38.9 percent. Longer routes and higher logistics costs continue to increase import expenses and expose domestic markets to supply-chain risks.

Exchange Rate

The Afghani depreciated marginally by 0.5% in October to an average of AFN 64.9/USD. Nevertheless, it remained 2.4% stronger than a year earlier and 7% above its three-year average, helping moderate imported inflationary pressures despite elevated transportation and trade costs.

Inflation (August 2026)

Headline inflation reached 7.8% year-on-year, its highest level since 2022, while food inflation climbed to 8.9%, approaching double digits. Higher costs of food, housing, healthcare and transportation continue to weigh on household budgets.

Fuel and Logistics Costs

Diesel prices remained high in October at AFN 80.4/litre, standing 3% above last year and 13% above the three-year average, sustaining pressure on transportation and market operating costs.

title: UNICEF Nigeria Humanitarian Flash Update No. 2 (Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease), 13 November 2026
content:

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 18 November 2026
content:
Key Highlights

  • An Israeli airstrike on Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis area of Gaza killed six people and damaged critical surgical facilities, further undermining efforts to restore the Strip’s severely overstretched health system.
  • As Gaza enters its fourth winter since October 2023, early seasonal rainfall has already caused flooding and damage to thousands of shelters, while humanitarian partners have called for the urgent entry of winter supplies and access to safer locations.
  • Food Security Sector partners highlighted the urgent need to facilitate the entry of veterinary kits into Gaza to protect livestock, preserve herding livelihoods and address parasite infestations that pose risks to human, animal and environmental health, particularly during winter.
  • In Jericho, West Bank, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot and killed by an Israeli settler. Overall, 40 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage were recorded across 30 communities in one week.
  • Settler attacks and related access restrictions displaced 68 Palestinians, including 31 children, in Hebron and Ramallah governorates during the same week. The Jordan Valley has accounted for 44 per cent of Palestinians displaced in this context in 2026.
  • Since the beginning of 2026, more than 5,150 Palestinians have been displaced across the West Bank due to demolitions, settler violence and related access restrictions, and evictions, averaging more than 16 people per day.

title: WFP Palestine Emergency Response External Situation Report #100, 21 November (Reporting period: 1-31 October 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

Although humanitarian assistance and commercial supplies increased following the October 2025 ceasefire, they remain insufficient against the scale of needs, and the crisis is far from over.
  • Some 1.4 million people, or two-thirds of the population, are acutely food insecure, with deteriorating weather conditions expected to further deplete their already limited capacity to safely store food and access cooking fuel.

title: Lebanon: Inter-Agency Response Update #2 (As of 15 November 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Limited alternatives for IDPs amid ongoing consolidation of collective shelters. Some 1200 IDPs moved out of collective shelters during the first two weeks of the month, underscoring limited alternatives available for those unable to return home. Planned shelter closures continue, requiring coordinated efforts to identify suitable relocation options and ensure that IDPs can relocate safely and voluntarily.
  • Food insecurity remains widespread, with further deterioration projected in 2027. According to the latest IPC analysis, 1.05 million people face crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity currently, projected to rise to 1.15 million from March 2027.
