title: Yemen Market and Trade Bulletin October 2026 - Issued on 21st November 2026
content:
SHORT-TERM OUTLOOK AND IMPLICATIONS ON FOOD SECURITY:

While Yemen’s acute food security crisis—with roughly 18.7 million people (over half the population) facing acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or worse)—remains driven by heavy import dependency, rising food and fuel prices, severe humanitarian funding deficits, and climate and rainfall shocks, conditions have deteriorated sharply amid renewed frontline conflict and regional spillover effects. Since July 2026—and intensifying in September around Ta’iz, along the western coast, and across southern flashpoints—escalating hostilities and displacement have placed severe strain on overstretched services and existing displaced populations, while access constraints and road/maritime disruptions have slowed trade flows, pushed up freight and fuel costs, and restricted humanitarian reach. These compounding shocks—aggravated by funding shortfalls and climate stress—are eroding household purchasing power and driving acute deprivation, with millions facing IPC Phase 3 or worse conditions and localized emergency/catastrophe risks in late 2026.

KEY HIGHLIGHTS:

  • EXCHANGE RATES: Currency stability continued. The exchange rate remained broadly stable in GoY-controlled areas, trading 4% below its level a year earlier and 8% below the three-year average—indicating a firmer Yemeni rial against both benchmarks.
  • FOOD PRICES: Key staples became more expensive. In GoY-controlled areas, flour and basmati rice prices rose by 7.4% and 6.3% month-on-month, while sunflower oil and beans increased by 3.3% and 3.6%, respectively.
  • MINIMUM FOOD BASKET (MFB): Food-basket costs increased. Minimum Food Basket (MFB) costs in GoY-controlled areas rose 2% month-on-month from August, standing 7% above September 2025 levels and 2% above the three-year average—further squeezing household food affordability.
  • FOOD AND FUEL IMPORTS: Grain arrivals in GoY areas declined sharply. Recorded wheat and flour imports fell by 1.5% nationally and by 42.5% through southern ports. Recorded petrol and diesel imports also decreased by 9.9%; however, the absence of northern records limits the interpretation of this trend.
  • FUEL PRICES: Official diesel eased but remained elevated. Diesel prices fell by 4.5% month-on-month while petrol remained broadly stable; however, both fuels stayed substantially above last year's levels and their three-year averages.
  • TERMS OF TRADE (ToT): Flour purchasing power weakened. The Government of Yemen’s casual labor-to-flour terms of trade declined by 7.2% month-on-month and 23.1% year-on-year. Agricultural and composite livestock-to-flour ratios also decreased.
  • CASUAL LABOR WAGE RATES: Daily rates barely adjusted. In GoY-controlled areas, casual wages slipped 0.4% month-on-month and remained 9.7% below year-ago levels, while agricultural wages edged up by 0.4%.
  • LIVESTOCK PRICES: Modest recovery offered limited relief. Goat and local sheep prices increased month-on-month by 1.6% and 2.4%, respectively, but remained below their levels from the previous year.

title: Multi-country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak Situation Report No. 27 (9 - 15 November 2026)
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi, Central African Republic
content:
IOM REGIONAL RESPONSE AT A GLANCE

During the reporting period (9–15 November 2026), IOM supported 3,729,851 traveller screenings, bringing the cumulative total to 79,831,882 screenings since the start of the outbreak. Thirty-nine alerts were identified through IOM-supported surveillance – 28 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), 1 in Uganda and 10 in the Central African Republic (CAR) – bringing the cumulative total to 1,034 alerts.

At IOM-supported points of entry (PoEs) and points of control (PoCs) in DRC, five deceased persons were intercepted and referred for sample collection and safe and dignified burial, bringing the cumulative total to 271. One confirmed Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease (BVD) case was reported in a displacement site, bringing the cumulative number of confirmed cases detected through IOM-supported surveillance to 73.

IOM reached 3,073,123 people through risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) during the reporting period, bringing the cumulative reach to 68,933,505 people since the start of the outbreak.

title: IOM Hurricane Melissa Situation Report #20
content: IOM’s Situation Report No. 20 covers the Hurricane Melissa response in Jamaica from November 2025 to October 2026. While emergency debris-removal, cash-for-work, non-food-item and psychosocial support activities have concluded, shelter recovery continues: 4,105 households have received repair assistance, and four community centres have been repaired to support emergency shelter capacity. The report highlights progress, remaining priorities and the partnerships needed to sustain recovery and strengthen resilience.

title: Crop Prospects and Food Situation Triannual Global Report No. 3, November 2026
content:
Synopsis (short abstract)

The triannual Crop Prospects and Food Situation report provides a forward-looking global analysis of cereal production, market trends and acute food security conditions, with a particular attention on low-income food-deficit countries.

FAO estimates that 41 countries/territories require external assistance for food: 31 in Africa, eight in Asia, one in Latin America and the Caribbean, and one in Europe. Persisting conflicts and insecurity remain the primary drivers of the most severe levels of acute food insecurity, while weather shocks associated with the strong El Niño event are worsening conditions in several subregions. Looking ahead, El Niño-related impacts on production are expected to remain severe into 2027 in several subregions, likely aggravating acute food insecurity further.

The report also includes FAO's latest forecast for 2026 cereal production among the Low-Income Food-Deficit Countries (LIFDCs), pegged at 126.5 million tonnes, about 2 percent above both the 2025 level and the five-year average. The increase largely reflects a strong production recovery in Asia, particularly in Near East Asia, while production among African LIFDCs is expected to remain near-average.

title: Food Price Monitoring and Analysis (FPMA) Bulletin #9, 12 November 2026
content:
Synopsis (short abstract)

Global wheat and maize export prices declined in October 2026. Wheat prices fell amid subdued import demand and improving global production prospects, while maize prices declined from their September three‑year high amid seasonal harvest pressure in the United States of America and expectations of ample supplies from South America. Expectations of easing constraints on Black Sea export flows also weighed on wheat prices, although continued logistical disruptions in the region partly offset the downward pressure. By contrast, international rice prices increased, supported by harvest delays in some exporting countries, adverse weather conditions and rising production costs. In most domestic markets monitored by FAO, staple food prices remained relatively elevated in September and October 2026. In parts of East Africa and the Near East, conflict‑related market disruptions, currency depreciation and tight supplies continued to exert upward pressure on prices. In Far East Asia, weather-related production shortfalls and high production costs contributed to the increases in staple food prices, while in Eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Central Asia, high transport and import costs continued to exert upward pressure on domestic food prices. By contrast, the arrival of new harvests improved market supplies and contributed to seasonal price declines in parts of West Africa and Central and South America. However, strong demand, delayed harvests and unfavourable production prospects continued to drive price increases in some markets. In Southern Africa, ample domestic supplies and continued intra-regional trade helped contain seasonal price increases.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 94, as of 17 November 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Despite a still volatile context, some humanitarian movements have resumed around Zémio.
  • Infrastructure has been installed in Ouham-Pendé to help prevent agro-pastoral conflicts and reduce tensions between herders and farmers.
  • 3,900 students received school kits in Kaga-Bandoro and M’brès.

GENERAL CONTEXT

Haut-Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

The security situation remains volatile in the Zémio area, despite a relative improvement recently observed along certain roads around the town. In this context, humanitarian actors have gradually resumed some movements and activities in areas affected by movement restrictions that have been in place since September. A limited resumption of civilian movement has also been observed on the main road corridors, while staff from peripheral health facilities have been able to travel to Zémio to replenish medical supplies. No incidents have recently been reported on these routes. A humanitarian organization also conducted movements along the Zémio-Dembia axis to carry out assessments. Given the continuing volatility of the security environment, humanitarian partners are closely monitoring developments and maintaining existing security and risk-management measures.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Health

Haute-Kotto Prefecture – Central

On 11 November, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and its partner International Medical Corps (IMC) concluded their campaign providing comprehensive care for women living with obstetric fistula. A total of 33 patients received specialized treatment in Bria, with an 88 per cent success rate. 15 other patients faced transportation challenges in reaching Bria from Ndele in Bamingui-Bangoran Prefecture. To improve access to services in that area, a second two-week campaign is being conducted in Ndele from 12 to 26 November 2026.

Multi-sector

Vakaga Prefecture – North-East

On 11 November, the NGO COHEB, under a labour-intensive work project implemented through the Emergency Project to Support the Stabilization and Recovery of Refugees and Host Communities in the Lake Chad Basin (PASRRC), distributed cash assistance to 400 beneficiaries, including 150 Sudanese refugees and 250 members of host communities. Through the cash-for-work approach, each beneficiary received 30,000 CFA francs to support livelihoods and meet priority household needs.

title: Locust Watch: Seasonal precipitation predictions in the Desert Locust winter and spring breeding areas (December 2026–May 2027) (19 November 2026)
content: The extremely strong El Niño reaches its peak. Dry conditions are expected across most regions until the end of November, except for parts along the Red Sea coasts and in Mauritania. In the Western Region, above-normal rainfall is likely in December in the northern Sahel, with light rainfall in Mauritania and Western Sahara, which may favour continuation and expansion of ongoing breeding. Wetter-than-average conditions are forecast from February in Mauritania and Western Sahara, and may continue into spring and extend to southern Algeria, supporting locust breeding. In the Central Region, rains are likely around the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden from early December, becoming much heavier in February and persisting through March, thereby supporting breeding along the coasts in winter and in interior areas during spring. In the Eastern Region, near- to above-normal rainfall from December to May may allow small-scale spring breeding in Iran and Pakistan.

title: UNICEF Zambia Humanitarian Flash Update No.1 (Cholera Outbreak), 16 November 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Outbreak Overview: As of 16 November 2026, ZNPHI reported 3,099 cases and 68 deaths (CFR 2.2%) across 27 districts in seven provinces since 28 July. Children under 15 make up 24.9% of cases with age data (available for ~78.5% of cases).
  • Lusaka and Chibombo are the current hotspots accounting for 75.2% of cases (1,959 and 371 respectively).
  • Community engagement and communication: UNICEF-supported household visits reached over 1.2 million people, while dialogues engaged a further 30,000 people and 1,390 gatekeepers and influencers. This was reinforced by 31,600 communication materials (distribution underway) and a media campaign with an estimated potential audience of 7.8 million.
  • OCV: 701,354 vaccinations supported in Lusaka, Chibombo and Chongwe (23–26 October 2026).
  • WASH: UNICEF delivered 20 AWD kits to five districts and two tents to Chibombo for cholera treatment centres. It supported three inline chlorinators in Chibombo and WASH/IPC supplies to 20 health facilities in Chibombo and to treatment facilities in four Luapula districts.
  • Funding: UNICEF’s cholera response 2026/27 is only 9% funded, with a US$2.95 million gap (91%); Health has the largest gap (US$1.64 million). Urgent funding is needed to replenish WASH supplies and scale up treatment and community case finding before the rainy season.

title: RAIS Cumulative Assistance Summary – January to October 2026
content:
Find the RAIS assistance summary for January – October 2026, broken down by month, covering all organisations that reported into the system during this period. This is shared so each organisation can check what has been recorded against its name — month by month — and flag any corrections.

Missed reporting for a previous month? You can still back-report it in RAIS. Back-reported records will be included, so the figures will be correct in the next RAIS Assistance Report dashboard.

How to read this summary: each monthly column shows two figures. For in-kind and service assistance (CRI items, shelter kits and repairs, home visits, counselling), the top number is quantity distributed and the smaller number below is cases (no value shown). For cash-based assistance (Emergency Financial Assistance, EPCA, Protection Cash Assistance, MCAP, PCAP, ATM-credited cash, cash for food/education/shelter, NDA), the top number is cases and the smaller number below is value disbursed (USD). A dash (–) means no assistance of that type was reported by that organisation in that month.

A note on what "cases" means: the case figures in this summary are not unique beneficiaries. A "case" is a household or family that received assistance during that specific month. The same household may be counted more than once within this period — for example, if it received the same type of assistance in multiple months, or received different types of assistance (cash and/or in-kind) from the same organisation or from different organisations, during the same month or across different months. As a result, summing cases across months or across assistance types will overstate the number of distinct households reached.

title: Chad : Humanitarian Situation in Lac Situation Report N° 02 (30 October 2026)
content:
This report was produced by OCHA in collaboration with the authorities and humanitarian partners. It primarily covers the period from 1 to 30 October 2026 and incorporates findings from the July 2026 mid-term evaluation of the response to internally displaced persons (IDPs). The next report will be published at the end of November 2026.

KEY POINTS

  • 307,206 displaced people in the province according to IOM Round 26, including 268,064 IDPs, 17,100 returnees, and 22,042 former IDPs who have returned.
  • More than 75,000 IDPs have been hosted across 16 sites in the Fouli and Kaya departments since May 2026. New population movements continue to be reported and remain under verification.
  • An encouraging improvement in the cholera situation was observed between 13 and 26 October, followed by a resurgence of 12 new cases in Kiskawa. However, the case fatality rate remains high (5.78%), well above the WHO emergency threshold, requiring the need to strengthen prevention, surveillance, and WASH interventions.
  • The areas of Liwa, Kiskawa, Kadoulou, and Daboua are among those most exposed to security risks. This insecurity directly contributes to population displacement, loss of livelihoods, and reduced access to basic services.
  • Four incidents were reported in the departments of Fouli and Kaya, affecting several civilians and resulting in dozens of deaths as well as abductions, a toll that would have been even higher without the intervention of the defense and security forces.
  • Despite the scale of needs, the protection sector remains the least covered, with only 0.3% of targeted people assisted.
  • A concerning deterioration in livelihoods has been observed linked to low rainfall.
  • US$10.6 million has been mobilized through humanitarian emergency funding mechanisms, including CERF, the Regional Humanitarian Fund, and anticipatory action, to support the response.
  • Significant humanitarian needs remain unmet due to insufficient funding, particularly in protection, shelter and site management, education, health and nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and food security.
  • The revitalization of the Grand Cadre Nexus and the review of convergence zones offer an opportunity to strengthen integrated investments by linking emergency response, access to essential services, social cohesion, and resilience.

title: WFP Lebanon Country Brief, November 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• As needs continue to outpace initial planning assumptions, WFP requires immediate, flexible, and front-loaded funding at scale to sustain and expand assistance in a highly fluid operational environment.

• Since the beginning of the escalation on 2 March, WFP has reached around 1.1 million unique conflict‑affected people with food and cash assistance in shelters and across communities.

• In October, the Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MEHE), with WFP and UNICEF, launched Lebanon’s first National Nutrition and Food Environment Report, with findings establishing a national baseline and providing evidence to inform policies and programmes.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Lebanon's political and security environment remains fragile, amid unresolved conflict with Israel. Persistent Israeli military operations across southern Lebanon have caused civilian casualties, infrastructure damage, and disruption to livelihoods and essential services. Since the renewed escalation on 2 March 2026, Israeli military operations have resulted in 4,389 deaths and more than 12,424 injuries as of end-October 2026.

• Despite increasing returns, Lebanon’s humanitarian situation remains critical. By end of October, 965,000 people had returned to their area of origin of whom 27 percent are still locally displaced within their governorate. Meanwhile, over 304,000 remained displaced and 11,200 stayed in shelters.

• The September 2026 Integrated Food Security Phase classification (IPC) analysis shows that 1.05 million people (21 percent of the analysed population) are experiencing acute food insecurity, with conditions projected to deteriorate further in 2027. Lebanese residents account for the largest share of the affected population, representing 65 percent (686,000 people) of those acute food insecure. Conflict-affected areas, in southern Lebanon, continue to face significant food security pressures. The situation is primarily driven by persistent economic hardship, high living costs, limited employment, and localized insecurity.

• The conflict has severely disrupted education, with 86 teachers killed or injured and 436 education facilities affected as of end of October 2026. Additionally, 101 schools were damaged or destroyed, while 57 public schools remain occupied as collective shelters, limiting access to education.

title: Operational Update - Central African Republic - July - September 2026
content: UNHCR's operations in the Central African Republic (CAR) are built on protection through presence, the cornerstone of the humanitarian response. Amid volatile security conditions and the spillover of the crisis in Sudan, UNHCR also remains ready to respond to emergencies. Durable solutions are another top priority supporting the voluntary, safe, and dignified return of Central African refugees, their sustainable reintegration, and their contribution to national development. Together with the Government of CAR and its partners, UNHCR provides protection and multisectoral assistance to internally displaced people (IDPs) and refugees, including Sudanese and Chadian refugees, while promoting durable solutions for Central Africans returning home. Its work is aligned with national priorities: the National Development Plan, the National Strategy for Durable Solutions and the Solutions Support Platform established under the 2022 Yaoundé Declaration.

title: The Bundibugyo Ebola Outbreak in Africa: Six-Month Situation and Response Report
content:
Executive summary

This report examines the Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak and the continental response from the declaration on 15 May 2026 to the evidence available for preparation of the six-month milestone on 15 November. It integrates pathogen and transmission knowledge, zoonotic origin and One Health, epidemiology, clinical care, operational performance, country experiences, research, financing, logistics, essential health services, social consequences and preparedness.

The principal finding is that substantial response capacity was mobilized, but persistent transmission and mortality indicate that this capacity did not consistently translate into sufficiently early detection, timely access to care, complete identification of transmission networks and reliable local service delivery in DRC. The introduction that began the outbreak also remains unexplained, so the risk of further spillover in the affected landscape persists independently of progress against human-to-human transmission.

Key findings that should guide the next phase

1. The burden remains overwhelmingly concentrated in the DRC. Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria provide distinct experiences of managing cross-border or travel-associated infection. Their outcomes should be assessed against their own case histories and observation periods. France’s imported case and medical evacuations to other countries belong in a separate international account so that the same patient is not counted twice.

2. Early growth was exceptional, but historical comparison requires matched definitions. The early reported burden substantially exceeded burden observed during the comparable early periods of major 2014 and 2018 Ebola epidemics, although direct quantitative comparison is constrained by differences in case categories included, uncertainties in disease onset and official detection and declaration, ascertainment and observation intervals. Historical comparisons should therefore preserve the original case classifications and reporting periods.

3. Contact tracing misses most new cases: Only 11% of confirmed cases (1,146 of 10,659 with onset from week 19 to week 45) came from the contact lists, against a target of 95%. The response found the other 89% outside those lists, which means many transmission links were identified too late to list and monitor the contacts. The daily contact follow-up [text continues beyond the visible page].

Five headline numbers in the analytical snapshot

By 8 November 2026, five countries had reported 11,021 confirmed cases and 5,358 deaths, a crude case-fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.6%.

The DRC carries almost all of this burden, with 10,990 cases and 5,354 deaths (CFR 48.7%). Uganda reported 20 cases and 2 deaths, Kenya 9 and 2, Nigeria 1 imported case and no deaths, and France 1 imported case and no deaths.

In the DRC, 67 health zones in eight provinces have reported at least one confirmed case, and 51 of 67 health zones reported a case in the last 21 days.

National notifications have held at about 460 to 480 confirmed cases a week since late September; the epidemic is a sustained plateau and not yet declining.

title: Afghanistan Emergency Situation Report Issue No. 69 | October 2026
content:
Highlights

WHO-supported health care facilities provided 117 607 outpatient consultations and distributed 131 medical kits, reaching more than 1.9 million beneficiaries. In addition, 498 health workers were trained across multiple specialized disciplines.

A total of 16 884 travellers were screened, strengthening early detection and cross-border disease surveillance.

Dengue fever cases increased nearly fivefold compared with the cases reported in September 2026, while a decline was recorded in all other diseases.

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Crisis in Mali - October 2026
content:
During October, Mali continued to face persistent instability and complex protection challenges, including the forced recruitment of young people, widespread displacement of communities, and gender-based violence.

While the reopening of transit routes into Léré marked a significant improvement in humanitarian access for relief operations, comprehensive rapid assessments revealed critical gaps in front-line health facilities. These included severe shortages of basic pharmaceutical supplies, prohibitive out-of-pocket medical expenses, and an acute deficit of trained healthcare workers.

In response to the escalating hostilities and growing humanitarian needs, UNFPA rapidly scaled up its emergency response, expanding access to life-saving assistance across key locations through fixed and mobile service delivery points. Supported by 37 deployed community midwives, integrated mobile teams conducted extensive outreach to displacement sites and facilitated referrals to health facilities across Léré, Niafunké, Tonka, Macina, San, and Gao. Through these coordinated efforts, UNFPA provided essential sexual and reproductive health services to 16,024 people and reached more than 11,290 people with gender-based violence risk mitigation, comprehensive care, and protection services during the month.

title: UNICEF Somalia Humanitarian Situation Report No.3, 1 July - 30 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Somalia's humanitarian needs remained high during the quarter, driven by drought, conflict, displacement, disease outbreaks and declining humanitarian assistance. An estimated 5.1 million people faced acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3+), while 1.92 million children were projected to suffer acute malnutrition between July 2026 and June 2027. About 75,000 displacement movements and over 1,400 conflict events were recorded.
  • UNICEF sustained lifesaving assistance across priority sectors, reaching 98,241 children with SAM treatment, 244,022 caregivers with IYCF counselling, 145,671 people with primary health care, and 286,006 people with safe water. Education support benefited 71,644 children, while 48,991 people accessed child protection services. Monthly cash transfers supported 13,493 vulnerable women, strengthening household resilience.
  • The 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal was 27 per cent funded (US$32 million) against US$121 million required, leaving a US$89 million gap. Underfunding continued to constrain service coverage, operational capacity and emergency preparedness for anticipated El Nino impacts.

title: WFP Sudan Country Brief - November 2026
content:
• In October, WFP assisted 3.4 million people, including 795,000 people in areas at Risk of Famine (RoF).

  • WFP distributed 17,000 mt of food and provided USD 11.1 million in cash-based transfers (CBT).

  • WFP reached 1.4 million people with GFA, 280,000 children and pregnant and breastfeeding women and girls (PBWGs) with nutrition support, 200,000 students with school feeding activities and 18,000 people through resilience and livelihoods activities.

  • In October, WFP made significant gains; in reaching previously difficult-to-access areas, providing in-kind food assistance to 170,000 people in East Darfur and 48,000 in West Kordofan.

  • While funding constraints remain the primary obstacle for implementation of WFP operations, administrative approvals, and logistics constraints continued to impede operations.

  • Fuel shortages and power disruptions also affected transport, silo operations, agricultural activities and programme delivery this month.

title: Climate Watch Advisory: The Evolving Dry Conditions in the Northern Parts of Eastern Africa - Issued 21 October 2026
content: Below-normal rainfall in the last JJAS season in the northern parts of the region has contributed to the persistent dry signal across the northern sector of the Eastern Africa region from May through September, affecting Eritrea, Ethiopia, Somalia, South Sudan, and Sudan. Analysis of the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) for the July-September period indicates that these dry conditions extend southwards into parts of Uganda, western Kenya and northwestern Tanzania. Consistent with these rainfall deficits, environmental monitoring products show widespread soil moisture deficits, vegetation stress, or a combination of both across the affected areas (Figure1). Consequently, alert levels have increased, signaling an elevated risk of adverse impacts on agricultural production, pasture availability, water resources, and pastoral livelihoods, especially in Sudan, northern Ethiopia, and parts of Eritrea.

title: Doo Tha Htoo District Situation Update: Burma Army arbitrary arrests and extortion, domestic violence, drug issues, education difficulties, and healthcare challenges in Maw Sa Ko Township (January 2025 to May 2026)
content: This Situation Update describes events occurring in Maw Sa Ko (Paung) Township, Doo Tha Htoo (Thaton) District, during the period between January 2025 and May 2026. In several instances, villagers faced arbitrary arrest and extortion. On 31 January 2025, a 13-year-old boy and a 17-year-old boy from Zy--- village, Aye Waing village tract, were arbitrary arrested by militia soldiers under the control of the Burma Army on a road in Zy--- village, before being released the following day for a payment 2,500,000 kyats (1,190.48 USD) each. On 2 June 2025, the Burma Army arrested two villagers from Kyet Tu Way Thaung village tract and Thel Aay village tract, then demanded 2,000,000 kyats (952.38 USD) each for their release. On 24 November 2025, two villagers, from Jn--- village, Sakhangyi village tract, were arbitrarily arrested by two Burma Army soldiers. They were threatened with forced recruitment and had to pay 2,500,000 kyats (1,190.48 USD) each in exchange for their release. Then in 2025, exact date unknown, a 33-year-old from Tt--- village, Zakhangyi village tract, and a 27-year-old from Rk--- village, Kyet Tu Yway Thaung village tract, were arrested by Burma Army soldiers near a tollgate on the YangonMawlamyine Road. The Burma Army demanded 2,000,000 kyats (952.38 USD) each for their release. Between April to June 2026, domestic violence also occurred in Maw Sa Ko Township, with several reported cases that were handled locally by village leaders. The township additionally faced drug issues. On 27 May 2026, Karen National Union (KNU) township security arrested a 53-year-old man at Jv--- River, Vl--- village, Kyet Tu Yway Thaung village tract, with 3,800 pills of WY amphetamine. Meanwhile, all schools in the township are administered by the Burma military regime. Because the area is a mixedcontrol area, Karen Education and Cultural Department (KECD) schools could not be established yet. So, to implement the KECD curriculum in the township, 32 students were given support to study at a KECD high school in Thaton Township, Doo Tha Htoo District. Finally, in Maw Sa Ko Township, villagers mainly went to hospitals and clinics run by the Burma military regime for medical treatment. In 2026, after becoming aware of Karen Department of Health and Welfare (KDHW) health workers, some villagers started seeking treatment from them. However, it was still challenging for the health workers to provide healthcare regularly in the area.1

title: LOCAL Alert 001: Cyclone Akva​n - Third Cyclone in 24 Days - Pre-landfall update as of 18 November 2026, 1:30 pm IST · Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and South Odisha
content:
OVERVIEW

Severe Cyclonic Storm Akvan lay about 610 km south-southeast of Visakhapatnam at 5:30 am on 18 November, moving north-northwest at only about 3 km/h. It is forecast to cross the Andhra Pradesh-Yanam coast between Nellore and Visakhapatnam around noon on 20 November, with winds of 100-110 km/h gusting to 120 km/h; earlier bulletins had expected a very severe cyclonic storm with winds of 145 km/h. Akvan is the third cyclone to strike this coast in 24 days, after Arnab (28 October) and Murasu (3 November). All 10 districts on red or orange alert were hit by those storms, seven of them by both.

title: Cameroon: North-West and South-West Situation Report No.87, July to September 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • More than 1,600 protection incidents recorded in the North-West and South-West regions.
  • Nearly 900 people displaced in the North-West and South-West regions due to violence and insecurity.
  • More than 4,000 people affected by floods and landslides, with about 500 displaced and five deaths reported.
  • Four improvised explosive devices incidents recorded in the North-West region.
  • A total of 736 children with severe acute malnutrition received life-saving treatment in partner-supported treatment centres.

SITUATION OVERVIEW / HUMANITARIAN ACCESS

During the reporting period July-September 2026, the humanitarian situation in Cameroon’s North-West and South-West (NWSW) regions remained fragile and deteriorated further amid continued clashes between State security forces (SSF) and non-State armed groups (NSAGs). Persistent insecurity, including kidnapping for ransom, arbitrary arrests, the proliferation of illegal checkpoints, extortion, and roadblocks, continued to restrict population movements, hinder access to basic services and livelihoods, and heighten protection risks for affected communities.

The situation remained volatile, with at least 11 improvised explosive devices (IED) incidents recorded during the reporting period, including 10 in the North-West and one in the South-West. While these attacks primarily targeted SSFs and their convoys, civilians remained at significant risk of injury or death from accidental explosions.

Attacks and threats against education intensified ahead of the 2026/2027 school year. NSAGs enforced school-related restrictions, imposed school levies in some areas, and increased intimidation of education personnel, including the abduction of five teachers in Wum (Menchum division, North-West). In September, armed actors also attacked a secondary school in the North-West, disrupting learning activities.

Humanitarian needs remained severe across the two regions, exacerbated by successive lockdowns imposed by NSAGs between 1 and 21 September. The measures restricted movement, disrupted education, livelihoods, and economic activities and limited access to essential services. Lockdown enforcement through threats and sporadic attacks resulted in civilian casualties in both regions and further affected already vulnerable communities.

Continued clashes between parties to the crisis triggered new population displacement and humanitarian needs across the North-West and South-West. In Momo division, an estimated 875 people (175 households) were displaced from Diku to Tikom during the reporting period with many families seeking refuge in nearby bushes. Heavy rainfall that caused flooding and landslides on 5 August affected over 4,157 people, displaced more than 500, caused five reported deaths, including a pregnant woman, and destroyed or damaged 16 houses infrastructure, livestock, and community water systems in Limbe (Fako division), Kumba (Meme division) in the South-West, and in Tinifoimbi Village (Boyo division) in the North-West. While many affected households have returned, those whose shelters were destroyed or damaged remain displaced and in need of assistance. Priority needs include shelter, food assistance, health, WASH, protection, education and livelihood support. In coordination with OCHA and area-based coordination co-chairs, humanitarian partners delivered multipurpose cash assistance, shelter support, psychosocial services, and gender-based violence prevention interventions across affected communities, in addition to the assistance delivered by authorities.

Humanitarian access remained constrained due to insecurity, prolonged lockdown and the presence of illegal checkpoints along key road corridors, including the Bamenda-Widikum axis in Momo division and the Bamenda-Ndop road. These restrictions significantly hindered population movements and limited the transportation of agricultural produce. The operational environment remained highly challenging and required continuous access negotiations amid a fragile, volatile, and rapidly evolving context.

title: West Bank Protection Cluster Snapshot | Protection Monitoring | Reporting Period 1 Aug – 30 Sept 2026
content:
INTRODUCTION

Findings from August–September 2026 highlight the combined impact of settler violence, movement restrictions, demolitions, and loss of land and property on the safety, livelihoods, and wellbeing of communities across the West Bank. The highest protection risk severity scores were recorded for attacks on civilians and civilian objects, including unlawful killings (58%); theft, extortion, forced eviction or destruction of personal property (58%); and restrictions on freedom of movement, siege and forced displacement (57%). These findings reflect continued threats to civilian safety, housing security, and access to essential services.

Qualitative findings from five Focus Group Discussions across Hebron, Ramallah, Jericho, and Jerusalem governorates highlight settler violence and lack of accountability as central concerns among participating communities. Some groups reported increasing attacks, while others described levels similar to the previous period. Communities reported physical harm, displacement, disrupted education, and persistent psychological distress, with children exposed to unsafe school journeys and young men, including community protection volunteers, facing heightened risks of assault and detention. Women and girls, older persons, and persons with disabilities face additional barriers to safe movement, access to support, and participation in community protection activities. Protection Committees and local networks continue to provide early warning, emergency support, documentation, and legal referrals, although limited resources and threats to responders constrain their efforts.

The Protection Monitoring System (PMS), a joint initiative led by the OPT Protection Cluster, systematically collects, analyzes, and disseminates information on protection risks through Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) and Focus Group Discussions (FGDs), ensuring that community perspectives remain central to the analysis. Building on monitoring undertaken since November 2025, this snapshot presents protection risk severity scores across monitored locations and highlights community-reported concerns, impacts, coping mechanisms, and capacities to inform coordinated protection response and advocacy.

title: Central African Republic BVD Readiness - DREF Operational Update (MDRCF034), 18 November 2026
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

17-05-2026

What happened, where and when?

Between 15 and 18 May 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) declared an outbreak of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) caused by the Bundibugyo strain as a major public health emergency. This declaration was rapidly echoed by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).

At that time, the outbreak mainly affected three provinces in the DRC, namely Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu. As of 18 June 2026, a total of 33 health zones had reported confirmed cases, distributed as follows:

21 out of 36 health zones (58.3%) in Ituri;
11 out of 34 health zones (32.4%) in North Kivu;
1 health zone in South Kivu.

These figures confirmed that Ituri Province remained the epicentre of the outbreak.

According to WHO data available on 18 June 2026, the DRC had recorded 896 confirmed EVD cases, including 208 deaths and 78 recoveries. Cross-border transmission had also been reported in Uganda, with 19 confirmed cases, including two deaths and seven recoveries.

Although the Central African Republic (CAR) had not reported any confirmed EVD cases at that time, the country remained at high risk of disease importation due to its proximity to the affected areas of the DRC. This outbreak, the seventeenth recorded in the DRC and the second associated with the Bundibugyo strain, had progressively expanded towards provinces located near the CAR border, notably Haut-Uélé. Available epidemiological information indicated a high likelihood of ongoing undetected transmission in this province, which serves as an important population movement corridor towards the border provinces of Bas-Uélé and South Ubangi.

Furthermore, several public health alerts had been reported in areas close to the CAR border, including:

The report of a death associated with a suspected viral haemorrhagic fever in Libenge Health Zone, South Ubangi Province, which hosts Central African refugees;
A report dated 18 June 2026 from the Chief Medical Officer of Yakoma Health Zone regarding a suspected EVD case in a locality bordering Ouango-Gambo Health District in CAR.

In this context, the combination of proximity to areas of probable transmission, intense cross-border population movements, repeated epidemiological alerts, and limited preparedness capacities fully justified the activation of a DREF preparedness operation. The operation aimed to anticipate and reduce the risk of EVD introduction and spread in CAR through proactive preparedness, community-based surveillance, and community engagement activities.

However, the epidemiological situation evolved in a concerning manner, with the outbreak progressively spreading to provinces that share a direct border with CAR. In August 2026, Bas-Uélé Province, which borders CAR, reported its first confirmed EVD case in Buta Health Zone, becoming the sixth affected province in the DRC. The confirmed case was linked to travel from Haut-Uélé Province, highlighting the persistent risk associated with population movements between affected areas and border districts in CAR.

As of 19 August 2026, the DRC had reported 5,208 confirmed cases and 2,476 deaths, compared to 896 cases and 208 deaths on 18 June 2026. In addition, 84 per cent of identified contacts were under follow-up. On the same date, another confirmed EVD case was reported in Viadana Health Zone, Bas-Uélé Province, in close proximity to the Haut-Mbomou, Mbomou, and Basse-Kotto health districts of the Central African Republic.

The progression of the outbreak is particularly alarming. While three provinces and 33 health zones were affected as of 18 June 2026, the situation had expanded to six provinces and 55 affected health zones by 19 August 2026. This continued geographical expansion brought the outbreak significantly closer to the CAR border and substantially increased the risk of virus introduction into the country.

Since the launch of the preparedness operation, sixty-four (64) suspected EVD cases have been reported and investigated in CAR. All laboratory test results returned negative for Ebola Virus Disease.

By the end of October 2026, the regional situation had deteriorated further. Most DRC provinces bordering CAR were affected by EVD, including Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, South Ubangi, and North Ubangi. Geographical proximity, combined with the strong historical and family ties between communities living along the Ubangi River, facilitates significant formal and informal cross-border population movements.

As of 25 October 2026, the epidemiological situation in the DRC reported:

10,060 cumulative cases;
4,887 deaths;
2,684 recoveries;
1,008 patients admitted to treatment centres;
a case fatality rate of 48.6%;
a contact tracing rate of 81.6%.

These cases were distributed across eight provinces and 66 health zones or health districts.

At the same time, the Central African Republic has progressively strengthened its preparedness capacity. The national preparedness level increased from 42 per cent at the beginning of the operation to 68 per cent during the latest assessment conducted at the end of August 2026. The 30-day acceleration plan validated in early October 2026 aims to raise this level to 95 per cent.

As part of this acceleration plan, the Incident Management System has been decentralized to bring coordination closer to the highest-risk regions and their border health districts. Efforts are underway to make Ebola Treatment Centres fully operational in Obo, Bangassou, the Bimbo University Teaching Hospital, and PK24. Surveillance at points of entry has been reinforced, as have risk communication and community engagement activities, under the leadership of the Minister of Health.

The Central African Red Cross (CRCA), which leads the Safe and Dignified Burials pillar, has trained fifteen teams of ten volunteers each to ensure adequate coverage of high-risk localities.

Finally, on 22 and 23 October 2026, CAR and the DRC met in Bangui for a cross-border coordination meeting aimed at strengthening information sharing, exchanging experiences, and improving joint preparedness measures to prevent and control any potential spread of the outbreak in health districts on both sides of the border.

title: Somalia Weekly Weather Forecast - Valid From 18 - 24 Nov 2026
content:
Review Summary:

  • Significant local rains in the south, little rain in the centre and north. During 10–16 November, Bualle recorded 159.9 mm, Balcad 115.0 mm and Awdheegle 88.4 mm, while most stations in Bay, Hiraan and the centre recorded little or no rain. In the north, Las Dacawo recorded 50.0 mm and Elafweyn 31.5 mm. Satellite estimates (IMERG, 11–17 November) indicate 30–55 mm over Lower Juba and parts of Middle Juba and Gedo.
  • By 16 November, 37 stations, 33 of them with a Deyr normal above 15 mm, had already received their full Deyr normal, including Baidoa (405.5 mm, 176% of the Deyr normal), Galkacyo (253.5 mm, 390%), Awdheegle (265.2 mm, 169%) and Bualle (240.9 mm, 148%), which passed its normal this week. Borama (16%), Burao (21%), Luuq (25%) and Mogadishu (27%) remain far below normal.
  • River levels are rising slightly on the upper Shabelle and the Juba but remain well below flood-risk levels. Belet Weyne rose from 2.90 m on 15 November to 3.76 m today, 2.74 m below its moderate flood-risk level. Jowhar (2.90 m) and Bulo Burti (2.30 m) are falling, and Dollow (2.86 m) and Luuq (2.78 m) are rising slowly.
  • Flood water in Jowhar district is receding. Satellite images show about 55 km² of flood water in Jowhar district, down from about 87 km² last week. Radio Ergo callers (5–11 November) reported flash floods that drowned livestock at Garadag in Sanaag and a death in stagnant flood water in Hirshabelle, while many callers in the south and centre welcomed the rains and said they had not seen the floods mentioned in the alerts.

title: Conflict Escalation in Yemen - Situation Report #12 (Reporting period: 11 – 17 November 2026 | Issued: 17 November 2026)
content:
Key Highlights

  • Casualties continue, with Marib and Lahj carrying the burden. The HEOC count reached 12,779 (10,519 injured, 2,260 deaths) by 16 November, +1,024 in eight days. The daily average fell to ~128 from ~225, but reporting was incomplete (58–92% a day, none for 9–10 November), so the figures are a minimum. Between 11 and 15 November, Marib reported 266 casualties and 49 deaths and Lahj 234 casualties; Al-Dhale’e still has no funded WHO-supported trauma deployment.
  • The front line is moving towards Aden. Front lines moved rapidly through Lahj and are approaching Aden, which hosts the main referral hospitals, the Health Emergency Operations Centre and the warehouse supplying the response. Further movement may change casualty flows and displacement, disrupt referral and supply routes, and require WHO and partners to adapt their operations.
  • Measles–rubella campaign reached 92.3% of target. MoPHP results show 883,896 children aged 6–59 months vaccinated and 741,713 given vitamin A (77.5%). Al-Mahrah (61%) and Socotra (78%) fell short and 73,300 children were not reached. WHO-supported teams vaccinated 6,007 displaced children in five IDP camps in Aden and Lahj.
  • Displacement continues to be at about 3,150 households a week. IOM DTM has recorded 347,321 people displaced since 1 August, including 18,780 in the past week, of whom 55% went to Lahj and 30% went to Taiz.
  • Cholera is falling in the five most-affected governorates, but a complex outbreak is growing in Tarim. Suspected cases fell from 638 (W40) to 321 (W45). Tarim (Hadramout Al-Wadi) has reported 172 cases of acute diarrhea since W43, 78 RDT-positive and 22 culture-confirmed, with both suspected food and water. A diarrhea treatment center is being set up.
  • Fuel and medical supplies are critically short in Taiz. Severe shortages of fuel, surgical supplies and anesthesia medicines are disrupting emergency services, including operating theatres and oxygen generation for intensive care units, and hospitals cannot sustain the continuous pressure. WHO delivered 19.6 MT of medicines and supplies to three facilities, and IRY and FMF plan to support two city hospitals.
  • Shortages are also reported across the front line. Health facilities in areas under the control of the de facto authorities are reported to be short of medical and surgical supplies. Alternative delivery routes and access negotiations are needed to reach hospitals on both sides.
  • The trauma referral pathway has critical gaps. Only four of the 35 planned trauma stabilization points are funded, none of them in Aden or in the part of Lahj towards which the front line is moving, and referral dispatch is unfunded. Burn cases are rising, yet hospitals can offer little beyond initial stabilization and wound dressing. Mental health and psychosocial support and rehabilitation remain the weakest links, leaving patients without continuity of care.
  • Funding remains the binding constraint. All 32 WHO-supported trauma deployments are funded only until January 2027. WHO’s third CERF request is being consolidated at US$2.4 million, including sites, mobile teams and supplies proposed by UNICEF and IOM.

title: WHO Weekly Situation Update on Ongoing Health Emergency Events in South Sudan - Week #46, Date: 9 – 15 Nov 2026
content:

title: Ecuador ENSO Floods 2026 - DREF Operational Update (MDREC032)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

01-11-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 1 November 2026, heavy and persistent rainfall associated with the ongoing El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon triggered flooding, river overflows, landslides and mudslides across several areas of Ecuador, causing damage to housing, livelihoods, road infrastructure, water systems, health facilities, educational establishments and other essential services. The impacts were particularly severe in the provinces of Esmeraldas, Guayas, El Oro, Galápagos, Santa Elena, Los Ríos, Manabí, Bolívar and Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas. As of 3 November 2026, more than 55,000 people and over 12,000 homes had been affected, while damage to transportation networks, water systems and basic services further increased humanitarian needs and access constraints in affected communities.

The emergency occurred within the context of a strengthening ENSO event. Oceanic and atmospheric monitoring conducted by the National ERFEN Committee identified elevated ocean heat content extending toward the eastern Pacific, positive sea-level anomalies of up to 45 cm in the central-eastern Pacific, 40 cm around the Galápagos Islands and 35 cm along the Ecuadorian coast, the propagation of warm Kelvin waves and a deepened thermocline. Sea surface temperature anomalies in the Niño 1+2 region reached up to +5.2°C above average, creating favourable conditions for above-normal rainfall and increasing the likelihood of severe hydrometeorological impacts across the country.

Anticipating these conditions, the Government of Ecuador progressively strengthened preparedness measures and, on 29 August 2026, the National Secretariat for Risk Management (SNGR) declared a nationwide Red Alert through Resolution No. SNGR-238-2026 due to the risk of flooding, landslides and other hydrometeorological hazards. Based on the forecasts and available lead time, the Ecuadorian Red Cross activated its ENSO National Contingency Plan and launched an Imminent DREF operation focused on anticipatory actions in Esmeraldas, Guayas, Los Ríos and Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas, including community preparedness, strengthening of Early Warning Systems, temporary protection of homes, safeguarding of water systems, risk communication and institutional readiness measures.

During October and early November, forecasted impacts progressively materialized and expanded geographically, resulting in recurrent flooding, river overflows, landslides and disruptions to essential services across multiple provinces. Assessments and official reports indicate that the scale, severity and duration of impacts now exceed the scope originally envisaged under the 45-day Imminent DREF operation, requiring a transition to a Response DREF. The operation will support affected populations through emergency response activities while maintaining anticipatory actions in at-risk communities where forecast impacts have not yet materialized.

According to forecasts issued by INAMHI, the ERFEN Committee and NOAA, which estimates a probability of more than 90 per cent that the current ENSO event could reach a very strong intensity, above-average rainfall is expected to persist during the coming months and into the 2026-2027 rainy season. Additional flooding, river overflows, landslides and damage to critical infrastructure and essential services remain likely, particularly in coastal provinces, low-lying areas and communities exposed to recurrent flooding and territorial isolation.

title: WFP Ukraine Country Brief, November 2026 [EN/UK]
content:
HIGHLIGHTS:

  • WFP assisted an estimated 504,300 people across its activities in Ukraine in October, including 298,500 people provided with emergency food and cash assistance in frontline areas.
  • As Russian forces continued attacks across Ukrainian frontline and urban areas, October saw multiple incidents of hostilities impacting WFP and cooperating partner staff, assets, and infrastructure.
  • WFP and UNICEF have begun trialing integrated logistics and programme solutions in Kharkiv region, including shared warehousing and joint frontline deliveries

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Security Situation:

  • Russian attacks increase intensity in targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure and focus on Kyiv city in multiple large-scale attacks, weakening the country and capital further as winter approaches.
  • In frontline and border areas, drone attacks against civilian vehicles, humanitarian movements and emergency services continued, including multiple instances of “double tap” strikes impacting emergency response, recovery and repair activities.
  • Repeated damage to critical infrastructure across central, eastern, southern and western regions of Ukraine is increasingly affecting the reliability of services supporting humanitarian operations beyond the immediate frontline.

WFP Impact:

  • The number of armed conflict incidents in Ukraine involving WFP or WFP cooperating partners this year (January – October) is already 81 percent higher than in 2025.
  • On 14 October, a WFP cooperating partner staff member of a was killed in an airstrike in the city of Sloviansk (Donetsk region).
  • The attack came just one day after a cooperating partner warehouse was attacked in Barvinokve (Kharkiv region) on 13 October, injuring two people and leading to the loss of 23 mt of WFP food.
  • In two separate incidents, two trucks belonging to WFP-supported bakeries were attacked by drones in Kherson region on 19 October.
  • Deteriorating security conditions in eastern Ukraine are increasingly limiting the willingness and ability of commercial transporters and humanitarian partners to access frontline areas. As such, WFP is increasingly leveraging its own delivery capacity to sustain humanitarian supply lines in frontline areas.

title: UNHCR Ukraine Operation Factsheet: Cash Assistance - Q3 2026
content:
POST DISTRIBUTION MONITORING: CASH ASSISTANCE

As part of its accountability to affected people, UNHCR consistently conducts monitoring exercises during and after service delivery. The post-distribution monitoring (PDM) of UNHCR’s Multi-Purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA) programme in 2025 confirms the relevance, effectiveness and impact of cash assistance in helping conflict-affected households meet their most urgent needs. Key findings from the PDM report include:

  • Contributes to protection by improving overall living conditions & wellbeing: 57% of recipients reported improved living conditions following receipt of assistance, while 62% reported reduced stress levels.
  • Preferred modality: Recipients overwhelmingly preferred cash assistance, with 83% preferring cash only and a further 15% preferring a combination of cash and in-kind support. Only 1% preferred in-kind assistance alone.
  • Meets identified needs: Cash assistance enabled households to cover essential needs that otherwise would have remained unmet, including utility bills, rent, clothing, shelter-related expenses, as well as food and healthcare costs.
  • Cash assistance delivered in a safe, accessible, accountable, & participatory manner: 96% of recipients reported satisfaction with the assistance process, 96% experienced no difficulties during registration or enrolment, and 98% felt safe receiving, keeping and spending the assistance. • Market resilience: In almost all cases (96%), recipients reported that the goods and services they needed were available in local markets, while 88% reported access to quality goods and services.

title: Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo | Kenya | Nigeria Weekly External Situation Report 27, Data as of 15 November 2026
content:
Event description

The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues at a high and sustained level of transmission. During epidemiological week 46 (9 – 15 November 2026), 442 confirmed cases and 239 confirmed deaths were reported, compared with 458 cases and 228 deaths in week 45; the national seven-day average has remained between 62 and 65 cases per day, and a new health zone, Watsa in Haut-Uélé, reported its first confirmed cases. Over three epidemiological weeks (weeks 44 – 46 compared with weeks 41 – 43), reported cases decreased by 6.7% and deaths by 4.6%, with a decline in Ituri partly offset by continued intense transmission in Nord-Kivu, where Beni remains the health zone with the most cases, and by rising incidence in Mangala, Mambasa and Mutwanga. Deaths in treatment centres increased in week 46 and the proportion of deaths occurring in the community fell to 59% (142 of 239), its lowest weekly level since August. In Kenya, the last patient was discharged on 11 November, and all contacts have completed their follow-up; the 42-day countdown is under way, and the event has not yet been declared over. In Nigeria, all 62 contacts completed their 21-day follow-up on 13 November and no secondary case was identified; surveillance continues in both countries. Additionally, Nigeria started the 42 days countdown on 27 Oct after the case was medically evacuated to Switzerland on the 26 October 2026.

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, insecurity in Beni, Mabalako and Bafwasende, strikes over unpaid salaries in several provinces and community resistance to safe burials continue to constrain surveillance and response operations.

title: South Sudan MVD Readiness - DREF Final Report (MDRSS018)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

23-12-2025

What happened, where and when?

The Marburg Virus Disease (MVD) outbreak was declared in Ethiopia on 14 November 2025, prompting heightened preparedness measures in neighboring South Sudan due to the risk of cross-border transmission through frequent population movement, trade, and pastoral migration. On 23 December 2025, three suspected MVD-related deaths were reported in Kapoeta East County, including two individuals with a recent travel history to the affected areas of Ethiopia and one suspected community-linked case. These alerts triggered increased preparedness and readiness efforts by the South Sudan Red Cross (SSRC) in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and partners.

The operation was implemented from 30 December 2025 to 28 February 2026 in the high-risk border counties of Akobo, Maiwut, Pibor, and Kapoeta East, which had been identified as priority locations because of their proximity to Ethiopia and high levels of cross-border movement. Preparedness activities included volunteer training, community-based surveillance, risk communication and community engagement (RCCE), infection prevention and control (IPC), hygiene promotion, and Safe and Dignified Burial (SDB) preparedness.

During implementation, the epidemiological situation remained stable and no confirmed MVD cases were reported in South Sudan. Investigations into suspected alerts, including those reported in Kapoeta East, did not result in any confirmed Marburg cases, and one suspected alert investigated during the operation tested negative. However, operational challenges affected implementation. In Akobo and Maiwut, insecurity and localized conflict restricted access to some communities and required volunteers and staff to relocate temporarily to safer locations while continuing awareness activities where feasible. In Pibor, cattle-raiding incidents disrupted planned interventions and limited access to some target areas. In Kapoeta East, poor road conditions and the remoteness of border communities presented logistical challenges, although SSRC successfully reached border locations, trained volunteers, and implemented preparedness activities.

By the end of the operation, no confirmed MVD cases had been detected in South Sudan. The outbreak situation in Ethiopia had improved, transmission had been brought under control, and preparedness capacities in the targeted counties had been strengthened through trained volunteers, community awareness, surveillance systems, IPC measures, and SDB readiness mechanisms.

title: Ukraine Crisis Response Situation | September 2026 Fact Sheet
content:
World Vision started working in Ukraine in March 2022 through 6 and now 3 active offices in Ukraine (Kyiv, Dnipro, Mykolaiv), which currently support aid efforts reaching conflict-affected people. While also supported Ukrainian refugees and host communities in Moldova, Romania, and Georgia. WV UCR in Moldova concluded its operations in June 2025 and transitioned to WV Romania registered Moldova Foundation.

World Vision’s Ukraine Crisis Response and its local partners have reached over 2.4 million people, including more than 1 million children, providing essential support through food, non-food items, cash assistance, protection and education interventions, livelihood, and mental health & psychosocial support programming.

In 2025, World Vision intentionally incorporated early recovery and economic development into its programming, expanding livelihood opportunities for affected families and creating new jobs.

Its microfinance arm, VisionFund, is operating in Ukraine in the field of medium- to long-term recovery and development via financing small and medium-sized businesses for further growth, opportunities to generate income and create new jobs.

Ukraine Crisis Response Goal

The Ukrainian children, refugees and IDPs, as well as the host communities in Ukraine, Moldova, Romania, and Georgia have the support to overcome the humanitarian consequences of the war crisis.

UCR Strategic Objectives

1 Early recovery and economic development opportunities are created for IDP and refugee households, as well as host communities for improved and self-reliant livelihood.

2 Children, their families and communities benefit from enhanced social protection mechanisms and education opportunities in Ukraine and host countries.

3 Basic needs of vulnerable children, families and communities affected by the war are met in Ukraine and host countries.

4 Equitable and complementary partnerships with national and local actors are encultured and promoted to enable them take stronger leadership role in delivering the humanitarian response and managing the transition to rehabilitation and development.

September 2026 in a glance:

  • 2,809 people reached inside Ukraine (989 families, incl.1,781 children, 838 women, 190 men):
  • 2,693 – by MHPSS Support;
  • 63 – by Cash Assistance;
  • 53 – by Livelihoods Activities.

title: WFP Tajikistan Country Brief, November 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP sponsored a high-level Government of Tajikistan delegation to China, as part of efforts to strengthen a sustainable, nationally owned school feeding programme.

• WFP and the World Bank convened a high-level meeting in Dushanbe to advance Tajikistan’s wheat flour fortification agenda, agreeing on priority actions for the 2027-2030 national roadmap.

• WFP supported disaster risk reduction awareness sessions and evacuation drills in 20 schools in Rasht and Tojikobod districts.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Tajikistan is a landlocked, mountainous country with a population of 10.27 million, growing at 2 percent yearly, the highest rate in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. Half of the population is under 25 years, and a quarter resides in cities (TAJSTAT, 2020).

• According to the Tajikistan Demographic and Health Survey (TDHS) 2023, stunting among children under five declined from 26 percent in 2012 to 14 percent in 2023, while wasting decreased from 10 percent in 2012 to 6 percent by 2017 and remained at 6 percent in 2023, marking a substantial improvement on nutrition outcomes over the past decade.

• Tajikistan’s economy remains strong, with GDP growth exceeding 8 percent in 2024 and early 2025, supported by remittances, services, and industry, while inflation remains low. However, the economy remains vulnerable to external shocks, with remittances accounting for nearly half of GDP and export performance remaining weak.

• Poverty declined from 20.4 percent in 2023 to 19.8 percent in 2024, driven by economic growth and remittances. Nonetheless, rural households remain vulnerable due to limited employment opportunities and exposure to climate and economic shocks.

title: NCDC Lassa Fever Situation Report Epi Week 44: 26th October – 1st November 2026
content:
Highlights

• In week 44, the number of new confirmed cases increased from 9 reported in epi week 43 of 2026 to 13. These were reported in Ondo, Bauchi, Edo, Taraba and Nasarawa States (Table 3).

• Cumulatively, 278 deaths have been reported with a Case Fatality Rate (CFR) of 23.4% which is higher than the CFR for the same period in 2025 (18.3%).

Of the 87% confirmed cases, Ondo reported 37%, Bauchi 23%, Taraba 12%, Edo 10% and Benue 5%.

• The predominant age group affected is 21-30 years (Range: 1 to 93 years, Median Age: 31 years). The male-to-female ratio for confirmed cases is 1:0.9 (Figure 4).

• The number of suspected and confirmed cases increased compared to that reported for the same period in 2025.

title: Vanuatu Pertussis Outbreak in Penama Province, Vanuatu: Situation Report 7 - 16-Nov-26
content:
DISEASE INFORMATION

Suspected case definition: A suspected case is any person with cough illness lasting >2 weeks, with at least one of the following symptoms; fits for coughing, OR; ‘whoop’ when breathing in, OR; vomiting after coughing fits.

Confirmed case definition: A confirmed case is a person who meets at least of the following criteria: Isolatin of Bordetella pertussis bacteria from a clinical specimen; OR a positive PCR test for pertussis; OR a coughing illness in person epidemiologically link by time, person, place to a laboratory-confirmed case.

Mode of transmission: Spread from person to person through respiratory droplets produced when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Outbreak Threshold: Two epidemilogically linked cases occuring within one week.

title: Hait Situation Report October 2026
content: Haiti’s humanitarian situation remained marked by largescale displacement and persistent protection concerns in October 2026. New incidents of armed violence continued to trigger significant population movements, particularly in Artibonite Department, where violence displaced more than 13,900 people according to IOM DTM. The majority of individuals sought refuge with host families, while others relocated to displacement sites. This geographic spread of violence beyond Port-au-Prince into rural and peripheral areas is contributing to growing displacement pressures and deepening humanitarian needs across affected departments. Although sustained multisectoral needs outpaced available capacities in many locations, IOM and partners continued to deliver life-saving assistance, including shelter, WASH, health, protection and site management support, while advancing recovery and stabilization efforts where conditions permitted.

title: Afghanistan: Humanitarian Update, October 2026
content:
Funding shortfalls threaten winter response in Afghanistan

As temperatures begin to fall across Afghanistan, humanitarian partners are ramping up winter preparedness amid significant funding constraints. Aid organizations are pre-positioning supplies to enable them to deliver assistance before access to remote communities becomes more challenging. With needs expected to remain high, the humanitarian response enters the winter season facing a substantial funding gap, raising concerns about being able to reach all those in need and forcing difficult choices about how the limited resources are prioritized.

The 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan requires US$1.71 billion to provide life-saving assistance and protection across Afghanistan. However, as of October, only $550 million has been received through the Plan, meaning 68 per cent of funding requirements remain unmet. This shortfall threatens efforts to support vulnerable communities during one of the most challenging seasons of the year.

Winter often brings heightened humanitarian risks across Afghanistan. In many provinces, heavy snowfall and freezing temperatures can isolate communities, disrupt transportation routes and limit access to markets, health facilities and other essential services. For households already struggling with poverty, food insecurity, climate-related shocks and limited livelihood opportunities, the cold season brings additional pressure as families seek to secure food, heating fuel, warm clothing and adequate shelter.

As winter approaches, many vulnerable families are expected to face increasing pressure as food prices, heating costs and other seasonal expenses rise while livelihood opportunities decline. Yet several critical sectors remain significantly underfunded.

Food Security and Agriculture, the largest sector in the humanitarian response, has received only 18.2 per cent of its funding requirements despite continued concerns over food insecurity across the country. As winter conditions reduce income-generating opportunities and increase household expenditure on food, fuel and other essentials, many families are likely to face greater difficulties in meeting their basic needs.

Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items cluster, which provides vulnerable households with shelter support, essential household items and winter assistance, has received only 15.1 per cent of the funding required. Water, Sanitation and Hygiene programmes are similarly underfunded, with just 16.6 per cent of requirements met, while Nutrition activities have received 16.3 per cent. Health is funded at 45.4 per cent, leaving significant gaps in essential services, particularly as winter conditions increase the risk of respiratory infections and other seasonal illnesses.

Together, these funding shortfalls risk limiting access to food, shelter, health care, safe water and nutrition support during one of the most challenging periods of the year, potentially leaving vulnerable households with fewer options to cope.

title: IOM Yemen Dispatch Situation Overview September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

Yemen’s security and humanitarian situation worsened significantly throughout September, driven by the continued spread of ground fighting following August’s violent escalations. Ground hostilities expanded rapidly across southwestern fronts, with Ansar Allah (AA) forces intensifying offensives in Ta’iz and Lahj as they attempted to consolidate gains on the West Coast by securing the overlooking mountains. The fighting triggered a massive surge in displacement, forcing over 160,140 individuals to flee their homes, particularly from the Maqbanah, Jabal Habashi, and Al Ma’afer districts in Ta’iz. Vital supply lines, including the crucial road linking Mokha to Ta’iz City, were severely disrupted and cut off, stranding communities and impacting humanitarian access. The AA forces claimed to have targeted several sites in Riyadh and the Aramco facilities in Yanbu, a Saudi Red Sea port, with missiles and drones. Saudi Arabia requested air defenses for critical facilities from Egypt, France, Pakistan, and the UK. French President Emmanuel Macron said France would send military assets to help protect Yanbu following the attack, as the concerns over maritime security and global oil prices grew. Saudi Arabia also reportedly urged the Government of Yemen (GoY) to call for a general mobilization, which was announced in a speech marking the anniversary of the September 26 Revolution. On the other side, in a move to capitalize on its capture of the Bab al-Mandeb and the West Coast, the AA-affiliated Red Sea Ports and Tax Customs Authorities announced reductions in vessel and container fees and port taxes, effective 1 October. The sharp escalation in violence severely strained Yemen’s already compromised health infrastructure, with hospitals in Ta’iz, Ma’rib, and Hadramaut overwhelmed by casualties. Major health centers were forced to suspend non-emergency care—such as maternity and obstetrics services—to reallocate scarce beds and medical personnel toward trauma management. The cholera epidemic maintained a strong hold across southern and western governorates, with transmission exacerbated by population displacement and damaged water and sanitation infrastructure. Abyan and Lahj continued to report the highest concentration of suspected cases, while newly displaced clusters in Ta’iz and Aden saw rising incidence rates. According to the IPC, nearly five million people faced crisis levels of hunger or worse in government-controlled areas between March and May, including 1.4 million in emergency conditions, and it has been observed that food security has significantly deteriorated since the escalation began. Wheat flour prices increased by 10 per cent in parts of Ta’iz as of late September, while traders estimate wheat stocks will cover only about two months of demand. At the UN General Assembly, 80 countries supported a statement condemning “the Houthis’ decision to resume the conflict in Yemen, their continuous strikes on Saudi Arabia, and their reckless attacks on the Red Sea.” UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg met with AA negotiators in Muscat to avoid further escalation and held talks in Cairo with the regional powers, including Egypt and the League of Arab States.

title: IOM Yemen Dispatch October 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

Yemen’s security and humanitarian crisis worsened in October with the expanding ground offensives, intensifying cross-border air strikes, and severe strains on already fragile structures for essential services such as healthcare. Ansar Allah (AA) forces sustained their multi-axis offensives across southwestern fronts, continuing heavy assaults on the key frontlines in Taiz while launching multiple strikes at strategic structures including the Presidential Palace and International Airport in Aden. This led to large-scale movements, driving the cumulative number of newly displaced individuals to over 300,000 since June. Taiz became the main frontline and humanitarian concern when AA forces captured Al-Turbah and AsSafiyah, cutting the main Taiz–Aden Road and effectively encircling Taiz City. Key commercial and humanitarian transport corridors remained blocked or compromised, with severe access restrictions critically isolating the population in Taiz. AA forces expanded long-range ballistic missile and drone strikes against the International Airports, oil infrastructures, and military installations across Saudi Arabia, and Saudi-led coalition forces alongside the Government of Yemen (GoY) also intensified air strikes against key AA positions in Yemen. As of 27 October, OHCHR had documented 263 civilian casualties, including 67 people killed. Children accounted for 97 of the casualties and about half of those killed. With the surge in conflict casualties, major referral hospitals across Taiz, Lahj, Marib, and Hadramawt faced severe shortages of basic medical supplies, fuel, and medical oxygen, and were forced to suspend routine and elective care to prioritize trauma operations. The health emergency was compounded by damaged water treatment systems and overcrowded, unsanitary conditions in displacement sites across the top concentrated governorates such as Lahj, Abyan, Taiz, and Aden. Food security exacerbated as staple commodities and fuel prices increased steeply with the continuing supply chain blockades and worsening access situation. Depleted humanitarian stockpiles and severe underfunding raise concerns of acute malnutrition cases increasing, as estimated 5.4 million people in GoY-controlled areas are expected to be in IPC Phase 3 or worse food insecurity in the final quarter of the year. Both GoY and AA raised fuel prices in their respective areas of control in the last week of October, with official price of gasoline ranging between YR 570 per liter (AA-controlled area, 20% increase since midSeptember), YR 1,700 per liter (GoY-controlled area), and over YR 2,500 per liter in Taiz. The citizens are forced to purchase fuel in the black market, where petrol prices skyrocketed to over YR 150,000 for a 20-liter can, as most gas stations have shut down. Water production in Taiz city has fallen by about half due to the critical shortage of fuel.

content:

Russia is targeting Ukrainian healthcare facilities and workers ahead of winter while Ukraine targets Russian oil infrastructure.
