Strikes on three medical facilities in Kharkiv caused the highest number of casualties. At least 73 people were injured or are suffering acute stress reactions, and 226 patients were relocated. The latest attacks come amid a broader increase in attacks on healthcare facilities and healthcare workers, particularly in front line regions where health services have already been compromised by years of war. ACLED records an all-time high of 63 attacks against healthcare facilities and workers in October, up from 50 events in September. The attacks are likely to continue in November as Russia intensifies its campaign against critical infrastructure and services ahead of winter.

title: South Sudan - Concept of Operations, November 2026
content:
Summary

Humanitarian logistics operations in South Sudan continue to face significant access constraints driven by inadequate road infrastructure, seasonal flooding, insecurity and deterioration of key supply routes. Renewed conflict and localized insecurity further disrupt humanitarian supply chains, while much of the road network remains unpaved and highly vulnerable to seasonal deterioration. During the rainy season, critical routes frequently become impassable, resulting in delivery delays, higher transport costs and increased reliance on costlier alternative transport modalities. These constraints are particularly acute in Jonglei, Unity and Upper Nile, where poor road conditions, flooding and insecurity continue to restrict last-mile delivery to vulnerable and hard-to-reach communities. Despite ongoing improvements by humanitarian, government and private-sector actors, significant access gaps persist, underscoring the need for sustained donor investment in early prepositioning, coordinated access planning, critical route rehabilitation and maintenance, and common logistics services to improve cost-efficiency, reduce supply disruptions and ensure timely delivery of life-saving assistance.

title: UNHCR Ukraine Operational Update - 18 November 2026
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT & HIGHLIGHTS:

• Throughout October, the Russian Federation (RF) continued large-scale aerial attacks across Ukraine, increasingly targeting energy and other critical infrastructure as temperatures dropped and the winter season approached. Repeated attacks damaged energy facilities and disrupted electricity and water provision and other essential services, increasing risks for civilians during the cold season, particularly older people and persons with reduced mobility. According to the UN HRMMU, at least 372 civilians were killed and 1,981 injured in October 2026.

• Humanitarian operations are increasingly facing security challenges, with at least seven incidents affecting UNHCR partners while implementing UNHCR’s programmes in October. These included strikes impacting humanitarian personnel and operations, damage to humanitarian vehicles and partners’ premises, and repeated damage to interim evacuation points. While no fatalities were reported among UNHCR or partner personnel, the incidents underscore the volatile operational environment and continued risks to humanitarian activities.

• UNHCR supported the working visit of the delegation of the Ministry of Social Policy, Family and Unity of Ukraine (MoSP) to participate in the 77th session of the UNHCR Executive Committee (ExCom). Speaking at the ExCom session, Minister Uliutin underscored the importance of international humanitarian support to Ukraine, protection of internally displaced people (IDP) and investment in long-term solutions.

• In the fifth year since the start of the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and more than 12 years since the war began, UNHCR’s pro gramme in Ukraine increasingly aims to help war-affected people and displaced people to find durable solutions, particularly through housing and strategic protection advocacy.

title: Yemen - Alert: A prolonged, tightened siege would likely lead to Famine (IPC Phase 5) in Ta’izz City (November 17, 2026)
content:
FEWS NET assesses a credible risk of Famine (IPC Phase 5) in Ta’izz City starting during February-May 2027 in the event of prolonged and tightened siege conditions. Since July, conflict in Yemen has escalated into a high-intensity, multi-front war marked by fluid battle lines, localized territorial shifts, and deepening regional involvement, with Ta’izz and Lahij governorates emerging as the epicenter of fighting (Figure 1). On October 4, the Sana’a-based authorities (SBA) captured the last major road linking Ta’izz City to government-held areas, effectively enclosing the city under a de facto siege. An estimated 600,000-750,000 people, many already displaced to the city from other locations, face worsening shortages of food, fuel, cooking gas, and water. Under the most likely scenario, limited quantities of food and other essentials will likely continue to be smuggled into the city via small mountain roads, sustaining Emergency (IPC Phase 4) and Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) outcomes. However, if fighting for control of the city persists for several months or longer and if siege conditions tighten – further restricting already limited food supply inflows and generating price spikes that render food increasingly unaffordable – then extreme food deprivation would likely drive acute malnutrition and hunger-related mortality above the Famine (IPC Phase 5) thresholds.

Prior to the siege, residents of Ta’izz City had already depleted much of their coping capacity after more than a decade of sustained conflict and economic contraction. Competition for limited informal labor opportunities and macroeconomic instability have placed substantial pressure on household budgets and resulted in widespread slight-to-moderate food consumption gaps over multiple years. Post-harvest food security data collected in late 2025 and analyzed in early 2026 indicated considerable food consumption deficits across the city’s three districts, even during a time of the year when seasonal improvements in food and income are typically observed as labor opportunities tied to agricultural value chains increase and prices decline modestly. At least 20 percent of surveyed households had a poor Food Consumption Score (FCS), while Household Hunger Scale (HHS) results indicated moderate to severe hunger among at least 20 percent of surveyed households, indicative of Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse. Even larger shares of the population reported using food consumption and livelihood coping strategies associated with Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse outcomes, such as reducing meal size and frequency, reducing health expenditures, sending children to work, and sending family members to eat elsewhere.

Household food deprivation likely became more widespread and severe as intensifying conflict coincided with the peak of the lean season in September, before the siege began in October. Although recent representative Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) survey data are unavailable for Ta’izz City, estimates modeled by the Yemen Nutrition Cluster using historical nutrition treatment admissions data suggest that GAM prevalence among children under five would likely remain within Critical levels (15-29.9 percent) prior to the siege. High levels of acute malnutrition are driven by a combination of inadequate food intake, poor water, sanitation, and hygiene conditions, suboptimal infant and young child feeding practices, and inadequate access to health and nutrition services, in addition to reduced household spending on healthcare to prioritize food purchases.

Under the most likely scenario, the siege of Ta’izz City is expected to persist in the near term but is not expected to be protracted. Limited quantities of food and other essentials are expected to continue entering the city through informal mountain routes, preventing a complete collapse in food availability while leaving markets severely disrupted. Prices will likely remain well above average and increasingly unaffordable due to constrained supply, the high costs of smuggling goods into the city, and falling household incomes. Given severely limited household purchasing power and coping capacity, Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes are expected to persist, with a rising portion of the worst-affected households in Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5). While available information suggests that current siege conditions are less restrictive than during the peak of the 2015 siege on Ta’izz City, households now have substantially fewer resources to withstand them. Interviews with multiple key informants indicate that severe food consumption deficits are already emerging among poor households, who are reducing meal size and frequency, prioritizing feeding children at the expense of adults, and selling off their few remaining assets to purchase food and other basic needs. Some poor households are reportedly scavenging from accumulating trash, while even middle- and better-off households are increasingly relying on dwindling, overstretched support from relatives and community networks. Worsening sanitation conditions due to the lapse of waste collection services, coupled with shortages of medicines and medical supplies, are expected to increase communicable disease risks and constrain treatment capacity at a time of year when disease incidence is already typically elevated following the rainy season. The interaction between worsening food consumption deficits and disease is likely to accelerate deterioration in nutritional status, particularly among children, pregnant and lactating women, and the elderly.

Under the credible alternative scenario, the siege would persist for several months or longer while restrictions on remaining supply routes progressively tighten, substantially reducing or effectively cutting off food inflows. Food shortages would become increasingly severe as traders become unwilling or unable to transport goods through active conflict zones and checkpoints. As existing stocks become depleted, remaining market supplies would become prohibitively expensive for poor households, while collapsing income-earning opportunities and the exhaustion of coping options would make it increasingly likely that at least 20 percent of the population would experience extreme food consumption deficits consistent with Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5). With modeled estimates already indicating Critical levels of acute malnutrition prior to the siege, sustained severe food deprivation, compounded by worsening disease exposure and increasingly limited access to healthcare and nutrition treatment, would likely drive GAM prevalence beyond the Famine (IPC Phase 5) threshold. The combined effects of severe malnutrition, disease, and diminished treatment capacity would be expected to drive hunger- and disease-related mortality beyond the Famine (IPC Phase 5) threshold.

Recommended citation: FEWS NET. Yemen Alert November 17, 2026: A prolonged, tightened siege would likely lead to Famine (IPC Phase 5) in Ta’izz City, 2026.

title: WFP Togo Country Brief, November 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• Despite improving economic conditions, refugees, IDPs and host communities affected by the Sahel crisis, together with climate-affected households, remain vulnerable to food insecurity and malnutrition, requiring sustained humanitarian and development support.

• WFP rolled out the training of 200 members of 30 school feeding complaints committees to strengthen protection, and safe community feedback.

• Continued investment in resilience, food systems, social protection, and climate adaptation is critical to protect recent gains and strengthen long-term food security. WFP shares the Government’s vision around resilience and welcomes investments made in strengthening food systems; social protection; and climate adaptation. As a trusted partner, WFP remains committed to supporting these approaches to ensure strengthened agricultural communities and sustainable food security across the country.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Togo has experienced relatively strong economic and agricultural performance in recent years, with real GDP growth over six percent since 2023, supported by public investments and policy measures.

• Favorable harvests and market supply have contributed to generally adequate food availability with staple food prices remaining below the previous year and five-year average in August 2026, supporting food access, including for vulnerable households.

• However, localized climate-related shocks such as land degradation, soil erosion and irregular rainfall continue to constrain agricultural productivity and undermine resilience in affected areas.

• Additionally, in the Savanes region, the spillover effects of the Sahel crisis have led to an influx of over 55,515 refugees and asylum seekers and more than 13,400 IDPs with an additional 3,169 people estimated to be awaiting registration, according to the latest governmental data, increasing pressure on markets, services, and natural resources in areas hosting large numbers of displaced populations.

• Against this backdrop, WFP supports the Government in addressing immediate needs while strengthening longer-term resilience through an integrated approach combining emergency assistance, resilience-building and national system strengthening under the Country Strategic Plan.

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Lebanon Crisis (9 October – 8 November 2026)
content:
The humanitarian situation in Lebanon remains fragile. Continued hostilities, movement restrictions and explosive ordnance contamination in southern Lebanon are limiting access to essential services and hindering safe returns. As of 28 October, 304,520 people remained internally displaced, 53 per cent of whom are women and girls.

Damage to health facilities, road closures and movement restrictions continue to limit access to care in parts of southern Lebanon. Three hospitals and 21 primary healthcare centres remain closed, while 17 hospitals have sustained damage.

Since the onset of the crisis on 2 March 2026, UNFPA has reached over 57,000 women and girls with sexual and reproductive health services and more than 56,500 people with gender-based violence prevention and response activities. UNFPA has supported 5,423 women to give birth safely in health facilities, and distributed dignity kits to nearly 37,350 women and adolescent girls.

title: WFP Benin Country Brief, November 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• Insecurity in northern Benin continues to drive population movements and increase requests from local authorities for WFP assistance, placing additional pressure on emergency response funding.

• In October, an estimated 10,341 new displaced populations (2,100 households) arrived in Kalalé, and WFP assisted 35,345 beneficiaries through USD 568,059 in cash assistance in the north.

• WFP provided financial and technical support for the Cadre Harmonisé analysis that covered 54 of 77 communes.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• In October, flooding affected several communities, particularly in Zou, rapid assessments are underway with humanitarian partners and local authorities for possible food assistance.

• Northern Benin is experiencing a rapid deterioration of food security, driven by escalating insecurity which drives up displacement and limits livelihood opportunities.

• The departments of Atacora, Alibori and Borgou host refugees and asylum seekers from Burkina Faso, Niger, Togo and Nigeria, as well as internally displaced persons (IDPs) fleeing violence.

• The insecurity risks and ongoing displacement in the northern and central regions of the country limit vulnerable population access to basic services and disrupts education, livelihoods, and community protection systems.

• WFP supported data collection for the Cadre Harmonise exercise. Updated results will provide an opportunity to analyze and classify current and projected food and nutrition insecurity across the country.

• Continued displacements due to insecurity, recent flooding-with damage to homes, agriculture and livelihoods-and the current Quelea birds infestation in the north are compounding needs for preparedness, targeting and resource mobilization.

title: UNICEF Panama Humanitarian Situation Report No. 7 (Earthquake), 1-13 November 2026
content:
Key Highlights

  • UNICEF and Global Brigades contributed to improving access to safe water for approximately 220 people displaced from Isla Cañas and relocated to La Pericada, through the connection to a potable water system, the installation of water storage facilities, and chlorination measures. In addition, training activities are being conducted on the operation and maintenance of water systems, hygiene promotion, and menstrual hygiene management. Concurrently, sanitation improvements have commenced in the Agua Buena settlement, including the construction of showers, latrines, and a septic tank with the support of local partners.
  • The Education in Emergencies (EiE) response continued to expand. As of 13 November, 5 of the 12 Temporary Learning Spaces (TLSs) were operational across Veraguas and Los Santos, reaching 391 students (52% girls) and 217 mothers, fathers, and caregivers. The remaining 7 TLSs are progressing through installation, teacher training, and preparatory activities to begin educational programming and psychosocial support services.
  • UNICEF and RET International trained 229 teachers, supervisors, and educational and administrative personnel (59% women) in Education in Emergencies and psychosocial support.
  • A total of 98 children and adolescents, along with 17 caregivers, are participating in recreational and psychosocial support activities in Child-Friendly Spaces established in four shelters across Veraguas and Los Santos.
  • A joint assessment conducted by UNICEF and Global Brigades at the Los Pozos Temporary Hospital identified priority needs to strengthen sanitation infrastructure associated with the expansion of temporary health services. As a result, support was agreed to enhance the wastewater treatment system through complementary solutions that will help ensure adequate sanitary conditions for patients, healthcare personnel, and communities served by the facility, which provides coverage to approximately 8,000 people.

title: Food Security Monitor - October 2026
content:
Summary

AGRA’s monthly Food Security Monitor serves as a vital tool for sharing timely data with key stakeholders, supporting informed, evidence-based decisions across the agricultural sector. Below are key highlights from the October 2026 Food Security Monitor edition:

Global Market Updates

  • Global food commodity prices eased in October 2026 but remained elevated compared with a year earlier, indicating that underlying price pressures persist despite short-term relief. The FAO Food Price Index fell 1.2% to 133.9 points, driven by declines in cereals, dairy and meat, while vegetable oils rose marginally and sugar surged 6.6%; overall food prices remained 5.9% above October 2025 but 16.4% below the March 2022 peak. Similarly, the International Grains Council Grains and Oilseeds Index declined 4.8% month-on-month, with wheat, maize, soybeans and barley all falling, but remained 8.8% above year-earlier levels. Rice was the notable exception, rising 4.0% during the month and 27.6% year-on-year, highlighting continued upward pressure in the rice market despite the broader easing in global grain and oilseed prices
  • Global fertilizer markets showed mixed but generally firm trends, with phosphate fertilizers and potash strengthening while urea prices eased. DAP, MAP and potash prices increased by 0.7%, 1.3% and 2.2% month-onmonth, respectively, whereas urea declined 2.0% to US$669/MT. Despite this monthly easing, urea remained 11.9% above its year-earlier level, the strongest annual increase among the fertilizers tracked, while DAP, MAP and potash were also higher year-on-year. Overall, fertilizer prices remain elevated, with phosphate and potash markets showing continued upward pressure and the nitrogen segment, particularly urea, remaining more volatile.
  • Fertilizer price trends across selected African markets remain highly divergent, with Rwanda experiencing the strongest and most persistent price pressures, including year-on-year increases of 40.7% for NPK and 67.1% for urea, while Uganda has seen a recent rebound despite generally weaker annual prices. In Southern Africa, Malawi and Mozambique continue to face elevated year-on-year fertilizer costs despite recent easing in some products, whereas Zambia has recorded modest monthly increases, but prices remain below six-month levels. West African markets appear comparatively softer, with Ghana recording particularly sharp declines in urea prices and Nigeria experiencing broader short- and medium-term price moderation. Overall, fertilizer affordability remains a significant concern in parts of East and Southern Africa, even as easing prices in several markets provide some relief.

Food Commodity Prices Updates

  • Maize prices exhibited mixed and divergent movements across the monitored regions between September and October in USD terms. In Eastern Africa, prices increased across all monitored markets, signaling broader upward price pressure across the region. South Sudan recorded the strongest increase (+13.0%), followed by Rwanda (+10.6%), Uganda (+8.3%), Ethiopia (+4.8%), Tanzania (+3.5%), and Kenya (+2.1%). South Sudan remained by far the highest-priced market at USD 1,137/MT, while Tanzania remained the lowest at USD 235/MT. Overall, the broadbased increases point to tightening maize availability and sustained regional demand following the earlier postharvest easing, with particularly pronounced pressures in South Sudan, Rwanda, and Uganda.
    In Southern Africa also, there is a general price increase, although the magnitude varied considerably across markets. In USD terms, Mozambique recorded a particularly sharp increase (+47.5%) from USD 316/MT to USD 466/MT, signaling significant short-term market pressure, while Malawi rose more moderately (+4.4%) and Zambia remained broadly stable. Local-currency trends similarly showed strong upward pressure in Mozambique (+47.5%), alongside increases in Zambia (+5.2%) and Malawi (+4.7%). Mozambique’s prices were also 44.6% above six-month and 17.1% above year-earlier levels, signaling sustained market tightening. In contrast, despite recent increases, Zambia remained 28.7% below six-month and 11.9% below year-earlier levels, while Malawi was still 18.2% lower year-on-year, indicating that recent upward movements have not fully reversed earlier price easing.
    Prices in West Africa exhibited considerable divergence with strong increases in Burkina Faso and Mali contrasting with declines in Nigeria and Niger. In USD terms, Burkina Faso recorded the largest increase (+17.0%), followed by Mali (+9.6%), while Nigeria (-7.5%), Niger (-4.2%), and Togo (-0.9%) declined and Ghana remained broadly stable (+0.7%). Local-currency trends reinforce the strong upward pressure in Mali, where several markets recorded double-digit monthly increases, while selected Burkina Faso markets also rose sharply. Conversely, Niger generally recorded declines, Nigeria fell by 5.8%, and Togo continued to experience broad-based easing. Yearon-year prices nevertheless remained below previous-year levels across many markets, suggesting that localized October increases have not fully reversed the broader regional price normalization.
  • Rice prices also showed mixed and divergent trends across regions between September and October in USD terms. In East Africa, movements were generally moderate: Tanzania (+1.2%, to USD 835/MT) and Kenya (+0.7%, to USD 1,380/MT) edged up, with Kenya remaining the highest-priced market, while Uganda (-7.0%, to USD 895/MT, due to currency depreciation), South Sudan (-4.1%) and Rwanda (-1.5%) declined. In Southern Africa, Mozambique recorded the sharpest increase (+9.9%, from USD 710/MT to USD 780/MT) as supplies tightened ahead of the lean season, and Malawi rose modestly (+1.1%, to USD 2,125/MT), remaining the highest-priced market at the official exchange rate, while Zambia fell by 8.5% (to USD 1,681/MT), reflecting currency depreciation. In West Africa, prices rose modestly in Mali (+4.6%), Niger (+3.0%), Burkina Faso (+1.6%) and Togo (+0.5%), reflecting poor production prospects and declining stocks in the Sahelian markets, while Nigeria recorded the sharpest decline (-10.6%, to USD 336/MT) amid good market supplies and Ghana was broadly stable (-0.2%, at USD 961/MT) and remained the highest-priced market.

Food Security Updates

  • Across East Africa, food insecurity is expected to remain severe through May 2027, driven by rainfall deficits and crop losses, conflict and displacement, high staple prices, declining household stocks, and constrained humanitarian assistance. Ethiopia faces worsening conditions in drought- and conflict-affected areas, with pockets of Emergency (IPC Phase 4), while South Sudan remains the region’s most acute crisis, with widespread Emergency outcomes, pockets of Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) and a continuing risk of Famine in some areas. In Kenya, 3.5–4.0 million people are expected to require assistance, although improving rainfall should support gradual recovery in many pastoral areas, while flooding remains a localized threat. Uganda is also expected to remain strained, particularly in Karamoja and refugee settlements, with assistance needs projected to peak at 3.0–3.49 million people in April–May amid poor harvests and high food prices. Overall, seasonal rainfall and harvests will provide some localized improvements, but these gains are likely to be uneven and temporary as conflict, climate shocks, weak purchasing power and reduced humanitarian support sustain high food assistance needs across the region.
  • In Southern Africa, food insecurity is expected to worsen through the 2026/27 lean season and into 2027, driven by declining household food stocks, weakening purchasing power, high food and transport costs, and increasingly adverse El Niño-related rainfall conditions. Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are projected across significant parts of Mozambique, Malawi, and Zimbabwe, while Stressed (IPC Phase 2) conditions are expected to expand across Zambia. In Mozambique, conflict and displacement further compound food insecurity in northern areas, while across Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe, and central and southern Mozambique, below-average and erratic rainfall is expected to constrain planting, crop development, agricultural labour opportunities, livestock production, and the 2027 harvest. Although current and early-season harvests are providing some temporary relief, these gains are expected to diminish as stocks fall and market dependence increases, with the full effects of El Niño likely to become more pronounced after May 2027 and potentially peak during the late-2027 to early-2028 lean season.
  • Across West Africa, food insecurity is expected to worsen into the 2027 lean season, particularly across conflictaffected parts of the central Sahel and northern Nigeria, where insecurity, displacement, poor or disrupted harvests, rainfall deficits, declining household stocks, weak livelihoods, and high food prices are increasing market dependence. The most severe conditions are projected in Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, and northeastern Nigeria, with Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) widespread in affected areas and pockets of Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) in Mali. In contrast, conditions are generally less severe in Côte d’Ivoire and Togo, where food insecurity remains more localized, although cross-border insecurity, refugee pressures, flooding, and weaker agricultural incomes are increasing vulnerability. Overall, seasonal harvests are providing temporary relief in several countries, but their benefits are expected to fade as stocks decline, with humanitarian food assistance needs rising and generally peaking between March and May 2027.

Update on El Niño conditions

  • By October 2026, El Niño had strengthened into a very strong event, but its food-security impacts varied considerably across Africa. The Greater Horn faced heightened flooding risks from above-average October– December rainfall, threatening crops, infrastructure, markets and humanitarian access, even as improved rainfall supported pasture and livestock in some areas. Conversely, Southern Africa and parts of unimodal East Africa faced delayed and below-average rainfall, high temperatures and growing risks to crop production, agricultural labour and livestock. West and Central Africa experienced more localized climatic impacts, with conflict, displacement and market disruptions remaining the dominant drivers of acute food insecurity.
  • The most severe food-security effects were expected to emerge from early 2027 onward, as poor rainfall reduces production, household stocks decline and dependence on increasingly expensive markets grows. Southern and unimodal East Africa face particularly elevated risks from January to June 2027, while flooding could cause more immediate disruptions in the Greater Horn. Across the continent, conflict and displacement are expected to magnify climate shocks, especially in Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, the Sahel, eastern DRC and northern Mozambique. Overall, the outlook points to rising humanitarian needs through 2027, with the severity ultimately determined by rainfall performance, harvest outcomes, staple-price trends, market functioning, humanitarian access and the scale and timeliness of national and international responses.

Food Trade Updates

  • Ethiopia has officially joined the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), enabling its financial institutions, businesses, and consumers to participate more efficiently in cross-border payments across Africa and strengthening the country’s integration into the continent’s financial and intra-African trade ecosystem. The National Bank of Ethiopia and PAPSS also announced that Addis Ababa will host PAPSS COWRY 2026 on 26–27 November, bringing together African and global payment leaders to advance continental payment connectivity, innovation, and economic integration.
  • Ghana became the first country to sign the Accra Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents, alongside 25 other countries, establishing a harmonised legal framework that allows cargo documents across road, rail, air and sea transport to serve as documents of title. The Convention aims to expand access to trade finance, particularly for SMEs, facilitate cross-border trade, strengthen supply chains and support trade digitalisation, while advancing AfCFTA objectives. Ghana has committed to early ratification, reviewing relevant domestic laws and piloting the new system with transport, customs and financial institutions ahead of implementation.

title: Ukraine - Concept of Operations, November 2026
content:
Background

As the war continues and the 5th year of the full-scale invasion is approaching, 10.8 million people in Ukraine continue to be in need of humanitarian assistance, with those living the near the frontline facing the most acute and lifethreating risks, as outlined in the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP). Since that day on 24 February 2022, the population is experiencing a steady escalation in the intensity of attacks, resulting in continued destruction and damage to the civilian infrastructure, interrupting critical services and supply chains. Recent frontline shifts prompted new displacements and evacuations. While the number of people in need dropped by 15% compared to last year, reduced funding and limited resources are challenging organisations’ capacity to respond to this evolving humanitarian crisis.

To support responding humanitarian organisations in their delivery of assistance to affected populations, the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) Cluster Approach was activated in Ukraine for Logistics on 3 March 2022.

title: WFP Philippines Country Brief, November 2026
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT
• Home to 116 million people, the Philippines has made significant progress in reducing poverty and improving food security, despite the impacts of climate shocks, inflationary pressures, and sporadic conflict.
• The Government is ramping up preparedness efforts for the very strong El Niño peaking at the end of 2026, with severe drought conditions forecasted nationwide through April 2027.
• In July 2026, the Philippines was designated an upper-middle income country. However, intensifying El Niño effects and the impact of the Middle East conflict have driven food price inflation to three-year highs, with vulnerable populations affected the most.
• While the poverty incidence dropped to 9.7 percent in 2025, stunting prevalence among Filipino children aged 0 to 5 years old increased from 23.6 percent in 2023 to 25.3 percent in 2025.

title: Vanuatu Dengue Outbreak Situation Report #16 (Efate, Santo, Tanna and Malekula Island)
content:
Suspected case definition: Any person with an acute fever illness that lasts more than 2 days with two or more of the following: anorexia and nausea; aches and pains; rash; low white blood cell count; tourniquet test positive; warning signs

Confirmed case definition: A suspected case with laboratory confirmation through: Isolation of dengue virus or detection of dengue-specific antigen or antibodies in tissue, blood, CSF or other body fluid by an advanced laboratory test.

Outbreak threshold: Four confirmed dengue cases reported within a single epidemiological week.

Circulating serotype: 16 samples were referred for confirmatory testing and serotyping. All 16 samples were confirmed as Dengue Virus Type 1 (DENV-1) for both Efate and Santo Island. Tanna Island serotype still pending.

title: WFP Lesotho Country Brief October 2026
content: In September, WFP strengthened Lesotho’s preparedness and resilience while sustaining essential assistance. WFP provided nutritious school meals to 48,485 children across more than 2,400 ECCD centres and assessed 391 smallholder farmers to strengthen local sourcing for home-grown school feeding. It supported government to advance shock-responsive social protection, impact-based forecasting and anticipatory action systems ahead of El Niño, while updating disaster risk reduction frameworks. WFP also targeted climate-vulnerable households for resilience support and completed field data collection to inform the scale-up of climate risk financing and agricultural resilience interventions.

title: WFP Nigeria Country Brief, October 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW
• The food security condition across conflict-affected areas remains fragile despite the onset of the harvest season in September. While household food stocks typically improve during this period, persistent insecurity continues to undermine farm yields, limiting the positive impact that seasonal harvests would ordinarily have on food availability and access.
• According to the National Bureau of Statistics, year-on-year food inflation reached 19.59 percent in September 2026, compared with 8.89 percent in January 2026. High food prices continue to erode purchasing power, and wide food consumption gaps are projected to persist among poor households, particularly internally displaced people.

title: WFP Afghanistan Country Brief, November 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW
The new IPC analysis has highlighted a mounting, unprecedented hunger crisis in Afghanistan.
The data projects that 19.2 million people (38% of the population) will face crisis levels of acute food insecurity or worse (IPC 3+) during the November - April lean season. This is an increase from 17.4 million projected for the same period a year earlier. An estimated five million of those who are acutely food insecure will be facing emergency levels of hunger (IPC 4), representing double the number projected for April - September 2026.
The malnutrition crisis is also escalating: an estimated 4 million children are expected to require treatment for acute malnutrition in 2027, a 10 percent increase compared to 2026. This includes nearly 1.1 million suffering from severe acute malnutrition. The number of pregnant and breastfeeding women requiring treatment is also projected to increase to 1 million.

title: Mozambique Health Cluster Bulletin October 2026
content:
1 Introduction

October marked an important step in restoring access to health services in areas affected by conflict and climate-related emergencies. During the month, three health facilities resumed operations, two in Cabo Delgado and one Niassa Provinces, restoring access to essential health services for vulnerable communities. While considerable progress has been achieved, significant challenges remain, including funding shortages, population displacement, and limited access to hard-to-reach areas. Continued collaboration among government institutions, partners and donors is essential to ensure that life-saving health services reach those most in need. We extend our appreciation to all Health Cluster partners for their dedication and commitment throughout the response.

title: Ukraine Cash Working Group: Accountability to Affected People (AAP) Package for Winter Group Cash Transfers in Ukraine
content:
The Winter Group Cash Transfers (GCT) AAP Package provides practical guidance and tools for humanitarian organizations and implementing partners to integrate Accountability to Affected People (AAP) into the design and implementation of Winter Group Cash Transfers

The plan is structured around three complementary pillars:

  1. Information provision: Ensure communities receive timely, clear, accessible, and consistent information about the purpose of Winter GCT, eligibility and selection processes, available assistance, implementation arrangements, and how to raise questions or concerns.
  2. Two-way communication: Establish and maintain accessible channels for communities to ask questions, share feedback, raise complaints, and report concerns throughout the program cycle. A Winter GCT Frequently Asked Questions document is provided to support hotline operators and frontline workers in addressing people's questions and concerns related to the program.
  3. Participation and inclusion: Enable communities to meaningfully contribute to identifying solutions to the winter-related needs, and how interventions are implemented and monitored. Particular attention should be given to ensuring that older people, people with disabilities, displaced people, women and other groups who may face barriers to participation are included in decision-making processes.

Partners are encouraged to use this AAP Package alongside the Winter GCT Operational Guidelines and accompanying community engagement tools to strengthen transparency, participation, inclusion and responsiveness throughout the program cycle.

title: Mozambique Health Cluster Bulletin September_2026
content:
1 Context Overview
Mozambique continues to face a complex humanitarian situation driven by the combined impacts of climate-related shocks and protracted conflict, with significant consequences for the health and well-being of vulnerable populations. In 2026, severe flooding in the central and southern provinces caused widespread displacement, damaged health infrastructure, and heightened the risk of waterborne disease outbreaks, disrupting access to and continuity of essential health services.
At the same time, insecurity in Cabo Delgado continues to trigger displacement and place additional pressure on already fragile health systems. Humanitarian needs remain acute, particularly among displaced populations, returnees, and host communities, requiring sustained support for primary health care, emergency medical services, mental health and psychosocial support, and outbreak prevention and response.
In response, Health Cluster partners have maintained a coordinated humanitarian effort to ensure the delivery of life-saving and essential health services. Interventions have focused on integrated approaches, including mobile health services, disease surveillance and outbreak response, sexual and reproductive health care, mental health support, and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) activities. Despite these efforts, considerable challenges remain, particularly related to humanitarian access, funding constraints, shortages of critical resources, and the need to further strengthen health information management, monitoring, and reporting systems.

title: Attacks on Health Care in the occupied Palestinian territory (16 - 31 October 2026)
content:
Data collected by Insecurity Insight shows that over 3,500 attacks on health care took place across the State of Palestine between 07 October 2023 and 15 October 2026. 95% of all incidents were attributed to Israeli forces. In Gaza, where 2,413 attacks on health care were recorded, health facilities were damaged 459 times, 785 health workers were killed and 399 arrested. In the West Bank, where 1,046 attacks on health care were recorded, health facilities were damaged 33 times, 13 health workers were killed and 203 arrested while ambulances and health workers were prevented from providing vital medical care to people in need over over 630 times.

In Gaza, at least 37 health facilities were damaged multiple times in IDF aircraft and drone strikes and violent raids. Kamal Adwan Hospital was reportedly damaged on 46 occasions, including once since the October 2025 ceasefire. Three other hospitals that sustained repeated damage - Ahli Arab, Al-Aqsa Martyrs and Al-Awda hospitals - were also reportedly damaged since the ceasefire. These incidents highlight the repeated damage sustained by health facilities across Gaza, disrupting the provision of health care and putting patients' access to treatment at risk.

title: Somalia: Emergency Trend Tracking: Quarterly Overview — Q3 (01 July – 30 September)
content:
OVERVIEW

The third quarter of 2026 (July–September) continued the Emergency Trend Tracking (ETT) series initiated in June 2026.
Throughout the full quarter, DTM teams collected data in five districts: Baidoa, Dayniile, Diinsoor, Doolow and Kahda.
Coverage was expanded to 8 additional districts between 26 July (Week 07) and 2 September (Week 12), namely Baki,
Borama, Bossaso, Burco, Caluula, Hargeysa, Qandala and Qardho.

During the reporting period, DTM teams recorded 68,469 new arrivals across 7,032 settlements (83% urban and 17% rural), including 5,598 IDP sites. Drought accounted for most new displacements (56%), followed by conflict (33%), evictions (9%), other reasons (1%), while floods and other natural hazards accounted for less than 1 per cent.

title: DTM Sudan Displacement and Return Snapshot
content:
OVERVIEW

DTM Sudan defines a returnee as a person who was previously displaced from their habitual residence within Sudan due to an event dating from 2003 onwards and has now voluntarily returned to the location of their habitual residence, irrespective of whether they have returned to their former residence or to another shelter type. DTM Sudan also collects data on individuals who returned to their locality or state of origin, but not their exact location of origin.
This map is for illustration purposes only. Names and boundaries do not imply official endorsement or acceptance by IOM.

By the end of October 2026, DTM recorded an estimated 8,594,507 internally displaced persons (IDPs) and 5,395,491 returned individuals across Sudan. IDPs were originally displaced from all 18 states in Sudan, and were recorded across 185 localities, across all 18 states. The total IDP population decreased by 26 per cent compared to the highest-ever recorded population of 11,585,384 IDPs, recorded in January 2025.
Compared to the previous month, the number of IDPs decreased across 6 states and increased across the other 12 states.

During October 2026, the number of IDPs in Blue Nile increased by six per cent from 417,714 IDPs to 443,494 IDPs, primarily in Ar Rusayris and Wad Al Mahi localities due to continued insecurity across the state. The number of IDPs also increased across Khartoum (4% increase, primarily in Karrari and Sharg An Neel localities), South Kordofan (1% increase),
Kassala (3% increase), Central Darfur (<1% increase), East Darfur (<1% increase), and West Darfur (<1% increase).

In terms of specific events triggering displacement in October 2026, field teams reported nine incidents in Blue Nile (5), North Darfur (3), and South Darfur (1). Of the nine incidents, seven were conflict-related incidents, while two events were reportedly related to fires that displaced an estimated 185 individuals. DTM field teams also reported increased movement reportedly linked to water shortages, poor rainfall, crop failures, and limited livelihood opportunities, particularly across North Darfur and South Darfur.

In addition, returned households were recorded across 84 localities across ten states in October 2026. The vast majority of returned individuals moved back to their habitual residence (93%). A minority returned to other locations near their locations of origin.4 The majority of returns were recorded in Khartoum (2,884,725 returned individuals) and Aj Jazirah (1,312,110 returned individuals). The majority (81%) of returnees moved back from internal displacement, while 19 per cent reportedly returned from abroad. The number of returns increased by two per cent compared to the previous month. This report represents data collected between 30 September and 27 October 2026. It includes extensive data on both IDP and returnee populations, including sections for displaced and returned individuals across each state in Sudan.

Corresponding datasets, with data on state, locality, and location levels, are available on the DTM-IOM website. For further information, see the DTM Sudan Interactive Displacement Dashboard.

title: Somalia Cholera Response - DREF Operation (MDRSO028)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

15-10-2026

What happened, where and when?

An outbreak of Acute Watery Diarrhoea (AWD) with laboratory-confirmed cholera is affecting Balibusle village in Jariiban District, Mudug Region, Puntland State of Somalia. The first alerts were raised by Somali Red Crescent Society (SRCS) Community-Based Surveillance volunteers between 26 and 29 September 2026, after an unusual increase in AWD cases was observed in the community. By 26 September, 27 cases and one death had been recorded, and the number of reported cases continued to rise, reaching 69 by 18 October 2026. Laboratory analysis confirmed the presence of Vibrio cholerae in stool samples, while water-quality testing by the Puntland Water Quality Laboratory found significant E. coli contamination in community water sources, pointing to unsafe water as the likely driver of the outbreak.

The outbreak is primarily affecting Balibusle and surrounding communities in Jariiban District, placing an estimated 70,018 people (11,670 households) at risk. The situation is particularly concerning due to limited access to safe water, inadequate sanitation conditions, and strained local health services. Seasonal rains are expected to further increase the risk of contamination and disease transmission, especially among vulnerable households that rely on shared water sources and have limited access to healthcare.

The trigger date is 15 October 2026, based on the outbreak report issued by the Puntland Ministry of Health, which confirmed the growing public health threat posed by the AWD/cholera outbreak in Jariiban District. The report, together with laboratory confirmation of cholera and evidence of contaminated water sources, highlighted the need for an urgent response. The Ministry of Health also called on humanitarian partners to support efforts to contain the outbreak and prevent further spread of the disease.

title: Tanzania | Hazard - Riverine Floods: Early Action Protocol Activation (EAP No.: EAP2022TZ01, Operation No.: MDRTZ041), 11th November 2026
content:
Activation Overview

The Tanzania Red Cross Society (TRCS), with technical and financial support from the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), has an approved Flood Early Action Protocol (EAP), MDRTZ041, covering the period 2025–2030. The protocol aims to reduce the anticipated impacts of flooding through timely implementation of forecast-based early actions before the occurrence of a flood event.

Tanzania experiences recurrent flooding, particularly during the Masika (long rains) and Vuli (short rains) seasons. Flooding poses significant risks to communities living in flood-prone areas, including loss of life, missing persons, injuries, disease outbreaks, displacement due to destruction of houses, loss of livelihoods and disruption of critical social services. The TRCS Flood EAP covers nine river basins: Wami-Ruvu, Internal Drainage Basin, Pangani, Lake Victoria, Lake Tanganyika, Rufiji, Rukwa, Lake Nyasa and Ruvuma. The protocol aims to assist approximately 120,000 people through planned early actions across four sectors: Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR), Health, Shelter and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH).

Forecast Monitoring and Trigger Assessment

The flood risk is monitored through the five-day severe weather Impact-Based Forecasts (IBF) issued by the Tanzania Meteorological Authority (TMA). The forecasts provide information on the likelihood and potential impact of severe weather, including heavy rainfall and associated flooding risks.
According to the approved TRCS Flood EAP, the trigger is reached when the five-day forecast indicates severe rainfall warnings (Orange) or major warnings (Red) in more than 10 administrative regions across more than three river basins for at least two consecutive days within the five-day forecast period, accompanied by advisories (Yellow) on at least two of the remaining days.

The five-day IBF issued by TMA on Wednesday, 11 November 2026, covering the period from 11 to 15 November 2026, indicated varying levels of heavy rainfall risk across several regions of Tanzania, as detailed below:

  • 11 November 2026 (Wednesday): No warning was issued across the country.
  • 12 November 2026 (Thursday): Advisories (Yellow) for heavy rainfall were issued over some areas of Geita, Mwanza, Shinyanga, Kigoma, Tabora and Katavi regions. The forecast indicated a medium likelihood and medium impact, with localized flooding expected in some areas.
  • 13 November 2026 (Friday): Warnings (Orange) for heavy rainfall were issued over some areas of Kagera, Geita, Mwanza, Shinyanga, Simiyu, Mara, Rukwa, Mbeya, Songwe, Kigoma, Tabora and Katavi regions. The forecast indicated a medium likelihood and high impact. Additional advisories (Yellow) were issued over some areas of Arusha, Manyara, Singida and Dodoma regions.
  • 14 November 2026 (Saturday): Warnings (Orange) for heavy rainfall continued over some areas of the same 12 regions: Kagera, Geita, Mwanza, Shinyanga, Simiyu, Mara, Rukwa, Mbeya, Songwe, Kigoma, Tabora and Katavi. The forecast indicated a medium likelihood and high impact. Additional advisories (Yellow) were issued over some areas of Arusha, Manyara and Singida regions.
  • 15 November 2026 (Sunday): No warning was issued across the country.

Trigger Achievement and Activation

The warnings issued for 13, and 14 November 2026 indicate that the condition of severe rainfall warnings across more than 10 administrative regions for at least two consecutive days was met. However, confirmation of the remaining trigger conditions, particularly advisories on at least two other days and coverage across more than three river basins, is necessary to establish full trigger achievement.

Upon confirmation that all agreed trigger conditions have been met, TRCS will initiate activation in accordance with the approved EAP procedures, in coordination with the Prime Minister's Office – Disaster Management Department (PMO-DMD) and relevant stakeholders. The EAP provides an expected lead time of one to five days between trigger achievement and the anticipated flood impact. This period allows TRCS and its partners to implement planned early actions before flooding occurs.

Expected Lead Time and Activation Arrangements

The approved TRCS Flood EAP provides an expected lead time of one to five days between trigger achievement and the anticipated flood impact. This period is intended to allow TRCS and relevant stakeholders to undertake planned early actions before flooding occurs.

The Anticipatory Action Coordinator at TRCS is responsible for monitoring the forecast information and coordinating the trigger assessment in collaboration with relevant technical stakeholders.

The Prime Minister's Office – Disaster Management Department (PMO-DMD) is the designated government coordinating agency. Coordination with TMA, PMO-DMD, local government authorities and other relevant stakeholders is essential to ensure timely assessment, verification and implementation of early actions in accordance with the approved EAP procedures.

Geographical Coverage and Duration of Early Actions

The geographical coverage of the early actions will be determined by the areas identified as being at risk through the triggering forecast and the geographical distribution of the affected river basins. The 12 regions identified in the TMA forecast will therefore be assessed against the nine river basins covered by the EAP to establish the specific regions, districts and communities eligible for early action interventions.

The early actions will be implemented within the one-to-five-day lead time provided by the EAP, focusing on preparedness, community mobilisation, risk communication, evacuation support and pre-positioning or distribution of essential supplies before the anticipated flood impact.

Planned Early Actions

In line with the approved EAP and the IFRC Planned Operation Matrix, the following early actions will be undertaken:

  • Dissemination of early warning information to at-risk communities to promote timely preparedness and protective actions.
  • Support for evacuation of vulnerable individuals and households to designated safe areas.
  • Public health awareness campaigns focusing on flood-related health risks, disease prevention and hygiene practices.
  • Distribution of water purification tablets, handwashing and hygiene kits, and jerry cans to support access to safe water and promote hygiene.
  • Community mobilisation for cleaning drainage systems, pruning trees and clearing bushes to reduce localised flood risks.
  • Distribution of tents at designated evacuation centres to provide temporary shelter for displaced and affected populations.

Implementation will be undertaken in coordination with PMO-DMD, local government authorities, relevant technical agencies and other humanitarian partners to ensure alignment with government-led disaster preparedness and response arrangements

Early Action Targeting

The TRCS Flood EAP aims to assist approximately 120,000 people across the four priority sectors of Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR), Health, Shelter and WASH.

The early actions will target communities and households located in flood-prone and high-risk areas identified through the TMA forecasts and trigger assessment. Particular attention will be given to individuals and households who are highly exposed to flooding and have limited capacity to prepare for and respond to its impacts.

Priority groups will include women, children, older persons, persons with disabilities, pregnant and breastfeeding women, chronically ill individuals, female-headed households, child-headed households and households with large numbers of dependants.

title: Argentina: NEA Flooding - DREF Operation (MDRAR026)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

03-11-2026

What happened, where and when?

Since 9 October 26, extraordinary rainfall has been recorded in the upper basin of the Paraná River, associated with the El Niño phenomenon. In the west of the state of Paraná (Brazil), more than 250 mm fell in 96 hours, and towards the end of October, new rains of up to 350 mm were recorded on the Iguazú basin and the Itaipu reservoir. This caused simultaneous flooding of the Iguazú, Paraná and Uruguay rivers. On October 14, the Iguazú River reached a flow of 16,200 m³/s, about eight times its average, and discharges from the Yacyretá dam reached about 35,000 m³/s. In Ayolas (Paraguay), upstream of the Argentine section, the Paraná River reached 6.43 m in October, the highest height for that month in 55 years.

As of 19 October 2026, the Paraná River exceeded evacuation levels in Corrientes Capital, Itatí, Paso de la Patria, Barranqueras and Isla del Cerrito, and the flood wave advanced downstream towards Goya, Reconquista and La Paz. The number of displaced people went from 240 (16 October) to 2,296 (21 October) and to 4,190 as of 3 November 2026, according to the Argentine Red Cross's Situation Report No. 6: 2,239 in Chaco, 1,802 in Corrientes and 149 in Santa Fe, in 23 localities. Data consolidated by government authorities record 3,903 displaced people in 21 localities, of which 2,005 (51 per cent) are self-evacuated.
In total, the authorities estimate that more than 5,028 people have been affected, 2 people have died (Bella Vista, Corrientes) and 1 person has been injured.

In the Chaco, the impact is concentrated in the Gran Resistencia. Puerto Vilelas accounts for 60 per cent of the province's victims (1,350 people), followed by Colonia Benítez (450), Barranqueras (253) and Isla del Cerrito (142). Municipal records and the field survey of the Argentine Red Cross show a greater impact in Barranqueras. Isla del Cerrito continues to be isolated by land due to the closure of Provincial Route No. 63: essential transfers, health care and evacuations are made by boat. The internal and coastal roads of Colonia Benítez, Tres Bocas, Isla Soto and other places are disabled by flooding and mud. The catchment of the water treatment plants continues to be affected by camalots, turbidity and sediments, and the provincial water company maintains a restricted distribution or with reduced pressure at the peripheral points.
In Corrientes, there are 1,802 displaced people in 12 coastal municipalities, of which 1,393 (77 per cent) are self-evacuated. The most affected localities are Corrientes Capital (672 people, in riverside neighborhoods such as La Tosquera), Itatí (518) and Paso de la Patria (228), where the rupture of an embankment affected more than 300 homes and pumping and containment work continues. In Santa Fe, the flood has already affected Las Toscas, Tacuarendí, Reconquista and Santa Fe Capital, with 149 people displaced.

Although in recent days the river has registered decreases of a few centimeters in the upper section, the humanitarian impact does not improve: it is a pause within a scenario of prolonged high waters. As of 2 November 2026, the Paraná River marked 7.11 m in Corrientes (evacuation level: 7.00 m), after a peak of 7.35 m, and 7.00 m in Barranqueras (evacuation: 6.50 m). On 3 November, it dropped just 5 cm in Barranqueras. At that rate, the river will remain above evacuation levels for weeks and families will not be able to return to their homes.

Meanwhile, the flood wave is advancing downstream: Goya (6.09 m) and Reconquista (5.91 m) exceed their evacuation levels, La Paz (5.86 m) exceeded the alert level, and the National Water Institute (INA) forecasts that Paraná and Santa Fe will reach or exceed the alert level in the second week of November. Added to this is the Paraguay River, which remains at 7.55 m, and the Bermejo River, which rose 18 cm on 3 November.

The most worrying factor is the rain on an already saturated basin. For 3 to 4 November 2026, the National Meteorological Service (SMN) issued an orange alert for strong storms, some severe, throughout the province of Corrientes, with accumulated 40 to 80 mm and gusts of more than 90 km/h, and yellow alert in Chaco (20 to 40 mm), Misiones and Formosa. The Yacyretá Binational Entity forecasts between 2 and 4 November 2026 accumulated 20 to 50 mm in much of the Paraná basin, with up to 90 mm in some sectors. In southern Brazil, forecasts for November anticipate above-normal rainfall, with the highest excesses in the state of Paraná and risk of flooding over the unregulated basin of Alto Paraná and Iguazú. In Paraguay, rains and storms persist on the left bank of the Paraná and the Paraguay River basin, and the Paraná remains at 5.35 m in Ayolas, above alert and flood levels, with more than 3,200 people evacuated in that city alone. These figures are from a separate record and are not included in the displaced persons totals submitted for Argentina.

As the soils have excess accumulated moisture, each new rain immediately drains into the rivers. That is why the National Water Institute (INA) warns that it is likely to observe new spikes and a second wave of flood in the Paraná River, due to the volume in transit from the Upper Paraná and the rains on the Paraguay River basin and the Itaipu contribution area, with a new flood transit from the Iguazú River. It also forecasts that the Uruguay River will approach the alert level again in São Tomé and San Javier between 6 and 8 November 2026. The Yacyretá Binational Entity also anticipates a new increase in flow after the current slight decrease.

On a seasonal scale, the SMN forecasts above-normal rainfall on the Littoral for the November–January quarter. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center anticipates a strong to very strong El Niño, with a high probability of reaching historic intensity and persisting at least until the January–March 2027 quarter. In this context, an increase in hydrometeorological events (intense rains, severe storms, and floods) is expected until February–March 2027 throughout the La Plata Basin, including the Uruguay River and the Paraná Delta. The Civil Defense Directorate of Corrientes describes a long-term emergency, until March or April 2027, and the Government of Chaco estimates stays of 3 to 4 months in evacuation centers. With this scenario, some 200 additional families are projected to be affected (around 1,000 people) in the prioritized areas in the coming weeks, in addition to possible new effects in Santa Fe, Entre Ríos, and Buenos Aires.

Exceptional nature of the event. The magnitude of this flood is exceptional for the basin and, according to official forecasts, the situation has not yet reached its peak. Upstream, the Paraná River in Ciudad del Este (Paraguay) marked the historical maximum of its series of records (32.96 m, on 15 October 2026), and the stations of Cerrito, Panchito López and Itá Corá surpassed their records of November 2023. In Ayolas, the October height was the highest in 55 years. The Iguazú River reached about 17,700 m³/s on 26 October, almost 12 times its average flow, and the Devil's Throat was closed for 20 days. The flows entering Yacyretá, of about 35,000 m³/s, are equivalent to 2.4 times the historical average of October (14,400 m³/s, series 1971–2025). In Corrientes and Barranqueras the river has remained above the evacuation level since 19 October. The most worrying thing is not the current reading but what is coming: the INA and the Yacyretá Binational Entity predict new rebounds, a second wave of floods and new increases in flow due to the rains expected over a saturated basin in northern Argentina, southern Brazil and Paraguay. Added to this is an El Niño with a high probability of reaching historic intensity, which would sustain high waters until February-March 2027, in the middle of the dengue season.

To date there is no declaration of national or provincial emergency. The National System for Integrated Risk Management (SINAGIR) maintains the Red Alert for the region. The Chaco alert system maintains the red alert in Barranqueras, Puerto Vilelas and Isla del Cerrito, and in Corrientes there are 11 coastal municipalities on alert. Reconquista (Santa Fe) has a municipal emergency, and on 31 October 2026 a bill to declare a water emergency in the Chaco entered the Senate of the Nation, which has not yet been discussed.

title: UNHCR Romania Ukraine Refugee Situation Weekly Update #222 - 16 November 2026
content:
Highlight

On 13 November, the Inter-Agency Coordination platform led by UNHCR held the third edition of “Building Bridges” - A Stakeholder Meetup on Social Cohesion and Inclusion. The event supported the 43 organisations that are part of the Refugee Response Plan (RRP) for the Ukraine refugee response, in their work with refugees and with the Romanian host communities that welcome them. Co-hosted by the Embassy of Denmark, the Embassy of Finland, the Embassy of Sweden, the Romanian Diversity Chamber of Commerce (RDCC), and UNHCR, the event brought together over 150 participants from the government, embassies, international organisations, private sector, and civil society. Ms. Diana Punga, State Adviser, Department for Administration, Public Policies and Civil Society of the Presidential Administration, provided the opening statement. Ms. Ioana Ciocan, Minister of Culture, opened the panel discussion. Through panel discussions and a partner’s marketplace, participants exchanged experiences, explored practical approaches to fostering social inclusion and identified opportunities for new partnerships. Discussions highlighted how closer collaboration between civil society, the private sector and public institutions can strengthen social cohesion and build more inclusive communities in Romania.

title: Attacks on Health Care in Myanmar: 16 - 31 October 2026
content:
Data collected by Insecurity Insight shows that since the military coup on 01 February 2021 and 15 October 2026, at least 1,979 attacks on health care took place across Myanmar, with over 65% of attacks attributed to the Myanmar Armed Forces (MAF). Health facilities were damaged 521 times while 176 health workers were killed, 55 kidnapped and 940 arrested.

At least 493 incidents of damage to or destruction of health facilities were reported across Myanmar between February 2021 and September 2026. Reported incidents increased from 2023, peaking in the first quarter of 2024, amid an escalation in hostilities following the launch of coordinated opposition offensives in October 2023. During this period, the MAF increasingly relied on airstrikes as part of its military operations. Over half of incidents where health facilities were damaged or destroyed were attributed to airstrikes, including aircraft and drone strikes. Of these, 85% recorded aircraft strikes attributed to the MAF, particularly in Kayin, Magway, Rakhine, Sagaing and Shan regions and states, particularly affected by conflict. Conflict parties, including local defence groups, the Chin National Army, the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and the Karen National Union (KNU), were named in incidents where drone strikes damaged health facilities, although less frequently. Overall these incidents highlight the sustained threat aerial attacks pose to health infrastructure and the continued availability of essential health services.

View the incidents on our interactive map. Download the data. Data is continuously updated and numbers may change if/ when further information is made available. See here for methodology. For data enquiries, please get in touch.

Suggested citation: Insecurity Insight. 2026. 16-31 October 2026, Attacks on Health Care in Myanmar. Switzerland: Insecurity Insight. https://bit.ly/16-31Oct2026MMRHealth

Documented incidents

16-31 October 2026

The publicly reported incidents below are not a complete nor a representative list of all incidents that affected the provision of health care in Myanmar between 16-31 October 2026. The incidents have not been verified through ground investigations. There is a delay in reporting incidents due to our open-source verification protocol.

20 October 2026: Near Yay Chan Pyin village, Ye Chan Pyin village tract, Sittwe township and district, Rakhine state, a Myanmar military medical battalion was raided by the Arakan Army, and medicines were taken away. Source: Narinjara

As reported on 21 October 2026: In Kyindwe station town, Kanpetlet township, Mindat district, Chin state, bunkers were observed at a station hospital following the Myanmar military's recapture of the town. The town had previously been taken over by ethnic armed groups, including the Arakan Army, the Chinland Defense Force, and the Chin National Defence Force, in April 2024. Sources: Myanmar National Portal and NP News

24 October 2026: At an undisclosed location, a CDM-affiliated laboratory technician was killed in an airstrike by the Myanmar military. Sources: Facebook I and Facebook II

As reported on 28 October 2026: In Sittwe town, Sittwen township and district, Rakhine state, several wards of the state hospital were closed to public access as the Myanmar military was using the buildings to accommodate wounded soldiers relocated from the 100-bedded Myanmar military hospital under the Directorate of Medical Services near Thin Pone Tan village, Sittwe township, due to intensified armed clashes in the area. Sources: Mizzima and Narinjara

31 October 2026: In an unnamed IDP camp near Wan Ngaw village, Tee Lon village tract, Loikaw township, Loikaw district, Kayah (Karenni) state, a makeshift school was destroyed when two Myanmar military aircraft dropped approximately 20 bombs at around 1400hrs. Three children were killed at the scene, and five others were injured. All eight children were aged 9-16 years-old. Sources: Kantarrawaddy Times, Karenni People’s Voice, and Khit Thit Media
