title: El Salvador - Quarterly Update | July - September 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • In San Salvador, 110 Judicial Facilitators from the central region participated in the first National Convention of Judicial Facilitators, strengthening their knowledge of international protection, forced displacement and referral mechanisms. Through their community outreach, they help identify and refer people with specific protection needs, including those affected by forced displacement. Organized by the Supreme Court of Justice (CSJ) with UNHCR’s support, the event was the first of five conventions expected to reach some 700 facilitators nationwide in 2026.
  • UNHCR and Swisscontact signed a Letter of Understanding to expand socioeconomic inclusion opportunities in El Salvador for forcibly displaced people. The agreement will strengthen referral pathways and access to entrepreneurship programmes, inclusive finance and vocational training, while promoting private sector partnerships that support livelihoods and greater self-reliance.
  • As MIRPS Pro Tempore Presidency, El Salvador led a two-day Regional Event on Social Cohesion, Economic Integration and Durable Solutions with UNHCR’s support. Delegates shared initiatives for the inclusion of displaced people in host communities and visited the CUBO community centre in Santa Lucía, San Salvador.

title: UNHCR MCO Panama's Caribbean Coverage Factsheet, July - September 2026
content:
Highlights

During a mission to Cuba, UNHCR met with the Ministries of Foreign Aairs, Education, Public Health, and Labour and Social Security, as well as the Immigration and Foreigners Directorate. Discussions covered refugee protection and the new migration framework, particularly its implementing regulations. The mission also strengthened collaboration with the UN Country Team and included focus group discussions with refugees and asylum-seekers to better understand protection needs.

UNHCR continued to provide practical and technical support to Caribbean governments on refugee protection, including technical assistance on individual protection cases in Saint Lucia and the British Virgin Islands, in coordination with local authorities. UNHCR also maintained bilateral dialogue with Caribbean governments, sharing technical guidance on the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol, including for countries considering accession.

UNHCR visited Aruba and met with the Immigration Oce (DIMAS) to discuss refugee protection, asylum procedures, and opportunities for continued cooperation. The mission delivered a draft asylum law prepared by an expert consultant, donated equipment for asylum and regularization matters, and engaged with IOM and CEDE Aruba to strengthen coordination and support for forcibly displaced people.

In August, an asylum-seeker living in Cuba travelled to Mexico to study Technology through a HABESHA Protection Scholarship, following UNHCR support throughout the application and travel arrangements. The scholarship is part of a complementary pathways initiative that combines access to higher education with legal stay and integration support.

UNHCR focused on protection coordination in Trinidad and Tobago, working with UN agencies, government institutions, civil society, regional platforms, and the diplomatic community. Activities included discussions around the UN Multi-Country Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF), active participation in the Protection Working Group, and continued support to the Migration Regularization Framework (MRF).

title: WFP Sierra Leone Country Brief, November 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP and the Ministry of Agriculture trained 80 Farmer-based Organizations (FBOs) in post-harvest management and market linkages, strengthening livelihoods and reducing losses.

• WFP and the Government broke ground in Makeni for a fortified infant food processing facility.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Sierra Leone’s humanitarian needs remain driven by chronic poverty, economic fragility, high food insecurity, and climate-related shocks. Although inflation has eased from previous peaks, rising fuel costs and food prices continue to strain household purchasing power.

• The July 2025 Food Security Monitoring System survey reported a decline in the proportion of severely food insecure households by more than half—from 28 percent in 2023 to 13 percent in July 2025—representing a 15-percentage point reduction.

• Since late February 2026, there has been a 57 percent increase in diesel and 40 percent increase in petrol, driven by external factors.

• WFP’s new Country Strategic Plan 2026-2030 reflects a sharpened strategic focus on food systems, home-grown school feeding, nutrition, resilient livelihoods, women’s economic empowerment and youth opportunities. WFP’s response is increasingly centered on strengthening nationally led systems, while retaining the capacity to respond to shocks, including climate-related disasters, public health emergencies and seasonal food insecurity.

title: Afghanistan: Bi-Weekly Market Report, Issue 317: First Half - November 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Market Overview

During the first half of November, national average prices recorded generally modest movements during the reporting period, while several key food commodities remained elevated compared with last year and their threeyear averages. Rice and cooking oil prices continued to face supply-side pressures amid disruptions to regional trade routes and slower imports. In contrast, pulses remained relatively affordable, supported by increased domestic availability, local production and imports from Central Asia, while restricted export opportunities and weak demand contributed to lower prices. Fuel and fertilizer costs remained elevated, adding pressure to agricultural production, transportation and household purchasing power. Meanwhile, limited demand for improved seeds and animal feed, alongside increased local availability, contributed to lower prices for these inputs.

Food Categories:

National average food prices recorded limited changes during the reporting period, although notable annual and longer-term price disparities persisted across commodities.

  • Wheat and wheat flour prices increased marginally during the reporting period and show a slight increase yearon-year with wheat grain prices up by 6%, high-price wheat flour up by 3% and low-price up by 6%.
  • Rice prices also show a marginal increase from previous period (Both Palawi and Sholae) and a significant increase from last year, with Palawi rice 12% higher and Sholae rice 27% higher than last year. Moreover, both varieties remained 21% above their three-year averages.
  • Weekly movements in cooking oil, pulses, sugar, salt and bread remained limited. However, cooking oil and sugar prices remain 10% higher than last year, while pulses and bread show declines.
  • Vegetables prices show a significant increase with tomato prices up by 30.4%, potato 2.6% and onion by 9.1%. However, year-on-year comparison show notably higher prices of potato while tomato and onion show declines.

Non-Food Categories:

Terms of Trade (ToT): Purchasing power remained constraint for both labour-dependent households and pastoralists, as declining income and higher prices limit their access to food.

  • Unskilled Labour ToT: The nominal unskilled labour ToT marginally declined by 0.9% to 9.6 kg of low-price wheat flour, representing an 11% decline from last year and 14% below the three-year average. The continued deterioration indicates sustained pressure on labour income relative to food prices.
  • Labour Availability and Wages: Unskilled labour availability remained low at 1.9 days per week, 12% below last year and 20% below the three-year average. Unskilled labour wages also declined by 4% year-on-year, contributing to a 24% decline in the real unskilled labour ToT compared with last year and 31% below the three-year average.
  • Pastoralist ToT: A pastoralist could exchange a one-year-old female sheep for 257 kg of low-price wheat flour, 7% below last year's level and 8% below the three-year average, indicating continued pressure on the purchasing power of livestock-dependent households.
  • Fertilizers and agricultural input prices show marginal increases during the reporting period. However, year-onyear show mix movements; DAP and urea remained 5% and 25% higher than last year, respectively. Meanwhile, improved seed and animal feed prices remained below last year, by 7% and 5%, respectively.

title: Gaza Protection Cluster Snapshot: Protection Monitoring (Reporting Period from 1 - 31 October 2026)
content:
INTRODUCTION

Findings from the current reporting period highlight the cumulative impact of insecurity, deteriorating shelter conditions, and barriers to essential services on displaced populations across Gaza. The highest protection risk severity scores were recorded for attacks on civilians and civilian objects, including unlawful killings (82%), psychological and emotional abuse or inflicted distress (75%), and restrictions on freedom of movement, siege and forced displacement (74%). As winter approaches, communities reported growing fears of flooding and exposure to cold and rain, with damaged tents, overcrowding, and inadequate drainage undermining safety, privacy, and dignity. Damaged buildings, rubble, and suspected explosive remnants further threaten civilian safety, particularly for children moving or playing in hazardous surroundings.

Economic hardship and insufficient, irregular assistance are limiting households’ ability to afford food, medicine, transportation, and shelter materials. Older persons and persons with disabilities face additional barriers due to inaccessible facilities, unsuitable pathways, and shortages of assistive devices, increasing their dependence on caregivers. Families reported borrowing money and selling belongings or assistance items to meet immediate needs, while adults and, in some cases, children assume additional responsibilities to secure water and food. Community committees, volunteers, and informal support networks continue to facilitate assistance and resolve disputes, but their limited resources cannot meet the scale of needs.

The Protection Monitoring System (PMS) provides timely and systematic evidence through Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) and Focus Group Discussions (FGDs), combining quantitative severity scores with community perspectives. This snapshot presents findings for October 2026, examines protection risk trends since monitoring began in August 2024, and highlights community-reported concerns, impacts, coping mechanisms, and capacities to inform protection analysis and response planning.

title: UGA: Flood - 11-2026 - Floods and other Hydro-Meteorological Disaster Events in Eastern, Western and Northern Uganda (2026-11-07)
content:
The Uganda Red Cross Society (URCS) Regional Operations Managers, Branch Managers, RCATs are activated and have been disseminating Disaster Risk Information and Early Warning advisories based on the official Government of Uganda seasonal September - December 2026 forecast that includes predicted El Nino impacts in Uganda.

At the end of October 2026, the rains intensified. As November 2026 began, several disaster events were already being registered in disaster hotspot areas across Uganda.

In the period 7th - 15th November 2026, several disaster-prone areas in Eastern, Northern and Western Uganda experienced intensive prolonged rainfall that caused floods and other hydro-meteorological disasters affecting vulnerable communities in 11 districts. The rains continue and more disaster events are expected to be registered in various parts of the country.

title: UNHCR Ukraine Protection Update #12 - Q3 2026
content:
▪ In the first three quarters of 2026, UNHCR’s protection response reached 429,429 people. Of those, 68 per cent are females, 32 per cent are older people above the age of 60 years, while 19 per cent are children. Over 42,022 people supported are living with a disability.

▪ Community-based protection was central to the protection response in the first nine months of the year, while 38 per cent centred on service provision, including legal, social and psycho-social services.

▪ UNHCR and partners promoted legal and policy developments through 57 advocacy and judicial interventions aimed at improving access to rights and services for forcibly displaced and stateless people.

title: WFP Armenia Country Brief, November 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • Armenia positioned its National School Meals Programme as a flagship, government-owned model at CBD COP17, demonstrating how school meals can simultaneously advance nutrition, education, local food systems, biodiversity conservation, climate resilience, and human capital development.
  • WFP continued scaling the Transformative Home-Grown School Feeding model and nutrition-sensitive value chains through investments in school-based agriculture, renewable energy, and wholegrain bread production, fostering more sustainable and resilient school meals systems.
  • WFP is supporting efforts to strengthen national preparedness and response systems through improved early warning and forecasting tools, and enhanced food security monitoring and data systems.

title: World Vision Situation Report #6: Humanitarian Response to Flooding (November 12, 2026)
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

Cambodia continues to experience the impacts of flooding following prolonged heavy rainfall associated with low-pressure systems and seasonal weather patterns. According to the National Committee for Disaster Management (NCDM), flooding has affected 10 provinces, 53 districts and municipalities, and 255 communes and sangkats, impacting approximately 73,922 households nationwide.

As of 6 November 2026, flood conditions across Cambodia have generally improved, with floodwaters steadily receding in most affected areas. Nevertheless, the recent influence of Typhoon No. 31 (In-Fa) has generated moderate to heavy rainfall over the past two days, resulting in localized flash flooding in several districts, particularly along the Cambodia-Thailand border. Water levels in key waterways, including the Sangke River (Battambang Province) and the Mongkul Borey Stream (Banteay Meanchey Province), have increased in response to the rainfall. According to the Tonle Sap Authority, these rivers and streams remain under close observation due to elevated flows and the potential risk to lowlying communities, agricultural lands, and local infrastructure.

Furthermore, the Ministry of Water Resources and Meteorology (MOWRAM) forecasts that the ongoing development of Typhoon No. 31 (In-Fa), combined with monsoonal conditions, may continue to increase precipitation across Cambodia, necessitating continued preparedness and monitoring by relevant authorities and at-risk communities.

content: This monthly bulletin of seasonal monitoring provides information on rainfall, temperature, soil moisture, river-water level and vegetation. It also provides climate and disaster-impact information.

title: Djibouti Storm Surge 2026 - DREF Operational Update (MDRDJ010)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

27-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 27 July 2026, between 5:00 and 6:00 p.m., Mouloud locality in the Dikhil region of Djibouti was struck by a severe windstorm accompanied by heavy rainfall. This was the second storm to affect the locality within a few days, following an earlier event on 24 July 2026, which caused no significant damage.

Preliminary reports indicated that more than 4,160 people (693 households) were affected. Approximately 290 households (1,740 people) experienced partial or complete damage to their homes, while more than 168 families were displaced after their houses lost their roofs.

The disaster resulted in two fatalities, an elderly man and an infant, and left 10 people injured, including three children. The injured were evacuated to Ali Sabieh Regional Hospital and Dikhil Hospital for medical treatment. The detailed needs assessment identified an additional 684 people (114 households), bringing the total affected population to 4,844 people (807 households).

At the time of the emergency, temperatures in the affected area exceeded 42°C, compounding the impact of the storm and increasing risks for households living in damaged or makeshift shelters. Several isolated domestic fires were also reported, with strong winds heightening the risk of fire spread and further endangering affected communities.

The disaster underscored the vulnerability of Mouloud and the wider Dikhil region to multiple, concurrent hazards, including severe windstorms, heavy rainfall, extreme temperatures and wind-related fire incidents. These hazards have exacerbated existing vulnerabilities, resulting in shelter damage, displacement and increased health, protection and safety concerns among affected populations.

Although the risks associated with extreme heat have decreased following improvements in climatic conditions and a more favourable seasonal outlook, significant water shortages persist in Mouloud, further exacerbating the humanitarian needs. Access to sufficient and safe drinking water remains a critical concern, particularly for displaced families whose living conditions and access to essential services have been disrupted by the disaster.

The persistent water shortage constitutes an additional and ongoing humanitarian need that requires a strengthened response. The initial WASH intervention targets have proved insufficient to address the scale of needs among affected communities, particularly IDPs and other vulnerable households facing barriers to accessing safe water. Consequently, extending WASH interventions is necessary to expand coverage, reach additional households and improve access to safe and adequate water for affected populations.

Despite the improvement in climatic conditions, households whose shelters remain damaged or inadequately repaired continue to face potential exposure to adverse weather. The combined effects of shelter damage, displacement and limited access to safe drinking water continue to undermine the well-being of affected communities. Continued monitoring, targeted assistance and close coordination with local authorities remain essential to address these interrelated needs and support the transitioning.

title: Uganda Drought Assessment (2026) - DREF Operation (MDRUG059)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

07-09-2026

What happened, where and when?

Uganda’s Karamoja region is in a severe drought after an exceptionally dry second half of the March to September 2026 rainy season. Between June and late August, cumulative rainfall was about 200 mm below average across most of the sub-region, and up to 500 mm below average in parts of Kaabong, Kotido and Nakapiripirit. By late August, vegetation greenness was only 60 to 80 percent of the seasonal average.

Prolonged dry spells since early June have caused crop losses of 50 to 75 percent across much of the sub-region, and main-season cereal and pulse production is expected to be extremely poor or to have failed in most areas. Pasture and water shortages have worsened, and livestock body conditions are declining.

The drought followed a significantly underperforming March to September rainy season, characterized by prolonged rainfall deficits, vegetation stress, crop losses and deteriorating food-security conditions. The event occurred during a period of strengthening El Niño conditions globally. The IPC update of 7 September 2026 attributes the deterioration in Karamoja to El Niño-related shocks, rising food prices and reduced humanitarian assistance, and Save the Children links the rise in child malnutrition to El Niño-linked dry spells. The available evidence therefore supports El Niño as a contributing climatic factor, rather than a confirmed sole cause of the drought.

Food insecurity has deepened. Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected across all nine Karamoja districts through January 2027, with some households in Emergency (IPC Phase 4). IPC projections to February 2027 put 432,109 people in Phase 3 and 41,259 in Phase 4, out of about 1.5 million people in the sub-region. At least 16 people were reported to have died from hunger by July 2026. An August 2026 nutrition survey found critical levels of global acute malnutrition in Kaabong (12.1 percent) and Nabilatuk (10.5 percent), and GAM is expected to remain Critical in Kotido and Kaabong through February 2027. The situation has since worsened as documented by ACT Alliance in July,

Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) in August, and through the IPC update of September indicating about 673,000 people were in Phase 3 or worse in August to October, the highest since 2018. For the early actions, the forecast trigger is the IPC projection that Crisis outcomes continue through January 2027 and deteriorate from January as household stocks run out, together with rainfall about 200 mm below average since June and vegetation at 60 to 80 percent of normal.

Water scarcity raises the risk of poor hygiene and water-borne diseases, and puts pressure on households, livestock and the communal valley dams and earth water pans that many communities rely on during the dry season. The Government has distributed food relief, but there are still major gaps in primary information on the scale, location and characteristics of needs beyond food, especially for water, health, hygiene and livelihoods. URCS will therefore carry out a multisectoral assessment to generate primary evidence on needs and gaps, and will begin limited, no-regret early actions in the five most-affected districts to reduce the impact of the drought while the assessment is under way.

title: Dengue Outbreak 2026 in Chad : DREF Operation (MDRTD027)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

27-10-2026

What happened, where and when?

Chad is facing an outbreak of dengue, a viral disease transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. The outbreak was officially declared on 3 October 2026 by the Secretary of State for Public Health and Prevention through Order No. 150/MSPP/SE/SG/COUSP/2026. The Ministry of Public Health and Prevention (MSPP) urged anyone with fever or headache to seek medical care without delay.

According to MSPP dengue Situation Report (SitRep) No. 003, covering data as of 26 October 2026, 4,600 suspected cases, 353 cases confirmed by RT-PCR and 14 deaths (case fatality rate: 0.30%) have been reported. Of the 750 RT-PCR results available, 353 were positive (47% positivity). The attack rate is 69 per 100,000 inhabitants in the affected provinces. Between 24 and 26 October, 596 new suspected cases and 42 new confirmed cases were reported, 83% of them in N’Djamena.

The outbreak peaked in epidemiological week 41 and is now declining: weekly suspected cases in N’Djamena fell from around 1,130 in week 41 to around 160 in week 43 and confirmed cases from 95 in week 42 to 41 in week 43. However, transmission remains active, particularly in N’Djamena, and the MSPP stresses that surveillance must be maintained.
Sex and age disaggregation (MSPP SitRep No. 003): suspected cases (3,199 cases with complete data) mainly affect people aged 5–34, with a predominance of women and girls, especially aged 15–34, and decrease sharply after 45 years. Confirmed cases (288 cases) mainly affect people aged 15–44, with a peak at 25–34 years and a fairly balanced distribution between sexes (male/female ratio 1.2; median age 30 years, range 2–77); children are under-represented among confirmed cases. The higher share of women among suspected cases may reflect greater exposure at home, where Aedes mosquitoes bite during the day, and greater use of health services; this will be explored through the community consultations planned under PGI. Data disaggregated by disability are not available from the MSPP; the CRT will collect sex, age and disability data in its own CBS and activity records.

Six provinces and 21 health districts have reported cases. This DREF focuses on the three provinces where new cases continue to be reported (situation as of 26 October 2026):

  • N’Djamena (Centre, South, East, North and 9th arrondissement districts): 2,045 suspected cases, including 495 new, 288 confirmed and 9 deaths. The capital concentrates most new and confirmed cases.
  • Ouaddaï (Abéché, Adré and Hadjer Hadid districts): 418 suspected cases, including 64 new, 21 confirmed and 1 death.
  • Sila (Goz Beïda district): 104 suspected cases, including 22 new, and 3 confirmed.
    Wadi Fira, where the outbreak started in the Kounoungou refugee camp, has recorded 1,971 suspected cases, 27 confirmed and 4 deaths, but is now close to zero new cases (6 new suspected cases). Batha (52 suspected cases) and Ennedi Ouest (7 suspected cases) report very few cases. These three provinces are not covered by this DREF but will continue to be monitored through MSPP surveillance.

The first suspected cases were detected in July 2026 in the Kounoungou refugee camp (Guéréda district, Wadi Fira), which hosts Sudanese refugees, through the EWARS Mobile surveillance platform. The first case was confirmed by RT-PCR on 24 July 2026 at the Medical Biology and Epidemiology Laboratory (LaBiEp) in N’Djamena. The outbreak was declared on 3 October 2026, and the Incident Management System (IMS) was activated on 5 October 2026.

A first meeting with technical and financial partners was held on 16 October 2026. On 19 October 2026, the Public Health Emergency Operations Centre (COUSP) invited the Red Cross of Chad (CRT) to a meeting at which it requested its support for the response. On 26 October 2026, the dengue situation was the first item on the agenda of the monthly health sector consultation meeting chaired by the Head of State. On 27 October 2026, the Minister of Public Health and Prevention formally requested the technical and financial support of the CRT through letter No. 0996/MSPP/SE/SG/COUSP/2026.

The situation is ongoing. Although the dry season will reduce outdoor breeding sites, Aedes mosquitoes continue to breed in water stored by households, so transmission can persist, particularly in N’Djamena.

Aggravating context: This is the second documented dengue outbreak in Chad in three years, after the 2023 outbreak (1,342 suspected cases, 41 confirmed and 1 death as of 1 October 2023), which had Ouaddaï as its epicentre. Several factors justify a targeted community response despite the current decline:

  • Risk of severe dengue: 23.8% of tested people were IgG-positive, which shows previous dengue circulation and exposes the population to severe forms in case of reinfection.
  • Limited testing: only around 16% of suspected cases have an RT-PCR result, and rapid diagnostic tests are not always available. The true extent of transmission, particularly in Ouaddaï and Sila, is likely underestimated.
  • Weak data and entomological surveillance: data completeness and timeliness remain insufficient, and no entomological assessment has yet been conducted.
  • Vulnerable communities: most suspected cases are aged 5–34, with a predominance of women aged 15–34. Eastern Chad hosts Sudanese refugees and host communities with precarious living conditions and limited access to health services.
  • Weak preparedness: there is no national arbovirus preparedness plan, and the response depends heavily on partner funding.

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 13 November 2026
content:
Key Highlights

  • Flooding in Gaza has compounded an already dire situation, with the Site Management Cluster reporting about 46,000 households affected and over 40,000 family shelters damaged. Response is held back by Israeli restrictions alongside funding shortfalls.
  • Sewage-contaminated stormwater poses public health risks, compounded by flooded health facilities, suspended services, medicine shortages and a rise in probable meningitis cases and other diseases.
  • The latest rainfalls left thousands of young students in over 100 learning spaces without access to education, damaged 15 child and psychosocial spaces, and caused the collapse of a safe space serving 200 women and girls.
  • In the West Bank, demolitions by Israeli forces displaced 150 Palestinians in one week, including in areas affected by the E1 settlement expansion plan and the Jordan Valley, as well as in East Jerusalem.
  • Education-related incidents nearly doubled in the third quarter of 2026 compared with 2025, affecting 149 schools and nearly 28,000 students and education personnel across the West Bank.
  • Settler violence and access restrictions continued to displace families and disrupt the olive harvest, with 410 harvest-related settler attacks recorded since 1 September 2026.

title: WHO Sudan: Sudan Health Spotlight - October 2026
content:
Monthly highlights

  • WHO supported the first phase of the polio outbreak-response vaccination campaign targeting more than 6 million children under 5 years of age across 12 states, out of the 11 million targeted in 2 phases across all 18 states.
  • WHO and partners conducted a reactive oral cholera vaccination campaign in Gharb Bara, North Kordofan, targeting more than 271 000 people amid ongoing cholera transmission and disruptions to essential water and sanitation services.
  • WHO strengthened Ebola preparedness in collaboration with national health authorities, including assessments of isolation capacity in Red Sea State that identified critical gaps in infrastructure, equipment and staffing to guide further readiness measures.

title: UNICEF Burundi Humanitarian Situation Report No. 25, 30 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • UNICEF strengthened Ebola preparedness through enhanced surveillance, risk communication, WASH and health system readiness.
  • Over 33,000 Congolese refugees remained at Busuma, sustaining significant humanitarian and basic service needs.
  • Water availability reached 21.45 litres per person per day, although sanitation gaps persisted.
  • Heavy rains and soil erosion increased risks to shelters and WASH infrastructure at Busuma.
  • 123,238 children and women accessed primary healthcare, reaching 110% of the annual target, reflecting increased service coverage.
  • 60,147 children, adolescents and caregivers accessed community-based MHPSS services, expanding access to psychosocial support.
  • October was marked by strong health service delivery and continued humanitarian assistance, alongside persistent pressure on refugee services and growing climate-related risks to infrastructure at Busuma.

title: Situation Update No.7: Escalation of Hostilities and Displacement Across Yemen (As of 10 November 2026)
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • Reporting period: 1 August – 10 November 2026
  • Displacement continues, with nearly 330,000 people now displaced. IOM DTM has recorded 329,117 people (54,846 households) displaced since 1 August, about 48,000 more than in the last update. Most new movements originate in and within Lahj and Ta’iz.
  • Fighting in Lahj is driving new displacement. Heavy fighting around Al Madaribah Wa Al Aarah, Al Maqatirah and Tur Al Bahah has forced more families to flee, many of them to Tuban, where reception capacity is under strain, and further displacement towards Aden is expected.
  • Civilian casualties increase. OHCHR has documented 284 civilian casualties in 107 incidents since 1 August, including 70 people killed and 214 injured. Children account for 103 of the casualties and half of those killed.
  • People in Ta’iz City face growing hardship. Key routes linking Ta’iz with Aden and the West Coast have been repeatedly disrupted; cooking gas has reportedly been prevented from entering the city since early October; and shortages are affecting health services, water production and food availability.
  • 256,872 internally displaced people (36,696 families) have been reached with first-line RRM assistance. Nearly 8,900 registered families are awaiting support, mainly in Lahj and Ta’iz, where insecurity, stock-outs and road blockages have interrupted distributions.
  • Strikes on fuel infrastructure in Al Hodeidah threaten essential services. Repeated strikes at the Ras Isa oil terminal, sharply reduced port activity, and rising fuel prices raise concerns about fuel shortages that could disrupt food supply chains, water pumping, and health services across northern governorates.
  • Second-line assistance is expanding but remains far behind needs. Emergency cash has reached 84 per cent of verified households and food assistance 64 per cent of verified households (first cycle), while shelter and WASH support has reached only about one in four households in need.
  • Health partners have reached more than 103,000 internally displaced people, and a measles–rubella vaccination campaign launched on 7 November has reached more than 600,000 children in southern governorates. Damage to health facilities and fuel shortages in Ta’iz threaten continuity of care.
  • Protection risks are rising. Partners report more family separation, explosive ordnance risks, eviction threats and a growing risk of gender-based violence, while five safe spaces for women and girls have closed on the West Coast.
  • Access remains constrained. Active hostilities, disrupted transport routes, movement restrictions and administrative procedures continue to delay humanitarian movements and the delivery of assistance.

title: East Africa Seasonal Monitor: An erratic start of September through December rainfall season across East Africa, November 13, 2026
content:
Key Messages

  • Poor rainfall performance, prolonged dry spells and above-average temperatures during the June–September season led to below-average crop production across high production regions of northwestern (north-rift) Kenya, Karamoja in Uganda, Sudan, South Sudan and the Kiremt regions of Ethiopia.
  • At the start of the October – December season heavy rainfall has been reported across much of Somalia, and eastern Ethiopia resulting in localized flooding, high river levels, particularly within the Juba and Shabelle river catchments.
  • Despite forecasts indicating a high likelihood of an early onset and above-average SOND rainfall, much of Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi has experienced a relatively dry start in September and October. False starts across coastal counties of Kilifi and Kwale in Kenya triggered planting which will likely lead to replanting.
  • Pasture and surface water resources that had extremely deteriorated across most pastoral regions are starting to recover as the season becomes established.
  • The strong El Niño and positive Indian Ocean Dipole are likely to enhance cumulative SOND rainfall across much of East Africa with the peak rainfall month likely to be November, in line with the typical progression of the seasonal rains. However, uncertainty remains regarding the spatial and temporal distribution of rainfall. Episodes of intense rainfall could increase flood risk and waterlogging. El Niño conditions are likely to persist into early 2027.

June – September Season

Context: Between June and September, the following are the areas and names of the rainy seasons underway in parts of East Africa: long rains in unimodal Uganda (Karamoja) that extends from March to September and Kenya (areas of western Kenya) that extends from March to November; Kiremt rains (June to September) in Western, Central, Northern, and Eastern Ethiopia; main rainy season (June to September) in the unimodal zones of South Sudan and Sudan; long rains in unimodal Uganda and Kenya; Karan/Karma rains (July to September) in northern pastoral areas of Ethiopia, Sitti and Fafan zones of Somali (Ethiopia), the northern sector of Somalia and Djibouti; and second rains (July to November) in South Sudan bimodal zone.

Poor rainfall performance, prolonged dry spells and above-average temperatures throughout the June–September 2026 season resulted in significant moisture stress and below-average crop production across several major agricultural production zones of East Africa. In Kenya, Trans Nzoia, Uasin Gishu and Nakuru counties experienced substantial rainfall deficits during critical cropping stages, with preliminary assessments indicating national maize yield deficits of approximately 28 percent and losses of up to 43 percent across high-potential production counties. In Uganda, April through August was characterized by dry and hot conditions which negatively affected sorghum production. In Sudan, delayed planting and reduced area under rainfed sorghum were reported in key production states, including Sennar, Al Jazirah, Blue Nile, North Darfur and North Kordofan. Similarly, in South Sudan, persistent rainfall deficits affected the unimodal eastern agricultural zones of Jonglei, Upper Nile and Unity, while in Ethiopia, poor Kiremt rainfall performance adversely affected the Meher season, particularly in Tigray, eastern Amhara, Afar and eastern Oromia. Observed rainfall indicates that June–September rainfall totals were generally 45–90 percent of the long-term average across the in-season cropping regions (Figure 1). Although some improvement in rainfall was observed towards the end of the season, particularly in parts of central and western Ethiopia, the late-season rains were insufficient to reverse the accumulated deficits.

title: Europe — Afghan nationals travelling to and through the Western Balkans in 2026
content:
Between January and August 2026, national authorities across the Western Balkans (WB) registered 3,941 Afghan nationals entering their territory. During the same period, DTM operations in the WB interviewed a total of 1,045 Afghan nationals in 22 locations across Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH), Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, and Kosovo1.

Drawing on official registration data and DTM survey findings, this report provides an overview of trends of arrivals and transits of Afghan nationals to Europe and the Western Balkans, and crossings into the United Kingdom. Using survey data, it depicts their demographic and socioeconomic characteristics, reasons for leaving, journey organisation, immediate needs, intended destinations and return intentions.

The findings relate only to the people surveyed while travelling to and through the Western Balkans and should not be interpreted as representative of all Afghan nationals travelling to Europe. Finally, the report shows the main figures on presence of Afghan nationals in the European Union and the United Kingdom, exploring the relationship between newest flows and overall stock in the European continent.

title: Displacement Tops 340,000 in Yemen as Restrictions Hamper Humanitarian Response
content:
Geneva/Aden, 13 November 2026 – More than 340,000 have been forced to flee their homes amid continued hostilities and growing insecurity in Yemen, as restrictions on key transport routes threaten to further disrupt the delivery of life-saving assistance, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) warned today.

“Imagine having to leave everything behind, not knowing where your family will sleep that night or how you will find food and clean water for your children. This is the reality for hundreds of thousands of people in Yemen,” said Abdusattor Esoev, IOM Yemen Chief of Mission. “With access issues delaying the delivery of essential aid and humanitarian needs continuing to grow, we urgently need more support to reach these families before an already desperate situation gets worse.”

The latest displacement figures highlight the mounting toll of the crisis on communities already struggling after years of conflict. Almost all of those displaced originate from three governorates: Taiz, accounting for 224,819 people (66 per cent); Lahj, with 72,018 (21 per cent); Al Hodeidah, with 40,782 (12 per cent). Many have been displaced within their own governorates, placing additional pressure on communities already struggling to meet basic needs.

For families uprooted by violence, finding safety is only the first challenge. Many face an uncertain future without adequate shelter, reliable healthcare, or access to clean water. As displacement continues, the growing demand for essential services is stretching already limited resources, leaving humanitarian organizations struggling to keep pace.

Ongoing hostilities, insecurity and restrictions on key transport routes are compounding the crisis, delaying the delivery of essential supplies and making it harder for humanitarian teams to reach people in need. For displaced families already struggling to survive, these delays can mean going longer without the assistance they urgently need.

Despite these challenges, IOM continues to deliver emergency assistance across affected governorates. Since 1 August, IOM has worked with local authorities, UN partners and local organizations to provide emergency shelter, essential household items, clean water, sanitation and hygiene supplies, as well as cash assistance to help families meet their most urgent needs. Together, these efforts have reached 21,384 families.

IOM has also provided protection assistance to 8,242 vulnerable people and delivered 70,535 primary healthcare consultations, helping displaced families access essential medical services amid mounting pressure on the health system.

Through its Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), IOM continues to monitor displacement trends and share timely information with humanitarian partners and local authorities to help direct assistance where it is needed most. However, with needs outpacing available resources, sustained humanitarian access and additional funding are critical to preventing the situation from deteriorating further.

“Every day that assistance is delayed puts more families at risk,” said Esoev. “People need safety, access to essential services and the means to rebuild their lives. Without increased support, the gap between what families need and what we can deliver will only widen.”

For more information, please visit IOM’s Media Centre.

title: Aid in Danger Bi-Monthly News Brief (16 - 31 October 2026)
content:
Protection of humanitarian and UN personnel, premises and assets
In the 29 months since the adoption of the UN 2730 resolution, Insecurity Insight recorded 1,571 attacks and acts of violence against aid workers from the UN, humanitarian and civil society, resulting in 866 aid workers killed, 924 injured, 484 kidnapped and 748 arrested. These acts of violence underscore the need for strengthened collective action and improved security risk mitigation strategies to enhance aid worker safety and security and to provide crisis and post-incident support to affected individuals and their families.

The criminalisation of aid and the growing risks to aid workers
The arrest of 748 aid workers in 356 incidents across 29 countries between May 2024 and October 2026 points to a concerning pattern of criminalisation of humanitarian action. With 76% of arrests concentrated in just five countries - Myanmar, the State of Palestine, Sudan, South Sudan and Yemen - the figures point to aid-hostile environments in which humanitarian operations are increasingly difficult. Arrested aid workers are often threatened, interrogated and beaten while detained, and in some cases tortured. Nine aid workers have died in detention while fewer than 30% have been reported freed, raising questions about the fate and treatment of those still detained and efforts to secure their release.

The figures also expose a stark disparity in who bears these risks. Of those aid workers whose nationality was reported, 91% were national or local staff. Often closest to affected communities and central to the delivery of humanitarian assistance, local aid workers are frequently left with less visibility, protection and leverage when they face allegations or arrest.

Beyond the immediate threat to life and liberty, arrests can have far-reaching consequences for humanitarian operations. The threat of detention can create a climate of fear and intimidation, erode trust, constrain staff movement and decision-making, and undermine the ability of organisations to operate independently. For those arrested and their colleagues, the experience of arrest and detention can have a profound psychological impact, regardless of its duration, contributing to trauma, anxiety and lasting concerns about personal safety. Uncertainty surrounding the circumstances of arrest, the fate of those detained and the prospects of release can further compound these effects, raising wider concerns about the personal risks and sacrifices associated with humanitarian work

title: Asia and the Pacific: Snapshot of El Niño & Middle East Crisis (as of 12 November 2026)
content:
KEY MESSAGES

  • Drought is driving needs: Drought and extreme weather are starting to drive humanitarian needs across many parts of Asia and the Pacific, with millions facing increasing food and water insecurity from drought. Preparedness, response and financing should therefore be sequenced ahead of and against national and subnational impact windows.
  • Highest immediate concern: For the next two months, the countries of highest immediate concern are Myanmar, the Philippines, Timor-Leste, Papua New Guinea, and Tonga, considering both El Niño and price shocks.
  • Impacts will unfold in waves: Humanitarian impacts are expected to unfold in three successive waves over the next six months. Forecast confidence decreases with each successive wave, particularly for impacts further into 2027.
  • Children at risk: El Niño could compound existing vulnerabilities across Asia and the Pacific, with an estimated 190 million children exposed to unusually dry or wet conditions and heightened risks to food and water security, nutrition, health, education and protection.

title: UNHCR Yemen Operational Update, November 2026
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT

After more than a decade of conflict, Yemen remains one of the world's largest and most complex humanitarian crises. The country continues to face the cumulative effects of new and protracted displacement, economic deterioration, climate-related shocks, and limited access to essential services. title: IRQ: Pluvial/Flash Flood - 11-2026 - IRAQ: Flash Flood Erbil (2026-11-12)
content:

title: Cameroon | Cholera: Early Action Protocol Activation (MDRCM040) (07/10/2026)
content:
EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL ACTIVATION

Activation Overview

The Cameroon Red Cross (CRC) activated its cholera Early Action Protocol (EAP) following flooding in the city of Douala, Littoral Region.

On the night of 11 September 2026, heavy rainfall caused flooding in several neighbourhoods of Douala, particularly Bonamoussadi (Sable Banya and Denver) and Makèpè Missokè. The floods affected communities and several water, sanitation and hygiene facilities, increasing the risk of contamination of water sources and exposure to waterborne diseases, particularly cholera.

Field assessments conducted by Cameroon Red Cross volunteers identified approximately 500 affected households, representing nearly 2,300 people, as well as latrines/pits and water supply sources affected by the floods. Stagnant water, high population density, poor housing conditions in some areas and the ongoing rainy season further increase health risks.

Following analysis of the data collected and monitoring of the trigger criteria defined in the cholera EAP, the threshold for the first trigger was considered to have been reached on 18 September 2026. This led the Cameroon Red Cross to activate the cholera EAP in Bangué Health District, Douala, Littoral Region.

Anticipatory actions will be implemented over three months to reduce communities’ exposure to cholera and limit the potential consequences of a possible outbreak.

title: Eastern Africa: El Niño Status and Humanitarian Impact Flash Update No. 1 (12 November 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Heavy rains are intensifying across Eastern Africa, with above-average rainfall already recorded in parts of Somalia, southern and south-eastern Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda and Burundi.
  • In contrast, parts of Ethiopia and South Sudan continue to face worsening drought conditions after below-average rainfall between May and October 2026.
  • Flooding is already causing widespread humanitarian impacts, including displacement, damage to homes and infrastructure, and heightened disease risks.
  • Somalia has recorded some of the most severe early impacts of the October rains, with nearly 170,000 people affected across several regions.
  • Preparedness efforts are underway, but significant funding and response gaps remain.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

The October-December 2026 rains have started strongly across Eastern Africa, but their temporal and geographic distribution remains uneven. In early October, the IGAD Climate Prediction and Applications Centre (ICPAC) reported wetter- to much-wetter-than-normal conditions in parts of Somalia, south-eastern Ethiopia, Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, Burundi and Kenya, with more than 100 mm falling in ten days in south-eastern Ethiopia and neighbouring Somalia. Parts of Kenya, Somalia, Ethiopia and Tanzania remained drier than average. Overall, the pattern matches the El Niño-driven, above-average seasonal outlook. The rains should improve water availability and crop conditions, but they also raise the risk of flash and riverine flooding, particularly in the Juba, Shabelle and Tana river basins. Preliminary reports already point to flooding, displacement, infrastructure damage and heightened disease risks in Burundi, Kenya, Somalia and South Sudan. With above-normal rainfall forecast through December, the risk of further flooding and rising humanitarian needs remains high, and rainfall, river levels and impacts require close monitoring. Across the region, the emerging transition from drought towards wetter conditions raises the prospect of overlapping drought recovery and flood exposure before affected communities have restored their livelihoods, according to the the October Africa Drought Watch.

title: Panama: Earthquake in Azuero & Veraguas - Situation Report No. 09 (as of 11 November 2026, 12:30)
content:
KEY POINTS

  • One month after the magnitude 7.5 earthquake of 9 October, around 2,700 people remain in 100 shelters, almost a fifth fewer than a week earlier.
  • The Ministry of Social Development (MIDES) has surveyed more than 8,000 affected households to target assistance, including the cash assistance WFP plans to start in early December.
  • Work continues on temporary learning spaces that could benefit some 5,500 students in Veraguas and Los Santos.
  • Sanitation gaps persist at displacement sites and temporary health facilities, such as the temporary hospital in Los Pozos.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

One month after the magnitude 7.5 earthquake of 9 October, with its epicentre 39 km north-west of Tonosí (Los Santos), the National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC), through the National Emergency Operations Centre (COEN), is following up on 19,666 families (62,665 people), including 2,781 people with disabilities and 202 pregnant women. The toll remains two deaths and 27 injuries.

According to the latest Damage Assessment and Needs Analysis (EDAN) figures, from 2 November, teams have assessed 19,865 homes in ten provinces and the Ngäbe-Buglé Indigenous Territory: 4,633 have total damage, 11,107 moderate or partial damage and 4,125 minor damage. In the Indigenous Territory, about 16 of the 130 homes assessed have collapsed structurally.

The number of people in shelters continues to fall: 2,731 people remain in 100 shelters, down from 3,356 in 113 shelters on 2 November. The 353 MIDES staff working in shelters have provided 5,652 psychological consultations and 10,808 social work interventions.

Between 9 October and 8 November, SINAPROC recorded 13,259 reports of collapses, 182 floods, 73 landslides, 104 rockfalls and 10 fires, and it has a seasonal rain advisory in place.

Authorities have delivered 6,544 family hygiene kits, 6,450 cleaning kits, 4,506 kitchen kits, 1,085 baby kits and 6,428 mattresses, and the Agricultural Marketing Institute (IMA) has distributed 81,229 bags of food. The UN system continues to support the Government-led response in education, food security, health, protection, water, sanitation and hygiene, logistics and telecommunications.

title: VNM: Flood - 11-2026 - Heavy rainfall caused flooding and landslide #4 (2026-11-12)
content:
Sources for data marked as Other

Viet Nam Red Cross Situation Update

Description

According to the latest information reported by the Viet Nam Red Cross Society (VNRC), based on updates from the Department of Dyke Management and Disaster Prevention and Control (DDMPC) and provincial authorities, heavy rainfall between 8 and 11 November 2026 has caused flooding, landslides and damage across several provinces in Central Viet Nam.

As of the latest reporting, the reported impacts include:

  • Casualties: Two people injured in Hue.
  • Housing: One house collapsed in Quang Ngai, while 47 houses were damaged or partially unroofed in Quang Tri (12), Hue (8), Quang Ngai (24) and Dak Lak (3). A further 41 houses were affected by landslides in Da Nang (9) and Quang Ngai (32).
  • Flooding and isolation: A total of 356 houses remain flooded in Dong Xuan and Xuan Phuoc communes, Dak Lak, while two villages in Xuan Lanh remain isolated. In Phuoc Giang, Quang Ngai, some houses remain inundated, with water levels reported at approximately 0.5–0.9 metres.
  • Agriculture and livelihoods: Flooding has affected 126 hectares of crops and 82.3 hectares of aquaculture ponds. Reported losses include 9,850 poultry and 14 livestock, mainly in Thanh Hoa and Quang Tri.
  • Transport and access: Flooding and landslides have disrupted national, provincial and local roads, particularly in Quang Tri, Hue, Da Nang, Quang Ngai and Dak Lak. While some routes have reopened, access remains disrupted in several locations.

Evacuations

Local authorities in six provinces and cities have evacuated a total of 1,260 households from areas at risk of flooding and landslides, including:

  • Thanh Hoa: 153 households
  • Hue: 20 households
  • Da Nang: 214 households
  • Quang Ngai: 151 households
  • Gia Lai: 102 households
  • Dak Lak: 620 households

All 153 evacuated households in Thanh Hoa have reportedly returned to their homes and started clean-up activities. Evacuations remain an important preventive measure in areas exposed to further flooding and landslide risks.

Weather and Flood Situation

Between 8 November and 07:00 on 12 November, accumulated rainfall reached 200–600 mm across much of the area extending from Thanh Hoa to Khanh Hoa. Some locations in Hue, Da Nang and Quang Ngai recorded rainfall exceeding 800 mm.

Water levels in rivers across Central Viet Nam are generally receding or fluctuating. However, the risk of further flooding and landslides remains, particularly in mountainous areas and low-lying communities.

According to the latest warnings cited by VNRC, 230 communes and wards across Hue, Da Nang, Quang Ngai, Gia Lai, Dak Lak and Khanh Hoa remain at risk of flash floods and landslides. Further heavy rainfall was forecast for 12 November, particularly in areas from Hue to Khanh Hoa.

The situation remains dynamic, and continued monitoring is required, particularly in communities experiencing prolonged inundation, isolation and disrupted access.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: No

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by National Society

Summary

According to VNRC's latest report, VNRC Headquarters, through its Social Work and Disaster Management Department and NDRT, is maintaining 24-hour monitoring, consolidating provincial damage and needs information, and sharing Government warnings and instructions with provincial Red Cross branches. VNRC is reviewing its emergency relief stocks, including quantities, quality and readiness for possible allocation and distribution. Provincial Red Cross branches are maintaining monitoring and coordination with local authorities, preparing available personnel and resources, and continuing damage and needs assessments. VNRC is maintaining communication with IFRC and partners regarding the evolving situation and potential support requirements. As of the morning of 12 November, no affected provincial Red Cross branch had submitted a request for emergency assistance from VNRC Headquarters. VNRC noted that assessments and verification of needs are still ongoing, and that the available information does not yet provide sufficient grounds for assistance under its Decision No. 135 (this is VNRC internal document guiding the disaster response and activities).

Actions taken by Federation

Summary: IFRC continues to coordinate with VNRC and monitor the situation, including any emerging requirements for further support.

Actions taken by RCRC

Summary: N/A

Actions taken by others

The Government and local authorities continue evacuation, search-and-rescue, traffic management, reservoir monitoring and flood-response activities. On 7 November, the Prime Minister issued Official Telegram No. 73/CD-TTg, directing preparedness and response measures for heavy rainfall, flooding and landslides in Central Viet Nam. The DDMPC also coordinated the dissemination of approximately 8 million warning messages to residents in potentially affected areas. Provincial authorities have undertaken evacuations, road clearance and drainage operations, and temporarily suspended classes in some flood-prone localities.

title: WFP Timor-Leste Country Brief, November 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• Through the US Global Award, WFP strengthens Timor-Leste’s El Niño preparedness through food assistance, food security assessments and analysis, and capacity strengthening for government institutions, supporting timely and coordinated action.

• In September, the BdMK SANUTRIO pilot became fully operational across all Community Health Centres in Covalima, Ermera and Oecusse, delivering integrated social protection and nutrition services, with a target of reaching 10,000 beneficiaries in over 8,000 households.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Timor-Leste, a least-developed small island state of 1.3 million people, has made notable progress in reconstruction, human rights, and development since independence in 2002, yet it still faces major nutrition and food security challenges, exacerbated by natural hazards.

• Stunting among children under five remains among the world’s highest. The 2024 IPC analysis shows 27 percent of households are acutely food-insecure, while the 2023 cost-ofdiet study found that 75 percent cannot afford a nutritious diet, with food prices up 78 percent since 2019. Low agricultural productivity, poor maternal and child nutrition practices, high poverty rates, limited safety nets, and frequent climatic shocks further weaken food systems and household resilience.

• WFP’s country strategic plan (CSP 2026-2030) supports the Government of Timor-Leste's vision for zero hunger and contributes to the National Strategic Development Plan 2011- 2030. The overall goal of the CSP is to improve food security and nutrition by strengthening existing social protection programmes (Bolsa da Mãe Kondisionál, Merenda Eskolár), the food value chain, supply chain management, and emergency preparedness and response.

title: Sudan: Ardamata Site Factsheet - Ag Geneina, West Darfur (as of 4th August 2026)
content:
Site Overview:

Ardamata Site, located in Ag Geneina, West Darfur, was established in 2002 and is divided into two sections: East Ardamata (new site) and West Ardamata (Ardamata 1, 2, 3 and 4). Originally hosting approximately 37,000 individuals, the site has experienced multiple shocks in recent years, including severe flooding in 2022 and 2024 and a cholera outbreak in 2025, highlighting persistent vulnerabilities and pressure on basic services and infrastructure.

Displacements continue to shape the site, with 65 newly arrived households recorded in July 2026 from Khartoum, Al Jazera, Nyala, Al Fasher and Kebkabiya. Community representatives reported that approximately 60% of former residents have moved to Chad, reflecting continued displacement and cross-border movement trends.

title: Sudan: As Salam Site Factsheet - Nertiti, Central Darfur (as of 12th July 2026)
content:
Site Overview:

As Salam Site, Nertiti, Central Darfur, was established in May 2026 to relocate displaced households sheltering in schools across the locality and allow schools to reopen. Community consultations were reportedly conducted prior to relocation, and households agreed to move to the site.

The relocation process was planned in two phases, with 986 households relocated from 12 schools during Phase I and approximately 3,000 additional households expected during Phase II. The site is located approximately 1 km from Nertiti town and is divided into North and South blocks. Local authorities secured landowner approval for the South Block in July 2026.

The site faces several environmental and humanitarian concerns. The South Block is reportedly prone to flooding during the rainy season, potentially affecting shelter conditions. The nearest health facility, Nertiti Rural Hospital, is located approximately 5 km away and remains overstretched. The area also experienced confirmed cholera cases in 2025, highlighting the need for strengthened WASH and disease surveillance measures. Fire hazards remain significant due to the widespread use of makeshift shelters constructed from local materials (Shargan mats)

title: Sudan: Kalma Site Factsheet - Beliel Locality, South Darfur (as of 14th July 2026)
content:
Site Overview:

Kalma IDP Site, located in Beliel Locality, South Darfur, was established in 2004 and remains one of the oldest and largest displacement sites in Darfur. The site covers approximately 9 km² and is located 17 km from Nyala. Recent arrivals originate from Nyala, surrounding villages, and Al Fasher in North Darfur. While many HHs have transitioned to more durable mud-brick shelters after years of displacement, vulnerable groups including female-headed households, elderly persons, and newly displaced families continue to live in makeshift shelters constructed from sorghum stalks, grass thatch, and palm-leaf mats.

Healthcare access remains a major challenge, with the nearest hospital located in Nyala and no ambulance services available, particularly during night-time emergencies. Seasonal flooding affects Centres 1, 3, 5, and 8, while poor drainage continues to affect Centre 4 and other low-lying areas.

title: Sudan: Zink Al Khudar Factsheet - Golo, Central Darfur (as of 26th July 2026)
content:
Site Overview:

Zink Al Khudar Site (also known as Souk Al Khudar) is the largest displacement site in Golo in terms of both population and geographic coverage. The site was established during early 2025 after collective centres within Golo reached maximum capacity due to the continued arrival of IDPs from across Darfur. The first displaced households were accommodated in a former vegetable market originally constructed by UNAMID.

As insecurity intensified across Darfur, particularly following the deterioration of the situation in Zamzam in April 2025 and subsequent events in Al Fasher, the site experienced successive waves of displacement. Between April and October 2025, large numbers of HHs, primarily from North Darfur, settled in the site. Zink Al Khudar subsequently expanded into two sections, the New Block and the Extension Block, with the last major influx recorded in October 2025.

title: UNHCR Somalia Operational Update: January to September 2026
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT & HIGHLIGHTS

Somalia’s humanitarian situation remained shaped by drought, conflict and insecurity, with over 804,000 internal displacement movements recorded by PSMN between January and September 2026. In September, political tensions over the electoral timetable and renewed violence in Baidoa and surrounding areas heightened protection risks and constrained humanitarian access and programme delivery. Regional instability, including conflict in Ethiopia and Yemen, continued to trigger limited refugee movements into Somalia, adding to preparedness and response needs. UNHCR declared a Level 1 Emergency for Djibouti, Somalia and Yemen in response to escalating conflict and humanitarian conditions in Yemen, strengthening preparedness for potential arrivals, including reception capacity in Berbera and Bossaso. By September, UNHCR, in coordination with NCRI, had facilitated the voluntary return of 470 Somali refugees from Yemen to Mogadishu through three Assisted Spontaneous Return (ASR) movements, supporting safe, dignified and sustainable return and reintegration. On 23 April, UNHCR, the Federal Government of Somalia and the African Development Bank launched the USD 20.5 million Strengthening Urban Resilience of Displaced and Host Communities in Dollow (SURDHT) project. Working with NCRDS and participating UN agencies, the project aims to advance durable solutions and resilience for displaced and host communities.

title: NGA: Epidemic - 11-2026 - Nigeria – Diphtheria Outbreak 2026 (2026-11-11)
content:
Description

Nigeria is experiencing its largest diphtheria outbreak on record. As of epidemiological week 44, 2026 (week ending 7 November), the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) reported 37,529 suspected cases, 28,151 confirmed cases and 1,126 deaths (case fatality rate 3.9%). They were in 26 states and the FCT, across 361 LGAs. Confirmed cases are 1.8 times the figure for the same period of 2025, and since the outbreak began in 2022, 68,277 cases and 3,269 deaths have been confirmed. Kano State is the epicentre, with 12,008 confirmed cases in 2026 (43% of the national total), and it reported the most confirmed cases nationally in the last four weeks (935). Bauchi State is the third most affected state (2,463 confirmed cases). Ungogo, Dala and Nassarawa (Kano) and Bauchi LGA are among the five most affected LGAs in the country. On 5 November 2026, the NCDC Diphtheria EOC surveillance update showed that the apparent decline in cases in October was due to late reporting rather than reduced transmission. Weeks 40–43 were revised upward by 77–203%, and week 40 is now the highest week of 2026. State reporting completeness remains low (Kano 20%, Bauchi 30%), so the true burden is likely higher. Two-thirds of confirmed cases are unvaccinated. Children aged 5–14 years and females (59% of cases) are most affected, and out-of-school and Almajiri children are at particular risk. Vaccine has been deployed for reactive vaccination, but uptake is low. Kano used only 26–33% of its deployed doses, and Bauchi started vaccination on 12 October in only 6 wards. In Kano, 13,785 contacts have been listed with none currently under follow-up. Only 50 vials of diphtheria antitoxin remain, and 282 people have died in the community. Late presentation and harmful practices, such as removal of the throat membrane by traditional barbers, continue to drive deaths.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: Yes

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by National Society

Health

  • RCCE for Health and hygiene promotion

Summary

Since early September 2026, NRCS volunteers in Kano, Bauchi and other affected branches have conducted small-scale community sensitisation on diphtheria signs, early care-seeking and vaccination, using the National Society's own resources. NRCS participates in the national Diphtheria EOC working groups and in the state EOC meetings in Kano and Bauchi. NRCS has received a formal request for support from Kano State and a request from the Bauchi State Primary Health Care Board. Both ask for community-based surveillance, active case search, risk communication and social mobilisation for vaccination. NRCS is requesting a DREF to scale up house-to-house RCCE, community-based surveillance and contact follow-up, and demand generation for reactive vaccination in eight high-burden LGAs of Kano and Bauchi.

Actions taken by Federation

General

  • Other

Summary:

The IFRC Country Cluster Delegation in Abuja and the Africa Regional Office reviewed the situation with NRCS between 12 and 30 October 2026. They are providing technical support for the DREF request and will support implementation, monitoring, financial management and reporting
